--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page serves as the Dutch preface to the first volume of "Geestelyke Natuurkunde" (Spiritual Physics), the Dutch translation of Johann Jakob Scheuchzer's monumental "Physica Sacra." The text is a celebratory poem, likely written by the translator or a contemporary admirer, praising both the intellectual depth of Scheuchzer’s work and the artistic quality of the engravings by Johann Andreas Pfeffel.</meta>

->UPON THE<-

### Learned, Excellent and outstanding Work,
->NAMED<-

# SPIRITUAL PHYSICS,
### Described in the Latin Language
->By the highly learned GENTLEMAN<-

# JAN JAC. SCHEUCHZER.
->And translated into Low Dutch,<-
->BY<-

# FLORENTIUS H. J. <small>VAN</small> HALEN.
->Adorned with matchless printed illustrations.<-

->THE FIRST VOLUME.<-

Exalted object of God's eternal wise guidance,
Shall I behold the wonders of that great Majesty
In you, enraptured by amazement?
What has more power here, my ears, or my eyes?
Here SCHEUCHZER’S spirit <note>Johann Jakob Scheuchzer (1672–1733) was a Swiss physician and natural philosopher who sought to explain biblical events through natural science.</note> flatters me with his learned language,
There PFEFFEL’S <note>Johann Andreas Pfeffel was a prominent German engraver responsible for the elaborate plates in this work.</note> hand competes again for the honor of victory,
Through Art-scenes, which never saw their equal.
Which of these two must I have wear the laurel crown?
Be silent, my Muse <note>original: "Digtnimf," literally "Poetry Nymph."</note>, for the judgment does not suit you;
As one sees here the marrow of art and true wisdom,
You must be content, with reverently bowed head
In their shadow, to contemplate God's wonders,
<margin>Plate 2.</margin>From that time when the Universe was still a Mixed-heap <note>original: "Mengelklomp," referring to the primal state of chaos before the elements were separated.</note>,
And Water, Earth, and Air, and Fire in one body,
And a single Chaos lay enclosed with each other;
When the dismal darkness could never be changed by the light,
Because an eternal night kept Everything covered,
Until God’s perfect Spirit stretched itself out,
And hovered upon the waters, to set the earth fast,
While every Element must listen to his laws,
And quickly be obedient to what his will pleases.
One sees with what wit Mr. SCHEUCHZER bears himself here,
To withdraw the great Word, GOD’S-SPIRIT, from errors,
And to discover to us that deep secret, following Moses' track.
<margin>Plate 3.</margin>But I see the first light shine upon the world-sphere:
Here the Abyss <note>original: "Bajert," a term for the primeval, chaotic mass of the world.</note> is stripped of its darkness:
The vapors break, the earth gradually comes to reveal itself.
The rough lump, upon which the Mortal had to dwell,
Received that new luster when GOD spoke: let there be light.

<column-break/>

Then the beginning of the Day and Night was established,
<margin>Plate 4.</margin>By the rising and setting of the Light and of the Darkness.
But I see the world there adorned with new luster,
The waters separated by GOD, with
The Firmament <note>original: "Uitspanzel," the expanse of the sky separating the waters above from the waters below.</note> between both, and each set its limit,
Both those that are above and those that flow below.
The firmament then received the name of Heaven,
Upon which now the evening of the second day approaches.
<margin>Plate 5.</margin>How wonderfully has GOD made that separation,
And lifted the upper waters so far on high,
As the others are driven into the abyss of the earth;
The heaven-water holds the world in its position,
And the Ocean embraces the extended land,
Dividing itself again into Seas and into Lakes.
One sees the streams here turn toward the depths
<margin>Plate 6.</margin>At the Divine command. The water foams and rustles
From cliff, from mountain and rock, as it roars along the fields,
To depart as quickly as possible to the gathering place.
One sees the Mountains reveal themselves for the first time,
And lift their peaked summits out of the stream
Of earthly waters, thus gradually the border
Of the earth to discover, which we further still behold,
When the eye is held up with wonder
<margin>Plate 7.</margin>Where one half of the world is still a mixed-heap,
A wild Chaos, and a formless body
Of earth and water, while on the other side the lands
Show themselves dry, and the sea by its shores
<margin>Plate 8.</margin>Finds itself bounded everywhere. Then the Deity spoke: let
The earth sprout herbs, which each contain its seed,
To, according to its own nature, come forth anew;
That the ground also adorns itself with green and fruitful trees,
Which each enclose their own seed according to their nature.
Then for the first time the green garment was born,
Which we see year after year clothe forest and field,

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<summary>This preface introduces the Dutch translation of Scheuchzer's "Physica Sacra," a work that harmonizes biblical creation with natural science. The accompanying poem guides the reader through the first days of Creation as depicted in the book's famous engraved plates.</summary>
<keywords>Jan Jakob Scheuchzer, Florentius H. J. van Halen, Physica Sacra, Spiritual Physics, Creation, Chaos, Firmament, Johann Andreas Pfeffel, Biblical Science</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the celebratory poem from the preface, moving from the initial state of Chaos to the specific works of the six days of Creation as detailed in Scheuchzer’s "Physica Sacra." It specifically covers the transition from the third day (plants) through the creation of celestial bodies, animals, and finally Man.</meta>

The new world was with new beauties
<margin>Plate 9.</margin> Provided on every side: this the **flowers** show us,
Which rightly boast of their scent and beautiful colors,
And can please every eye through their variety,
When we see **tree** and **herb** bear **flower** and **fruit**.
How much are we obliged to the Divine authority,
As He concludes the work of this third day.
<margin>Plate 10.</margin> Now to the fourth day, where the eternal Omnipotence
Decorated the wide **Firmament**, and the nine heavenly spheres,
With Lights, to reveal the distinction between Night
And Day to the generations to come.
O bright **Sun**, how manifold are your gifts?
What gratitude we owe to GOD for you?
The light delivers us from the dreary darkness,
Which otherwise would have remained spread everywhere;
The trees, flower, and herb must, from your bright rays,
With which you refresh the earth, fetch their warmth and food.
Everything rejoices at your coming and joyful break of day,
Until you, in your turn, go down in the west,
To give the world's other half a new day;
Then we see the Starry Host <note>original: "Starren-beir," literally "Star-bear," likely referring to the constellations or the starry sky in general.</note> float through air and clouds,
All led together in a row, by the shimmering of the **Moon**.
O Heavenly light! which must stand at the service of the night,
How wonderfully your power works upon trees, plants, seeds,
And all herbs, which are laden with fruit!
Who can report the influence by which you rule the sea,
And cause ebb or flow, according to your... <note>The sentence here seems to break or transition into a reflection on human limitation.</note>
O Wonders! which [show] man the darkness in his own eyes,
You bear the signs of God's eternal Omnipotence,
Who for you, O Sun and Moon! has determined your orbit,
So that you always shine upon the earth with moderation,
And that one part of the world should not die
From cold, or the other again be ruined by heat,
But remain in one state through the changing of time.
<margin>Plate 11.</margin> O Sun! O sphere of fire! who shoots your rays far and wide
To our joy, do you come to show yourself thus,
As art has sketched you here for our eyes?
And is your bright glow still stained with spots?
The telescope <note>original: "verrekijker." The poem refers to the relatively recent scientific discovery of sunspots, which Scheuchzer discusses as part of his "physical" examination of the Bible.</note> has thus put you on display,
And in the **Moon-sphere** also made the invisible seen.
But let us trust this matter to the wiser,
And pass by the **Eclipsing** <note>original: "Tánen," meaning the fading or waning of celestial light.</note> of the **Sun** and **Moon**,
So that the fourth day may herewith be ended.
<margin>Plate 12.</margin> There for the second time the Sun dawns in the east;
I see the **waters** bear a swarm of **Fish**,
The air pierced by the **Feathered creatures**, at the word
Of the eternal Supreme Power. How many various kinds
Of little creatures do I see here floating on their wings,
After the dried-out Ripeness <note>original: "Ryp." While this can mean "frost," in this poetic context of creation, it likely refers to the "ripening" or "maturation" of the creative elements.</note> has brought them into life:
GOD’S greatness makes itself known here in the small,
Through a thousand wonders and discovered rarities,
Which are enclosed in these little creatures for our sight,
To increase our attention in the investigation.
<margin>Plate 13.</margin> There I see the **Eagle**, the **Ostrich**, the **Hen** and **Rooster**,
<margin>Plate 14.</margin> And yonder the **Stork**, the **Heron**, **Duck** and **Swan**
Mirrored in the wetness of the sweet water-streams,
In the shadow of the low reeds, or high-crowned trees.
But has this silver brook so quickly, so unexpectedly,
<margin>Plate 15.</margin> Brought me to the shore of the Ocean?
O yes, I hear and see the rushing of its waves,
The newborn **Fish** seek to mate with one another.
What wondrous **Creatures** do I see here, both great and small,
The body of the Art-scene <note>Refers to the physical engraving/illustration in the book.</note> shows them all together,
For each has something from which GOD’S Omnipotence is to be read.
<margin>Plate 16.</margin> Here I see the **Whale**, there again the **Leviathan**,
Whose unsearchable strength no man can grasp,

<column-break/>

When he rages and blows in the midst of the streams,
Yet human ingenuity knows how to tame everything,
However fast, however wild, however bold in the water, or on the land.
<margin>Plate 17.</margin> What wonder do I see here? Can it be? Is this a tooth
Of the **Leviathan**? And may I believe this?
O yes! GOD’S wisdom goes far beyond our understanding;
Just as the **Whale’s** eye surpasses our eye.
<margin>Plate 18.</margin> There the **Shellfish** comes to show itself, in a state
That astonishes everyone, by beholding its strangeness.
But I intend to linger no longer at the sea,
Since the fifth day has descended into evening.
But before my desire for song is confined to the Ocean,
<margin>Plate 19.</margin> I cannot keep silent about the **Horns** or the **Shells**,
<margin>Plate 20.</margin> Their color, shape, and nature must also receive His glory,
To acknowledge, as I exalt them, GOD’S guidance,
Who has bound everything to His Omnipotence.
Now the sixth Day comes to enlighten the morning horizon,
And makes the mists yield before the sunbeams;
<margin>Plate 21.</margin> The four-footed Animals receive life: the **Ox**,
The **Horse**, **Camel**, and **Swine**, and the **Rhinoceros**
Comes to show itself together with the **Elephant**,
As the first Inhabitants who dwell upon the earthly round:
<margin>Plate 22.</margin> There follows the **Lion**, the **Bear**, the **Dog** and **Crocodile**,
The first-created Cattle live peacefully, gentle and still,
And seem not to know their own nature and wildness,
Possessed by no bloodthirst, or any predatory urge;
The **Little Sheep** grazes peacefully, by no **Wolf** plagued,
The swift **Deer** is not stalked by the **Tiger**,
But alas! how quickly shall that peace turn into war,
When the first-created Man dares to dishonor GOD’S command.
O Supreme-throne-monarch of all that has being!
Through whom all grows and blooms, moves and lives,
It pleased You, after the Universe had received its standing,
Through Your love for mankind and fatherly blessing
<margin>Plate 23.</margin> To fashion the first Adam after Your image
And even likeness. O wondrous thing! how You play
With attention through my senses in this Art-scene.
I see the first **Man**, from whom the family tree had to begin
Of all Peoples; I see him sitting by the stream
Of the Paradise flood, in the shade of a tree,
Shone upon by GOD’S light of grace from the heaven's vault:
The cattle seem delighted to unite around him,
And to greet him in his glorious state,
Where the delightful Eden serves him as a refuge,
A Paradise of luxury to live in without care.
I shall, driven by no desire for dispute or curiosity,
<margin>Plate 24.</margin> Investigate here where that pleasure-garden stood;
No, SCHEUCHZER’S clever spirit has done this perfectly,
And weighed many opinions against each other,
Yes, and with diligence brought together that which is most probable.
<margin>Plate 25.</margin> I also pass by the **Bdellium** <note>original: "Bedolah." A semi-precious resin or gem mentioned in Genesis 2:12.</note> and **Onyx** <note>original: "Sardonix."</note>,
I let others reconcile that dispute, in order for me
<margin>Plate 26.</margin> To turn anew to **Adam** and his pleasure-bower.
I see him ruling as King over all that is created,
Where he receives GOD’S will: *Eat freely in this Garden*
*Of all Trees, but beware of This one; or,*
*If you eat of it, you shall straightway die the death;*
The knowledge of Good and Evil would ruin you.
O threatening command! what disobedience
Is great enough, that in you it dares to violate
GOD’S Majesty, to live forever in sin and pain?
Look out for yourself, **Adam**! Fear the evil before it is committed,
For the misdeed is always followed by remorse.
<margin>Plate 27.</margin> There the mild GOD grants you **Eve** as a Wife,
Whom He caused to come forth from one of your Ribs,
While a deep sleep had taken hold of your spirit;
He grants this **Eve** to you for comfort in loneliness.

<summary>This page continues the poetic description of the Creation, covering the appearance of plants, celestial bodies, and the various animals of the sea, air, and land. It concludes with the creation of Adam and Eve in Paradise, emphasizing God's omnipotence and the initial state of natural harmony.</summary>
<keywords>Creation, Adam, Eve, Sun, Moon, Leviathan, Paradise, Scheuchzer, Natural History, Sunspots, Garden of Eden</keywords>

--- Page 15 ---
<meta>This page continues the poetic reflection on sacred history, transitioning from the completion of Creation to the Fall of Man and the subsequent events leading to the Great Flood and the construction of Noah's Ark, as depicted in the series of plates.</meta>

What joy you received through the eternal wise counsel,
By being given a partner in Paradise?
O Wonder Pair! Had you remained in your first state,
Your descendants would not have sighed under your fall and sin,
Since you embraced death by eating the fruit,
Which the Divine command had so strictly forbidden you.
<margin>Plate 28.</margin> Alas! There I see the *Serpent* enticing the innocent *Eve*
To the forbidden fruit. O first Mother! Be silent!
Close your ear and your sight to this hellish Serpent!
The bite of this fruit will make you mortal;
Rendering yourself and all your kin guilty of the death penalty.
But ah, the *Serpent* has flattered you too much with hope,
That the Knowledge of Good and Evil was prepared for you,
As soon as you had eaten the Fruit of this Tree.
Recoil, mortals! Recoil! How do you dare presume,
Upon the advice of the *Serpent*, to violate
The Divine command, to your punishment and the downfall of both.
Alas! It is done, your eyes are opened:
Scarcely has the taste of this fruit been enjoyed,
Or you are terrified when you see your own *Nakedness*,
And the threatening danger of disasters and sorrow.
<margin>Plate 29.</margin> What benefit can the *Fig leaf* give you now?
GOD calls you, while fear makes you shiver and tremble
At the hearing of the curse that fits your sin.
With what disasters you now see your shoulders burdened;
Overloaded with labor, pain, and illness, and death-anxiety.
The foul *Serpent*, who advised you to this evil,
Also feels her punishment, in crawling along the ground.
<margin>Plate 30.</margin> But whether this land-monster first stood on its legs,
I leave to others who are wiser than I;
I have no desire to wander from the path of the Bible,
But find a sweet fragrance in what God's word tells us:
How the *Serpent* was subjected to a curse and vengeance,
That she would see her *seed* crushed by the *Seed of the Woman*.
But unhappy Pair! You must leave blessed *Eden*
To till the land, where GOD'S hand
Clothes you with the *skins of beasts*. O mournful state!
Compared to what you once enjoyed in Paradise,
From which you now remain locked out by the *Cherubim*.
<margin>Plate 31.</margin> The Earth is cursed, the *Thorns* come forth,
The crops of the field are killed by *Thistles*,
In the sweat of your brow you must now till the land,
Until the earth beholds you as earth again,
*From which GOD'S hand first made you after His image.*
I saw you, O first Two! until now always naked,
<margin>Plate 32.</margin> Now I see you dressed in shaggy beast-skins,
So that no heat or cold would plague your naked skin,
Since the greenery of Paradise gives you no more shade,
Where you live together on the land as the first Country-folk.
<margin>Plate 33.</margin> What scent of sacrifice is offered here to the Godhead?
It is *Abel*, who thus seeks to please his Creator,
And is also graciously shone upon by Him in return,
While *Cain's* sacrificial smoke descends to the earth,
As unpleasant to GOD: this causes his anger to ignite;
Mad Frenzy causes him to defile his soul and hands
With the blood of a Brother-murder.
Flee, *Cain*! *Cain*, flee! Before GOD hears that abomination!
But ah! It is in vain to flee that all-seeing Eye.
These are, O bitter Envy! your very first fruits:
That you have bred Brother-murder upon the earth,
Whose bloodlust later played such a cruel role,
Driven by Pride, Greed, and Ambition,
Of which a thousand writings bear witness.

<column-break/>

But let us depart from *Strife*, *Envy*, and *Hatred*
To see the work that *Noah* undertakes, <margin>Plate 34.</margin>
To build for his Family at the Divine command.
What sea of doubt seems to hold back my song,
Through the dispute of what Wood this Ark was built!
GOD'S word gives us report here of the *Gopher tree* <note>original: "Gopherboom"</note>,
But who now discovers what the word *Gopher* means,
Or under what nature of wood this is to be reckoned?
Therefore I pass this dispute in silence,
To see the floating house being built, and to remind
Myself of the favor GOD showed to *Noah*,
When all that had life stood in fear of the death penalty.
There they strive in competition for the building of this work, <margin>Plate 35.</margin>
Which GOD Himself sketched, and the measure, size, and limits
He depicted to *Noah*, in order to preserve,
From the wild waves, a little of all that has life,
And thus to keep the work of creation in its state,
When the first keel would again rest upon the land.
Here we now see the difference of *measures* and *cubits* <note>original: "ellen"</note>, <margin>Plate 36.</margin>
With which one tries to calculate the greatness of the Ark,
Yet so varied that I discharge myself from it,
And proceed to see its division,
Where its *floor plan* appears before the eye, <margin>Plate 37.</margin>
And shows where the Man and the Cattle could dwell;
Where the Provisions are, gathered by *Noah*,
For in this Building shines God's spirit and high wisdom.
There we see the *Ark* appear completely built,
Yonder in *cross-section*. Who can contain themselves here, <margin>Plate 38.</margin>
When he clearly beholds how everything is divided?
Where the eye plays through the opening in every corner,
To clearly discover where everyone has stayed:
Here one can see the Ark again stripped of its *Roof*, <margin>Plate 39.</margin>
There it floats on the world's sea, which has covered the land.
O wretched sight! which awakens anxiety and fear in the heart,
By paying close attention to the plagues
With which GOD'S wrath has struck the wicked man;
But we do not yet see this punishment at its highest,
As the following Art-scene forbids me to stand still here,
To behold the first *Sea-ship*, though full of difference in being, <margin>Plate 40.</margin>
But must I fear no cliffs here,
Upon which the weak keel of my Poetry may shipwreck?
O yes! I recoil: it is also more than time.
I shall not linger a moment at the *Fluyt-ship* either, <margin>Plate 41.</margin> <note>A 'fluyt' (fluitschip) was a standard Dutch merchant vessel of the 17th century; the poet is likely comparing the biblical Ark to familiar ship designs of his era.</note>
I long to behold the bustle of the living Cattle,
Where the *Four-footed* and the *Creeping creatures* <margin>Plate 42.</margin>
Strive toward the Ark, while the *Birds* soar airily around,
And seem to greet their dwelling place while singing.
Happy Cattle, you who may find a shelter here,
To withdraw yourselves from the mournful water-flood,
Which the vast Universe must soon destroy,
To rob of life all that has life.

<summary>This page describes the biblical narrative from the Fall of Man in Eden and the first murder (Cain and Abel) to the construction and interior layout of Noah's Ark. The poet reflects on the physical dimensions of the Ark and the animals entering it to escape the impending Deluge.</summary>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the poetic commentary on the biblical narrative, moving from the immediate aftermath of the Fall of Man to the cataclysm of the Great Flood and the physical evidence of it found in the natural world, specifically referencing the work of Johann Jakob Scheuchzer.</meta>

<margin>Plate 43.</margin> An ocean roars from below and from above,
The sluices of the abyss are opened by GOD’S hand,
The water flows all around from the high to the low land,
To finally overflow the peaks of the mountains.
Desperate mankind, now, now the punishment has come,
Which *Noah* has foretold to you so long and so often;
Help now the water to increase through the tears you shed,
Now that you see the floating house closed,
And yourself, in this danger, cast off from all help;
GOD’S vengeance is not satisfied by sighs or weeping,
But by the death and downfall of you all alone.
O scene of mourning! I cannot behold your misery,
And remain able to withhold my tears,
Therefore I shrink back from you with a troubled mind,
So that a happier subject may sweeten this suffering again.
<margin>Plate 44.</margin> But what new dispute holds me back in my endeavor?
Shall I here contemplate the *instrument* <note>original: "werktuig". This refers to the scientific or mechanical cause of the flood, a major topic of debate among 18th-century scholars like Scheuchzer who sought natural explanations for biblical events.</note> of the deluge,
Through which the water was spread upon the globe?
No, I keep myself content with GOD’S omnipotence;
For He, who has caused everything to come from Nothing into Something,
Can easily cause the world to be flooded by water,
As soon as His thunderous voice breaks open the abyss,
And speaks with absolute authority to all the waters;
Accomplish my will, and do that which you are commanded.
No other Instrument, than GOD’S will, was needed here.
<margin>Plate 45.</margin> There we see the Earth entirely flooded with water;
The wild sea is bordered by no shores here,
No, everything is drowned in the depths of the roaring wet;
The *mountains, hills, and cliffs, and caves*
Are covered with the waves of the ocean,
From which the new state of the Earth is brought forth,
To provide a dwelling place for *Noah* and his seed.
<margin>Plate 46.</margin> O *Swiss Alps*, I feel my attention awaken through you,
To investigate this great miracle even further,
You show me upon your peaks the mark of the Deluge,

<column-break/>

Through all the *scars* <note>original: "ſtriemen". Literally "streaks" or "stripes," referring to geological strata or erosion marks interpreted as evidence of receding floodwaters.</note>, that the current has left behind.
Blinded Doubters, who seem to hate the truth,
The mute mountains make you silent, showing you
GOD’S power, and unnerving all the strength,
Which you dared to attribute, too recklessly, to Nature;
GOD first created Nature, therefore she must remain a creature,
That owes its being to a higher power.
What new wonders do I see again before my sight? <margin>Plate 47.</margin>
*Petrified Herbs and hardened field-crops*; <margin>Plate 48.</margin>
Witnesses, which rightly suit the great Deluge,
To withstand the opponents of the Truth,
And to strike them upon the face with shame and embarrassment.
The *Petrified Human-fish* <note>original: "Verſteende Menſſenviſch". This refers to the famous fossil "Homo diluvii testis" (Man, a witness of the Flood) discovered by Scheuchzer, which he believed was a human skeleton but was later identified as a giant prehistoric salamander.</note> shall reveal this even more, <margin>Plate 49.</margin>
To overthrow all doubt of the Deluge,
As also the *Molar of the great Elephant*, <margin>Plate 50.</margin> <note>A mammoth fossil, often cited in the 18th century as proof that large animals were drowned and buried by the Flood.</note>
Thus the truth of GOD’S holy Word remains standing.
O glorious Artwork, not to be valued by any treasures,
How shall I honor SCHEUCHZER’S name and his learning,
Who, supported by the Drawing-pen of PFEFFEL,
Rightly wears the laurel wreath of true wisdom?
Heroes of Art, with what thanks, with what reverence
Are we obliged to approach you in our hearts,
And to greet you with deep respect for the favor,
Which you show to everyone through your art?
Never was enough praise given to you according to your worth.
If ever *Seneca* <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher.</note> was exalted by the Roman,
Or *Zeuxis* <note>A famous Greek painter of antiquity.</note> praised for his art in Greece,
Suffer that you both be named by my Muse,
A new *Seneca*, and *Zeuxis*, whose power
Shall shine forth in everyone's eyes until the world's end,
And gleam like the Sun in her dawn,
Continue then, Heroes, follow the thread you have begun
Of your started work, which neither envy nor time shall mar,
Before your Names end with the end of the world.

->G. TYSENS.<-

# PREFACE
### AND
## INTRODUCTION
### TO THE
# SPIRITUAL
# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'D' featuring floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Prefaces, like books, do not all share the same reasoning nor the same objective. There are those who use them to praise their own works, much like wine shops use hanging ivy branches <note>original: "opgehange eilooftakken". An ivy bush was a traditional sign for a tavern; the author is referencing the proverb "Good wine needs no bush," suggesting some authors over-advertise their work.</note>; there are others that instruct, that offer excuses, or that remove prejudices. There are a few which openly present weaknesses and flaws, though most seek to cover them up. My intention is to make use of all these approaches—excepting only the first and the last—and above all to lay open the occasion of this undertaking and the method I have used to carry it out.

It happened that, for a five-year period, I undertook to explain texts of Holy Scripture according to the rules of modern Philosophy <note>The author likely refers to the "New Philosophy" of the 17th and 18th centuries, such as Cartesianism or Newtonianism, which sought mechanical and mathematical explanations for natural phenomena.</note> as the subject of the Physico-Mathematical lessons which the most Renowned Curators of our Illustrious School <note>The "Athenaeum Illustre" of Amsterdam, a prestigious center of higher learning.</note> had placed upon my shoulders. I was encouraged in this because I noted that commentators, for the most part, remain clinging to the "bark" <note>the surface-level meaning</note> of Sacred Literature; while others, having cracked the shell, seek only hidden kernels <note>mystical or allegorical interpretations</note>. Many treat those things belonging to Natural Philosophy either in passing, or unpleasantly, or incorrectly. The nearly infinite number of commentators on the Holy Books should have perhaps deterred me—those who, led by piety or moved by a desire to know and to teach, seem to have exhausted all matters—yet a new trail has added an innumerable number of objects to the path, revealing an immeasurable abyss of Scripture...

# PREFACE.

...and of Nature, a perspective <term>Doorzichtkunde: This refers to the science of optics or perspective, suggesting a way of looking at the world that reveals deeper truths</term> of things infinitely extended—yes, even of a matter changing infinitely according to the position of the eye—so that I could certainly imagine that perhaps something remains, if not is lacking, which could kindle some light, or even a tiny light, for the explanation of these or those Texts. I have sounded the depths and, over the course of many years, completed the task I had set for myself. Present at the Lessons were citizens of every rank, both the learned and the unlearned, as well as men venerable in age and authority; and students, though they were so few you could have counted them on your fingers. 

To the best of my ability, I have paired the holiness of revelation with the beauty of Nature. The wonder inspired by divine works lifted both me and my listeners to a wonder for the Creator Himself—as the most powerful, the wisest, and the best—and also toward His service. For I have long been convinced (as is abundantly clear from my other works) that medical matters <note>original: "Geneeskundige zaken". In the 18th century, this often encompassed the broader study of "physick" or the natural laws of living bodies.</note> are by no means to be viewed with an eye that is merely curious or irreligious, but should be applied to the exercise and practice of a religious piety <term>Godsvrucht: a deep, lived devotion to God</term>; that ideas must be sanctified, and that nourishment must be provided not only for the Understanding, but also for the Will and the Heart.

Having completed the assigned Work, I felt I had worked more for myself and satisfied my own curiosity rather than that of my listeners. Thus, I never even considered publishing this **Sacred Natural Philosophy**, much less illustrating it with Prints. Later, however, thoughts were born within me—as one arises from another—to add Prints to the Text, to reshape it, to improve it, and to expand it. Fortune has favored the bold <note>original: "Het geluk heeft den Kloekmoedigen geholpen," a translation of the Latin proverb *Audentes Fortuna iuvat*.</note>. I have examined various collections of Biblical Prints and seen that the majority of the most prominent ones were either purely historical or crafted according to the whims of Painters and Engravers. They were poorly formed and inaccurately expressed. Among so many works—to each of which I leave its own merit—I have not encountered any that presented Nature itself [to/for] the Creator...

# PREFACE.

by the world-renowned *Joann: Frickius* <note>Johann Frick (1670–1739) was a noted German theologian and historian.</note>, Professor of Holy Divinity, regarding the *Faith of Constantine the Great*, 1713. He visited the universities at Wittenberg in 1714 and at Leipzig in 1715. Having returned home in 1716, he was promoted to the holy ministry in 1718, and to the deaconship of the church at Leipheim in 1718. He was further promoted to its superintendency <note>a regional ecclesiastical leadership role</note>, which he has served with the highest praise since 1727.

In the first place, Regensburg must be named, a city-state highly renowned since the times of the Romans for the cultivation of arts and sciences. This fertile nourisher of learning and arts fosters the very noble *Joannes Andreas Pfeffelius* <note>Johann Andreas Pfeffel (1674–1748), a prominent German engraver and publisher.</note>, a most excellent man, who himself has long since earned the title of Engraver <term>Plaat-snyder: literally "plate-cutter," referring to the artist who etches the copper plates used for printing illustrations</term> to His Sacred Imperial Majesty due to his particular skill in his art, and has been promoted with the greatest praise. Out of his reverence for the Holy Scriptures, his affection for scholars, and for the art itself in which he excels, he has taken upon himself the care and costs of the entire work. He arranged and divided the copper plates among various engravers—each plate recommending itself by the diversity of its subject matter—so that he gave to each the part to work on in which they surpassed others. Some excelled in the art of landscape painting, others in history, the figures of humans, animals, or plants; finally, he gave the appropriate tasks to those who have the gift for adding ornaments, as seen on the borders of most plates. Each was given their specific task, not all to one, so that the engravings would appear perfect in all their parts.

In the High-German <note>standard German</note> printing are the parallel translations of the Great *Luther* and the *Zurich* <note>the Froschauer Bible</note> version. In the Latin edition, the *Zurich* appears again alongside the Common Latin <note>the Vulgate</note>, so that nothing should appear on the title page that could be an offense to anyone of the principal denominations of the Christian religion. However, in the treatise itself, having set aside all partisan zeal, I have everywhere paid close attention to the original text: the Hebrew of the Old [Testament], and the...

# P R E F A C E.

the Greek of the New Testament, not even a dot having been changed, so that even the strictest defenders of the Formula of Concord <term>Formulier van Gelykvormigheid: The "Formula of Concord" (1577) is a fundamental Lutheran confession of faith</term> should find nothing therein to take offense at. Regarding the *Zurich-Latin* translation, I must only inform you beforehand that it was produced by men outstanding in learning and piety, and very highly esteemed by the Roman Catholics themselves. Behold a testimony! and an excellent judgment, greater than all reservations, by *Jacobus Augustus Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617) was a prominent French historian and statesman known for his monumental history of his own times.</note>, President at Paris, a man beyond all praise, which is found in his *History*, Book XXXV, p. 714:

*Theodorus Bibliander <note>Theodor Bibliander (1506–1564) was a Swiss reformer and linguist.</note> died of the plague, where he publicly taught; a man of diverse learning, very old, who was succeeded in office by Johann Wilhelm Stucki. But to the edition of the Bible published in Zurich in the year 1543, which Leo Jud had begun—and, upon dying, had handed over to his colleagues, having solemnly sworn them to complete the work—Bibliander put the finishing touches, aided by the labor of Conrad Pellikan and Peter Cholin, most skilled in the Greek language. This translation Robert Estienne <note>Robert Estienne (1503–1559) was a famous Parisian printer and scholar.</note>, two years later, added to the old one in his edition, though he withheld mention of those who had worked on it; and Spanish theologians long after revised it again, and it was finally seen through the press by Guillaume Rouillé in Lyon.*

I have judged it necessary to relate this so that the origin of the translation, so highly esteemed by us and by the Spaniards themselves, would be known, and so that a distinguished proof would be displayed of what fruit can be drawn for God's glory from the books and diligence of our opponents, if we, setting aside all hatred, put on love and justice. He who desires to know more should read the *Defenses of Jacobus Huldrich regarding the Zurich Translation of the Bible against the warning of Jacob Gretser, a monk of the Society of the Jesuits at Ingolstadt, recently sent to foreigners by a bold accusation.* At Zurich, at the printing house of *Johann Rudolf Wolf*, 1616, in quarto.

neither read nor examined, and have only included the biographies <term>Levens-beſchryvingen: Literally "life-descriptions," referring to the biographical sketches of the authors or translators mentioned in the work.</term> of those which have come to my knowledge; these I have arranged in a somewhat disorganized <note>The author uses a "modesty topos" here, a common literary device where a writer downplays their own skill or organization to deflect potential criticism from scholars.</note> manner, so that no one may attribute any deficiency appearing here and there to a contempt for either the authors or their works. Therefore, every reader will be given ample opportunity to add to this those things which are missing. I could also have added my own judgment here concerning these or those writings, but I have preferred to omit such a thing, and leave to everyone the same freedom—as is the custom, so also the liberty—to think well or poorly of them as they see fit.

# LIST OF AUTHORS
### and their Writings mentioned in this Work.

### GUILIELMUS ADER.
*On the Sick of the Gospels* <note>original: "Over de Evangelische Kranken"</note>, at Toulouse 1620. 8vo. to be found in the 9th Volume of the *Critici Sacri* <note>A famous collection of biblical commentary by various scholars, first published in London in 1660.</note>.

### CHRISTIANUS ADRICHOMIUS, otherwise CHRISTIANUS CRUCIS,
born in Delft in the Netherlands, 1533; died in Cologne, June 19, 1585. He wrote, among other things,
*The Theater of the Holy Land* <note>original: "Theatrum Terræ Sanctæ"</note>.

### LEO ALLATIUS.
Born on Chios, he came to Rome as a youth and applied himself with such success to the knowledge of the liberal arts that he earned the favor of Popes Gregory XV, Urban VIII, Innocent X, and Alexander VII. The first of these sent him to Germany to transport the Heidelberg Library <note>The Bibliotheca Palatina, taken as a trophy of war during the Thirty Years' War.</note> to Rome; the latter appointed him over the Vatican Library. He died in 1667 at the age of 83, after having founded several houses for students in his homeland of Chios. From him, the following work is available:
*Treatise on the Ventriloquist* <note>original: "De Engastrimytho Syntagma." This work discusses the "witch" of Endor from the Bible, whom the Greeks called an "engastrimythos" or belly-speaker.</note>. In the *Treatises of the Library of Critics*, Part 6, page 331.

### PETRUS ALLIX.
An English theologian, Treasurer of the Church at Salisbury, previously a Preacher of the Divine Word at Charenton. After the Edict of Nantes was revoked <note>In 1685, this revocation ended the legal protection of French Protestants (Huguenots), leading to a mass exodus.</note>, he was exiled and sailed to England in 1685; he died at a great age in 1717. *Diatribe on the Year and Month of the Birth of Jesus Christ* <note>original: "Diatriba de Anno & Mense Natali Jesu Christi"</note>, at London 1712. *Memoirs of Trevoux* 1715, page 1298.

### GEORGIUS ALTMANN, of Zofingen
*On the Crowing of the Cock heard by Peter in the House of the High Priest* <note>original: "De Gallicinio à Petro in Ædibus Pontificis audito"</note>. In the *Bremen Library* <note>A scholarly journal of the time.</note> Vol. V, Class III, Part III, page 451.
Remarks on the Thyatiran Lydia, concerning the passage in Acts 16:14. In the *Bremen Library* Vol. V, Class IV, Part IV, page 670.

### ANASTASIUS, the Sinaite.
A Palestinian Priest and Monk on Mount Sinai. According to Nicephorus (XVII. 29) and the Roman Martyrology (April 21), he is considered the same person as the Anastasius who was Bishop of Theopolis (Antioch) from the year 1561 <note>This likely refers to the year 561 AD; the OCR date 1561 is an error in the original or the transcription.</note>, removed by an exile of 23 years in the year 570, restored in the year 593, and died in 599. However, this author is later in time, called <term>Μωϋσῆς νέος</term> <note>original Greek: "Mōysēs neos," meaning "the New Moses."</note> by the later Greeks because he relates things told to him by Alexandrians which supposedly happened after the times of Pope Eulogius of Alexandria (who died in the year of Christ 608) and mentions John, Patriarch of Alexandria, who held the Patriarchate from the year 677 to 686. *Fabricius, Greek Library* <note>original: "Biblioth: Græc."</note>, Book V, chapter 34, page 312.
*Twelve Books of Anagogical Contemplations on the Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "Anagogicarum contemplationum in Hexaëmeron Libri XII." Anagogical refers to a spiritual or mystical interpretation of the Bible.</note>. Of these, only the last book has been published in Greek at London, 1682, in 4to, with the translation by André Dacier. The first eleven books appear in Latin in the *Supplement to the Library of the Church Fathers* at Paris, 1579, and in other editions.
*<term>Περὶ τοῦ κατ᾿ εἰκόνα</term>* <note>original Greek: "Peri tou kat’ eikona," meaning "Concerning [Man] Created according to the Image [of God]."</note>. This was published in Greek and La-

<column-break/>

tin through the efforts of Jean Tarin at Paris, 1618, in 4to, with the translation by Fronto Ducæus at Ingolstadt, 1596, among the works of Gregory of Nyssa.

### JOHANNES JACOBUS BAJER,
Brother of the preceding. Born in Jena. Son of father *Joh. Wilh. Bajer* of Nuremberg, Professor of Holy Divinity, and mother *Anna Catharina*, daughter of *Joann. Musaeus*, likewise a famous theologian, and *Anna Margaretha Forster*, in the year 1677, on the 14th of June. From his tender youth, he applied his industry to Medicine, and to the study of Natural History which paves the way for it, having as teachers the very famous professors of the University of Jena: *Treunerus, Hambergerus, Wolffius, Schelhammerus, Wedelius, Slevogtius, Crausius*; and at Halle: *Hoffman* and *Stahlius*. Having given various proofs of a most singular scholarship, he departed in the year 1699 for Hamburg, Lübeck, Kiel, Schleswig, Friedrichstadt, Tönningen, Wismar, Schwerin, Rostock, and Riga. From here, having shipped across the sea-gulfs to Danzig via Königsberg; from there through Brandenburg to Berlin, Wittenberg, and Halle. After receiving the doctoral honors at Jena in 1700 and holding an inaugural debate on *Hair* <note>original Latin: "Hayren"</note>, he visited the places of Lower Saxony: Clausthal, Zellerfeld, Goslar, Brunswick, Wolfenbüttel, Helmstedt, and Magdeburg. Being accepted into the Society of Nuremberg Physicians, he

<column-break/>

married the daughter of *Joh. Casp. Bachmeyer*, Councilor and Secretary to the Duke of Württemberg-Weiltingen, and Barbara Sabina Herpfers, by whom he later fathered eight children, four of whom died very young. Of those remaining, the daughter *Susanna Maria* was given in marriage to *Sigismundus Jacobus Apinus*, Professor of Philosophy. The other daughter is *Anna Catharina*. The eldest of the sons is *Ferdinandus Jacobus*. The other follows the path of his father, the Hero. While he was successfully teaching the art of medicine at Nuremberg, he was appointed Field Physician on behalf of the Franconian Circle <note>A regional administrative grouping of the Holy Roman Empire</note>; being afflicted by pleurisy and side-pains, and fearing consumption or an wasting fever, he departed for Regensburg to settle there. However, immediately thereafter, the illustrious Overseers of the Altorf University called him to the Professorship of Medicine, vacated by the death of Mr. *Apinus* in the year 1703. In this new position, in the year 1704, he began his first public lectures on *Medical Matters mentioned in the Sacred Code of the New Testament* <note>original Latin: "Rebus Medicis, quæ in Sacro Codice Novi Fœderis commemorantur"</note>, which work—simultaneously useful and rare, and serving my present purpose very well—produced the academic proofs listed below. In the Imperial Society of Natural Investigators <note>The Academia Naturae Curiosorum, later the Leopoldina</note>, of which he is now an illustrious President and a most worthy successor to the very amiable *Lucas Schröckius*, he is enrolled under the name *Eugenianus* <note>A customary academic pseudonym within the society</note>. After the passing of Mr. *Bruno*, the care of Theoretical or Instructional Medicine was entrusted to him, and when Mr. *Joann. Maur. Hoffman* departed for Onolsbach, he received the first Chair of Medicine, a portion of the Medical faculty, along with Chemistry and Botany. Having lost his first wife, with whom he had lived for 19 years, he chose *Sophia Magdalena Schaener* of Nuremberg as his second companion. More details of his life and writings were published by the illustrious President himself in the *Biographies of the Professors of Medicine who ever lived at the Altorf University*, 1728.

- *Second Proof*. Respondent: *Christoph Maximil. Cnopff* of Hersbruck, also there, 1728, in quarto.

### THOMAS BARTHOLINUS,
A shining star of the North, and of the entire learned world. His father was *Casparus*, Physician, Philosopher, and Royal Professor of Divinity; his mother was *Anna Finck*, daughter of Mr. *Thomas Finck*; he was born on October 20, 1616, in Copenhagen. Among his teachers was Mr. *Paulus Moth*, personal physician to two Kings of Denmark. He diligently exercised his industry at the Royal University in general literature, philosophy, and Holy Divinity. However, having laid the foundations in Medicine, he moved in the year 1637 with his brother *Bartholus Bartholinus* (later a Royal Professor) to Leiden in Holland, where he had for teachers in Medicine *Vorstius, Walaeus, and Valkenburg*, and in general literature *Salmasius, Heinsius, Vossius, Golius, and Boxhornius*. Having left Leiden, he traveled to France and spent two years there, primarily in Paris and Montpellier; from there he crossed into Italy, where he was detained for three years by the Muses of Padua <note>meaning the University of Padua</note>,

...studies, devoted entirely to Anatomy <note>original: "Ontleedkunde"</note>, Botany <note>original: "kruidkunde"</note>, and Practical Medicine <note>original: "Oeffenende Geneeskunde"</note> under *Sylvaticus, Sala,* and *Vellingius*. Having seen the other cities of Italy, he became known in Rome to *Puteanus, Holstenius,* and *Servius*, and in Naples to *Severinus* and *Schipanus*. In Sicily, he met *Castellus*, where the Commonwealth of Messina offered him a distinguished Professor’s Chair. Having seen Mount Etna and the ruins of Syracuse, he arrived in Malta. After greeting Padua once more, he traveled through Switzerland to Basel, where he was honored with the Doctor’s laurel wreath in the year 1645, with *Joh. Casp. Bauhinus* bestowing it upon him. From there, he traveled through France, the Netherlands, and Germany in 1646 to return to his Fatherland. There, in 1647, following the death of *Longomontanus*, the Professor’s Chair was offered to him; to this was added the Professorship of Anatomy after *Simon Pauli* was called to the Court. Having held this office for the course of thirteen years, he discovered, among other things, the thoracic duct <note>original: "Melkader in de Borst," literally "milk-vein in the breast"</note> and the lymphatic vessels <note>original: "Water-vaten"</note> in man. In the year 1649, he chose as his wife *Elisa*, the only daughter of Burgomaster *Kristoffel Janzen*, through whom he became the father of five sons and four daughters. The sons were: *Kasper*, Royal Professor of Medicine and Anatomy; *Kristoffel*, Royal Professor of Mathematics and Secretary to the King; *Thomas*, Professor of National History and Politics; and *Joannes* and *Albert*. The daughters were: *Anna Margaretha*, who died as a maiden; *Margaretha*, married to *Kristiaan Muller*, Lord of Katterup; *Anna Margaretha*; and *Elisa Catharina*. In the year 1654, he succeeded *Olaus Wormius* in the professorship and the governance of the University. In 1656, upon the death of his maternal grandfather, *Thomas Finckius*, he became the Elder and Dean of the Medical Society. Weakened by various public and scholarly labors, he obtained a discharge from his university duties from the King in 1661, with the honorary title of Professor Extraordinary being added. In industrious retirement, having purchased a country estate called *Hagested*, he devoted his labor to works worthy of being engraved on cedar wood <note>A metaphor for works of enduring value</note>. In the year 1670, he was brought to the Court as Chief Physician by *Frederick III*, a favor which his successor *Christian V* increased that same year by raising his annual salary. In that same year, his country villa at *Tusculum* <note>Hagested was nicknamed Tusculum after Cicero's retreat</note> having burned down, he endured the significant loss of his library and rarest manuscripts with an unshaken spirit, and with the same bravery faced the death of his wife in 1675. In this same year, he was admitted to the High Royal Court of Justice. In the year 1678, he entered into a second marriage with *Magdalena Rhode*, with whom he lived for two years. In the month of August 1680, a difficulty in urinating increased so much that after the 3rd of November, a great weakening of strength followed, along with a loss of appetite. Bloody urine gave evidence of gnawing gravel <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>. Finally, after a fatal obstruction of water followed on November 30th, this immortal man piously and patiently ended his life on December 4th. More concerning his life can be found in the *Programma* of *Joh. Baggerus*, Vice-Rector of the Royal University, on the death of *Th. Bartholinus*; and in the funeral oration by *Wilh. Wormius* delivered in 1681; and *The Memory of this Danish Aesculapius* <note>The Greek god of healing</note> by *Oliger Jacobæus*.

*Dissertation on the Pierced Side of CHRIST. Including letters by the famous Salmasius and others concerning the Cross.* Leiden: Le Maire, 1648, in octavo.

*Four Memoirs on the Cross of CHRIST: 1. On the middle seat, 2. On the myrrh-infused wine, 3. On the crown of thorns, 4. On the sweat of blood.* Copenhagen: M. Marzam, 1651, in octavo. These are available revised along with the treatises of Lipsius and others on the Cross. Amsterdam, 1671, in duodecimo.

*Medical Miscellany on Biblical Diseases*, Copenhagen, 1671, in octavo. Frankfurt: Dan. Pauli, 1692, in octavo, which is the third edition. They are also found in Crenius’s *Historical, Critical, and Philological Dissertations*, Part IV, page 417.

*The Paralytics of the New Testament, illustrated with Medical and Philological Commentary.* Copenhagen, 1653, in quarto. Basel, 1662, in octavo, provided by Georgius Segerus. They are included in the fifth volume of the collection of works pertaining to History and Sacred General Literature. Rotterdam, 1695. Leipzig: Joh. Christian Wohlfart, 1685, in octavo. Crenius’s *Historical, Critical, and Philological Dissertations*, Part IV, page 306.

<column-break/>

### S. BASILIUS.

The Great, called "the great teacher of truth" <note>original Greek: "ho megas teys aleytheias didaskalos"</note> by *Zacharias Mytilenæus*, "The pride of the Church" <note>original Greek: "Kaucheyma teys ekkleyfias"</note> by *Athanasius*, and "the divine light of the world" <note>original Greek: "ho entheos teys oikoumeneys Phoofteyr"</note> by *Gennadius*. Born in Neocaesarea (formerly Mazaca) in the Pontic region of Cappadocia around the year of Christ 316. His parents were *Basilius* and *Emmelia*, and his grandmother was *Macrina*. He was the eldest brother of *Gregory of Nyssa*, *Naucratius* the monk, *Peter* Bishop of Sebaste, and his sister *Macrina*. Having performed the duties of Reader, Deacon, and Elder in the Church at Caesarea, he held the monastic life in higher regard; therefore, he withdrew to the Pontic wilderness, where he enjoyed the most pleasant company of *Gregory Nazianzenus*. In the year 370, he succeeded the deceased Bishop *Eusebius*. He passed away in the year 379 after the birth of Christ, on the first of January. See Fabricius’s *Greek Library*, Book V, chapter 19, page 60.

*On the Hexaemeron* <note>The six days of creation</note>, nine sermons on the six-day work, from which *Ambrose* expressed most things word-for-word in six books. Nic. Faber published the Latin translation by *Eustathius*. The same can be found in the *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1654, in the first part, and in the editions of *Basil* himself. The Latin translation by *Joannes Argyropulus* is in the works of *Basil*, 1565, in folio, at Basel, revised by *Godfried Tilman*; that of *Janus Cornarius* in the edition of *Basil*, 1552, in folio; and that of *Victorinus Strigelius*, Leipzig, 1566, in octavo.

*On Paradise*. Twenty-nine sermons on Genesis 2:8. *Cornarius* and *Franc. Combefisius* translated it; first part, page 525.

### JOH. CHRIST. BAUER.

*The Formation of Birds from the Earth*, regarding Genesis 2:19. Antwerp: Salomon Hermans, Otterwisch: in Meyssen. Published in Leipzig by the heirs of Brandenburg, 1706, in quarto.

### THEOPH. SIGEFRIDUS BAYER.

*A Unique Book on the Chinese Eclipse, examining the judgment of the Chinese regarding the solar eclipse believed to have occurred when Christ was put on the cross.* Königsberg, 1718, in quarto.

### JOH. BEAUMONT, the Younger.

*Considerations on a Book, entitled the Theory of the Earth.* 1693, in quarto.

### BEDE, surnamed THE VENERABLE.

An English priest, the most learned of his century. He was born in the year 672 at Jarrow <note>original: "Girwich"</note> in the territory of Durham. As a boy of seven years, he laid the first foundations of the sciences in the Monasteries of St. Peter at Wearmouth and St. Paul at Jarrow. In his 19th year he was made a Deacon, and in his 30th year, a Priest.

# LIST OF NAMES

<note>This entry continues the life of the Venerable Bede from the previous page.</note> In the year 701, having been summoned to Rome by Sergius to resolve differences in religious practice, he preferred instead to remain in the monastery and apply himself to scholarship until he was "dripping with sweat" <note>This is a literal translation of a Dutch idiom meaning to work with extreme intensity</note>. He died in the year 735 on May 26th, being 63 years old. Others claim his year of death was 729, 31, 32, 62, 66, or 76. He is buried in the monastery at Jarrow <note>original: "Girwich"</note>, with his bones having been moved to Durham. The following works are available:
> *Book on the Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "In Hexaëmeron Liber"</note>.
> *Book on the Site of Jerusalem and the Holy Places* <note>original: "De Situ Hieruſalem & Locorum Sanctorum Liber"</note>.
> *Book on the Temple of Solomon* <note>original: "De Templo Salomonis Liber"</note>.

The works were printed in 1545 and 1563 at Basel, and in 1612 at Cologne.

### MICHAEL BECK.
From Ulm, Minister of the Divine Word and Professor of Theology.
*Dissertation on the Great Grape of Canaan* <note>original: "Diſſ. de uva magna Cananea"</note>. The defender was Simon Gross. At Jena, 1679, in quarto.

### SIGISMUNDUS BEERMAN.
Teacher in the Church of the Holy Trinity at Wolfenbüttel.
*An Epistolary Dissertation, in which a program concerning the matters of Jonah is subjected to calm inquiry, regarding the most celebrated man Master Hermann von der Hardt, senior of the Julian Academy and Provost of Mariaberg* <note>original Latin title: "Diſſertatio Epiſtolica, in qua clariſſimi Viri Dni. Hermanni von der Hardt... Programma de rebus Jone placidæ diſquiſitioni ſubjicitur"</note>. At Wolfenbüttel by Gothofr. Freytag, 1719, in octavo.

### EDUARDUS BERNARDUS.
An Englishman born in 1638. He laid the foundations of his scholarly training in London and completed them at Oxford in the school of Saint John the Baptist; there, in the year 1667, he was chosen as the Proctor of the Academy. He traveled to Leiden in Holland with the purpose of searching through the written Oriental manuscripts, primarily the 5th, 6th, and 7th books of Apollonius of Perga on Conic Sections from the Arabic copy. Having returned to Oxford, he was promoted to the mathematical Chair by Christopher Wren; after that, he obtained a clerical post <note>original: "Geeſtelyke Prove"</note> from the Society of Saint John in the county of Surrey and became Chaplain to the Bishop of Bath. Returning to the mathematical Chair, he died while publishing books on January 12, 1696, aged 59 years.
*Three Books on Ancient Weights and Measures, second edition, purer and twice as large* <note>original: "De Ponderibus & Menſuris antiquis Libri tres..."</note>. Oxford, from the Sheldonian Theatre, 1688, in octavo.

### JOH. CHRISTIANUS BIEL, of Brunswick.
*A Dissertation on Lydian Purple, to illustrate the passage in Acts 16:14* <note>original: "De Purpura Lydia..."</note>. In the Bremen Library, Class II, Part III, page 409.

### JANUS BIRCHERODIUS.
Born at Birkerød in Zealand <note>Denmark</note> near Frederiksborg in 1623; his father of the same name was a minister there. In 1635 he was sent to the Herlufsholm School, and in 1640 to Copenhagen. In 1646 he went to Leiden, where he heard the lectures of Salmasius, Heinsius, Boxhorn, and others. In 1648 he departed through the Netherlands for France, and in 1651 was promoted to the Rectorship at Slagelse. Having undertaken a new journey to the Netherlands, France, Germany, and Switzerland, he returned home in 1657. He was called to Copenhagen in 1658 to the Professorship of Philosophy; in 1660 to the same in the Greek Language; and in 1668 to the same in Theology, in which faculty he was made a Doctor <note>original: "Leeraar"</note> in 1675. He died in 1686.
*Against Burnet* <note>original: "Anti Burnetius"</note>, Copenhagen, 1688.
*Traces of Sacred Antiquities regarding the origin of the World in Hesiod and other Greek Poets* <note>original: "Sacrarum Antiquitatum de ortu Mundi vestigia in Heſiodo aliisque Poetis Græcis"</note>.

### SAMUEL BOCHART.
Minister of the Divine Word at Caen, born in Rouen from a noble lineage. For his father, René Bochart, was the Minister <note>original: "Predikant"</note> of Champigny-Ménillet

<column-break/>

at Bordeaux and was the great-nephew of Jean Bochart, a Councilor in the Parliament of Paris in the year 1490. He was the nephew of Jean, who vigorously defended the case for King Francis I regarding the "Pragmatic Sanction" <note>A decree issued by Charles VII of France in 1438 to limit papal power over the French church</note> concerning spiritual offices and other ecclesiastical matters. He was the son of Etienne Bochart and Esther du Moulin, daughter of Pierre du Moulin, a very pious minister at Charenton. From these parents he was born in the year 1599. The precocity of his mind is evident from 44 poems which he composed in praise of Thomas Dempster in his 13th year, published in 1612, through which he laid the foundations of his scholarly exercises. In philosophy, he applied himself at Sedan, where he defended theses in 1615, and others at Saumur under the presidency of Cameron. He followed the latter to London. In the year 1621 he was in Leiden, where he applied himself to the Arabic language under the master Erpenius. Having been admitted to the Holy Ministry in France on September 24, 1628, he debated in September of that same year with a missionary Father at the castle in Caen <note>OCR says "Koudum," likely Caen given the context</note> in the presence of men of both faiths; he carried away the laurel of victory. Being summoned by the Queen of Sweden, he traveled there in the company of Huet in the year 1652. He passed away at Caen on May 16, 1667, from a stroke <note>original: "Beroerdheid"</note> during a learned discussion: a man who added to his profound learning an extraordinary modesty and tranquility of mind. His writings came into the hands of the Lord of Colleville, his nephew through an only daughter married to the Lord of Colleville of the lineage of Le Sueur.
> *Phaleg and Canaan, or Sacred Geography* <note>original: "Phaleg & Canaan of Geographia Sacra"</note>. Caen, 1646, in folio.
> *Hierozoicon, or a two-part work on the animals of Holy Scripture, of which the first part in four books treats of animals in general and of viviparous and oviparous quadrupeds; the second part in six books treats of birds, serpents, insects, aquatic creatures, and fabulous animals* <note>original: "Hierozoicon, ſive bipartitum opus de Animalibus S. Scripturæ..."</note>. With a seven-fold index: 1. Passages of Holy Scripture. 2. Authors who are cited. 3. Words of the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Samaritan, and Ethiopian languages. 4. Arabic words. 5. Greek. 6. Roman, which are explained throughout. 7. Subjects. Third Edition, according to the revision of Johannes Leusden. At Leiden by Cornelis Boutesteyn and Jordaan Luchtmans. Utrecht: Willem van de Water, 1692, in folio. The first printing appeared in London in 1663 by John Martyn and James Allestry, contaminated with infinite errors due to the absence of the author. The second in Frankfurt, 1675, in which David Claude testifies that he struck out several thousand printing errors, besides those which Bochart himself had placed among the list of errata and added to the end of both parts of the London printing. An abridgment <note>original: "Kort Begrip"</note> of the work was published in 1690 by Veczei, a Hungarian, at Franeker.
> *Collected Notes on the Earthly Paradise, Plants, and Precious Stones* <note>original: "Collectanea de Paradiſo Terreſtri, Plantis & Lapibus pretioſis"</note>. In Manuscript.

### LAURENTIUS DAVID BOLLHAGEN.
From Stargard, Bachelor of Holy Theology, Minister of the church at Jülich, and appointed assistant to the Synod.
*Inaugural dissertation on the third Jewish Temple* <note>original: "Inwydings-verhandeling over den derden Joodſchen Tempel"</note>. Presided over by Dr. Jo. Frid. Mayer, Professor of Holy Theology, etc., at Greifswald, 1707; reprinted there in 1717.

### C. J. BOMBLE, Minister at Wijk bij Duurstede.
*Analysis and Apocalyptic Chronology according to the mind of the celebrated Mr. C. Vitringa in the Apocalyptic Commentary of the second edition* <note>original: "Analyſis, nec non Chronotaxis Apocalyptica..."</note>. Amsterdam, 1721, in quarto.

# OF THE AUTHORS.

### JOHANNES BRAUNIUS.
Born in Kaiserslautern <note>original: "Keizers-Lauteren"</note> in the Palatinate in 1628. Having been deprived of his father, who was the Mayor, he came to Metz in his seventh year after the city was plundered by the Imperial forces. From there, he went to Leiden in Holland, intended for a career in commerce; however, through the advice of *Constantine l'Empereur* and *Coccejus*, he took up his literary studies again and, in his seventh year of study, joined the university ranks. In France, he stayed for some time in Paris and Saumur. In the year 1650, he undertook a journey through Germany and Switzerland; later, he was called to Zeeland by the Walloon Synod and served as a French Minister in Delft in 1661, and then in Nijmegen, where he entered into marriage. When the city was taken by the French, he suffered greatly and was fined a large sum of money. In the year 1680, he obtained the Chair of Professor of Theology and of the Hebrew Language at Groningen, as well as the position of Academy Preacher. He died there in the month of December 1708.

*The Clothing of the Hebrew Priests, or a most extensive commentary on Exodus XXVIII and XXIX & Leviticus XVI, and many other passages of Holy Scripture, in 2 Books* <note>original: "Vestitus Sacerdotum Hebræorum, sive Commentarius amplissimus..."</note>. Amsterdam, published by the Janssons of Waasberge, Dan. Elzevier, the Widow of J. van Someren, and Hendrik and Dirk Boom, 1680, in quarto.

### BUDAS.
Wrote on *the 70 Weeks of Daniel & Chronography* <note>original: "LXX. Hebdomadibus Danielis & χρονογραφίας"</note>; he continued the chronology up to the year 202 after the birth of Christ. *Eusebius VI. 7. Jerome Chapter 52. Fabricius, Greek Library, Book V, Chapter 1.* He is among the authors whose works are lost.

### THOMAS BURNET.
English Theologian, official over the Charterhouse Church <note>original: "Kathuizer Kerk"</note>. Died September 7, 1715, at a very great age.

*The Sacred Theory of the Earth, containing the origin and general changes of our world, which it has already undergone or will undergo in the future. To which are added Philosophical Archaeologies, or the Ancient Doctrine of the origins of things* <note>original: "Telluris Theoria Sacra..."</note>. Amsterdam, by Joann. Wolters, 1694, quarto.

The fourth edition was printed in London, 2 parts in octavo, with a three-part addition by the Author, 1719.

*Answer to the objections of Erasmus Warren.*

### CASPARUS BUSSING.
Minister in Hamburg, Professor of Mathematics.

*On the Situation of the Paradisiacal and Millennial Earth according to Burnet, aligned with the Ecliptic, which T. Burnet proposed in his Sacred Theory of the Earth. A Mathematical Dissertation, in which the obliquity of the Ecliptic is simultaneously demonstrated a priori* <note>original: "De Situ Telluris Paradisiacæ & Chiliasticæ Burnetiano..."</note>. Hamburg, 1694, quarto, printed by Ziegler.

### JOHANNES BUTEO DE BOTEON.
From Charpey near Valence in the Dauphiné, where he was admitted into the order of the St. Anthony Monks at Vienne. Thuanus claimed that he was descended from a noble High-German lineage. The Dauphiné being devastated by civil wars in the years 1561, 1562, and 1563, he fled to Morans, where he is said to have died of grief in 1564 in his 75th year; or, as *Chorierus* maintains, in 1560 in the Monastery of St. Anthony.

*On Noah’s Ark, what its form and capacity might have been. Among his Geometric works* <note>original: "De Arca Noë, cujus formæ capacitatisque fuerit..."</note>. Lyons, 1554, quarto.

### ABRAHAMUS CALOVIUS.
A very renowned theologian among the Lutherans, born April 16, 1612, at Mohrungen in Prussia; his father was *Petrus*. He pursued his studies amidst various vicissitudes of fortune <note>A common way of saying he faced many hardships or changes in status</note> at Thorn, under the teachers *Graserus, Meuserus, Schallerus, Gerhardus*; at Mohrungen under *Paulus Riccius*; at Königsberg under *Mauritius, Crusius, Hoppius*, and others, where he was received by *Joachim Hessius*. In Rostock in the

<column-break/>

year 1637, he was promoted to the honors of Teacher, and in Königsberg to the extraordinary professorship in Theology. In 1643, he was appointed to the Rectorship of the preparatory school <note>original: "Leerlingfchool"</note> in Danzig in place of *Joannes Botsaccus*, and at the same time added to the ecclesiastical pulpit. In the year 1645, he was present at the colloquy at Thorn. In the year 1650, he was called to Wittenberg as Professor of Theology, where he died as First Minister and General Superintendent on February 20, 1686, in the 74th year of his age.

*A Discussion on the Infallibility of the New Biblical Chronology of Christian Ravius, added as a supplement to the Biblical Chronicle* <note>original: "Discussio infallibilitatis novæ Chronologiæ Biblicæ Chr. Ravii..."</note>, with an addition of a special subject concerning the chronological root of the 70 Weeks of Daniel. Prefixed is his preface to the Lovers of Sacred Letters regarding the various deviations of Scaliger and others in Holy Chronology from the only infallible rule of Holy Scripture, and the blunders against the same, and the necessity and utility of a corrected Holy Chronology; likewise a Letter from Ravius sent to the Author. Wittenberg, 1670, quarto.

### CANDIDUS.
Wrote on the six-day Creation, according to *Eusebius V. 27* and *Jerome chapter 48*, and indeed was the first, if we believe *Nicephorus*. Yet, besides Philo the Jew, Justin Martyr had already done so. *Fabricius, Library, Book V, chapter 1*, among the authors whose works are lost.

### JACOBUS CAPELLUS.
*Triumph of Illustrious Epochs, with an explanation of several selected difficult passages of Scripture* <note>original: "Epocharum illustrium Θριαμβος..."</note>, are to be found in the *Hist. Philolog. Fasc. VIII. p. 377.*
*On the Temple of Jerusalem* <note>original: "De Templo Hierosolymitano"</note>.

### JOH. SAMUEL CARL.
Physician, and Chief Doctor at Isenburg.
*Sacred Dietetics: The Discipline of the Body, Conducive to the Sanctification of Souls, presented from correct natural principles, yet entirely in accordance with all Divine order . . . Particular Dietetics: 1. Dietary Rule from Holy Scripture. 2. of the Saints. 3. of the Philosophers. 4. of the Courts. 5. of the Poor* <note>original: "Diætetica Sacra, Die Zucht des Leibes..."</note>. Among the small works of moral medicine, which were published at Büdingen by Joh. Fr. Regelein, 1726, octavo.

### JOH. BENEDICTUS CARPZOVIUS.
A renowned theologian of the Lutheran Church, his father being of the same name and worthy of the same esteem; born in Leipzig, April 24, 1639, where he had as teachers *Müllerus, Rivinus, Rappoltus, Frankenstein, Thomasius*; at Jena in 1655, *Christian Chemnitius, Frischmuth, Bosius*; at Strasbourg *Bæclerus, Dannhauwer, Johan Sebastian Schmidius*. On his journey through Germany, he became known to *Wagnerus* in Tübingen, to *Zeilerus* in Ulm, to *Ursinus* in Regensburg, to *Dillherrus* in Nuremberg, to *Hackspan* at Altdorf, to *Hottinger* at Heidelberg, and to *Buxtorf* at Basel. Having returned to Leipzig, he completed his theological book studies under *Hülsemannus, Kromajerus, Gejerus, Scherzerus*. In the years 1662, 1668, and 1671, he was a preacher in St. Nicholas Church; in 1674, Archdeacon; and in 1679, Minister in St. Thomas Church. The University entrusted to him the Professorship of Ethics in 1665, of Oriental Languages in 1668, and the Theological Professorship in 1684. He died on April 23, 1699.

*A brief paper on coins showing Moses with horns* <note>original: "Ad Nummos cornutum Mosen exhibentes schediasma." This refers to a common historical mistranslation of the Hebrew for "radiant" as "horned."</note>. The defender was Paulus Stark from Vogtland. Leipzig, by Joh. Bauer, 1659, quarto.

### CHRISTOPH. CELLARIUS.
Born in Schmalkalden in 1638. He went to the Academy at Jena in 1656, where he, in the space of seven...

### OLAUS CELSIUS.
Teacher of Holy Theology and Oriental Languages at Uppsala.

In the year 1722, he began three exercises on the Palm Tree, the first of which deals with its excellence and nobility. II. Explains the passage in Genesis 10:27. III. The passage in Genesis 14:7. There shall follow fourteen other chapters, in which will be treated the palm trees at Elim (Exodus 15:27), the forms of the Tabernacles (Leviticus 23), and of the Holy Land; of Deborah (Judges 4:5); of Baal Tamar (Judges 20:33); of the palm trees in the Temple; regarding the passages Psalm 92:13, Song of Solomon 7:7, Jeremiah 10:5, Song of Solomon 7:8, Revelation 7:9; of the city of Tamar (Ezekiel 47:19); of the palm branches carried before CHRIST, and regarding those passages of Holy Scripture where translators have rendered "palm tree," even though no trace of it appears in the original text. *Bremer Boekzaal* <note>A contemporary scholarly journal</note> volume VI, Class: page 748.

He promises:
*Treatises on the Olive Tree, Vine, Fig Tree, and Mulberry Tree, and the varieties of Thorns* mentioned in the Holy Scriptures. Ibid.

### ROBERT ST. CLAIR.
*The Abyssinian Philosophy confuted, or Theory of the Earth* <note>original: "Telluris Theoria"</note> *neither sacred, nor agreeable to reason.* London 1697, Duodecimo <note>A small pocket-sized book format.</note>.

### GABRIEL CLAUDERUS
Physician to the Duke of Saxony.

Method for embalming human and other bodies without the removal of internal organs or the dissections customary until now. In which not only are various matters presented regarding the embalmings of the ancient Egyptians, Arabs, Hebrews, and particularly of CHRIST'S body, as well as those of modern times; but also the method is added as to how entire dead corpses could be embalmed without removing the entrails. There is also added a method for preparing various oils and chemical spirits instantly, without fire or distillation. At Jena, by Joh. Bielke, 1679. Quarto.

### DANIEL CLAUER, of Dresden.
*Prior Chronological Dissertation: On the Patriarchal Form of the Hebrew Year* <note>original: "Diss: Chronologica Prior, de Forma Anni Hebræorum Patriarchali"</note>. The Chairman was Dr. Henr. Klausing, Wittenberg, by Gerdes, 1716. Quarto.

### BERNARDUS CONNOR.

### HERMANNUS CONRINGIUS,
Born November 9, 1606, at Norden, a city in East Frisia. His father was named Herman, a minister there; his grandfather Joan had fled from Overijssel on account of religion. His mother was Galatea Copina, of whom our subject was the ninth child. Having been stricken by the plague in his fifth year, he fell into a malignant skin condition <note>original: "schurfdheid," likely scurvy or a severe rash</note> which tormented him so much that he was unable to attend school until his sixth year. In the year 1620, he greeted the University of Helmstedt <note>original: "Giulische Hogeschool," the Academia Julia</note>, having stayed here for two years. In the year 1625, he went to Leiden, where he also practiced Theology and Medicine. In the year 1632, he obtained the public laurel at the University. In the year 1636, having been declared a Doctor of Medicine, he entered into marriage with Anna Maria, second daughter of Joan Stuckins, a jurist; during which marriage, in 40 years and 7 months, he became the father of 11 children, having increased in books, children, and wealth. He exchanged the Profession of Natural Philosophy for that of Medicine. Recalled to his homeland, he was honored in 1649 by the most Serene Princess Regent with the office of Chief Physician and Privy Councilor. In the year 1750, having been called to Sweden by Queen Christina on very grand terms, he traveled thither; and returned from Stockholm after three months, gifted with very rich presents and the dignity of Councilor and Royal Chief Physician. The Queen had promised him an annual pension of 1600 Thalers. But the most Serene Dukes of Brunswick and Lüneburg, the pension having been increased and the Professorship of Political Science <note>original: "borgerlyke Voorzichtigheid," likely referring to the Latin 'Prudentia Civilis' or Statecraft</note> having been assigned to him, kept him. In the year 1652, he was appointed to oversee and arrange the state papers of the Duchy of Bremen, and called to Frisia regarding matters of the greatest importance. In the year 1651, he received the homage of certain Frisians in the name of the Princess Widow. Called by Charles Gustavus, King of Sweden, as Councilor and Chief Physician to Holstein on a pension of 1500 Joachim Thalers, under the condition that if he wished to move here with his family to Sweden, he would be paid twice as much annually. In the year 1660, he was by the most Serene Augustus...

### DAVID CONSTANT.
Born in Lausanne on March 15, 1638; admitted to the rank of Minister in 1660. Immediately thereafter, he was called to the Church of Copet by the Baron of Dhona. He was appointed to the Overseership of his local school in the year 1674; to the position of Head Teacher of the Holy Language and Ethics in 1684; and to the office of Professor in 1702.

*The Rainbow, or a Sermon on the words of Genesis 9:13. 1713. Octavo.* <note>An "octavo" (8.) is a book size where the printer's sheet is folded three times to create eight leaves.</note>

### RICHARDUS CUMBERLAND
Bishop of Peterborough, born in London in 1632. Having completed his studies at St. Paul’s School and Cambridge, he became Chaplain to Bridgman. Later, he was a Minister in Brampton, a post he exchanged for Stamford in the Province of Lincoln. Due to his sorrow over the affairs of state, which were in turmoil under King James II, he fell into a severe illness. He was deemed worthy by King William, upon his ascent to the throne, to be elevated to the Bishopric of Peterborough. He kept such a watchful eye on his diocese that in his 80th year he conducted a church visitation. Three years later, he applied himself with all diligence to learning the Coptic language. He died of a stroke in 1719, being 87 years old.

*A Book on the Weights and Measures of the Hebrews* <note>original: "De Ponderibus & Mensuris Hebræorum Liber"</note>.

*Most Ancient Origins* <note>original: "Origines antiquissimæ"</note>. Manuscript.

### ANTONIUS DEUSINGIUS.
Highly experienced in the Oriental languages, especially Arabic, which he learned in the house of Golius. He was born in Meurs in 1612, his father Johannes Otto Deusing being an Ensign under the Dutch military forces. Having obtained the title of Doctor of Medicine at Leiden University, he was appointed Professor of Mathematics in the year 1638. From here, in 1639, he went to

In the year 1647, he became Provincial Physician in Groningen, and at the same time Professor of Philosophy and Medicine. Finally, in 1652, he was appointed Court Physician to the Most Illustrious Count of Nassau, William Frederick, Stadtholder of Friesland. He died in Groningen in 1666, aged 54.
