### HERMANNUS DEUSINGIUS.
Born March 6, 1654. His father was Antonius, Professor of Medicine at the University of Groningen and the Ommelanden; his mother was Magdalena Modesta Scheidmann, daughter of Herman Scheidmann, a Jurist and Assessor in the High Court of the Roman Empire, a very godly and steadfast woman. In his childhood, he was pulled from the water almost by a miracle by his father, who happened to be passing by. He laid the foundations of his studies under Christoph Wittichius, Joachim Borgelius, Upmeyer, and Tobias Andreas. In Law, he received the Doctoral laurel in his 22nd year, conferred by Wessel Bertling in the year 1677. Having been chosen by the States of Groningen in 1682 as Professor of Law and the Greek Language, he declined this service, being content only with the lectures previously granted to him. Thereupon, he traveled through the Netherlands and Germany. Having returned to Groningen, he transformed legal philosophy through an amazing reformation into a demonstration of the historical symbolic system <note>The term "Leenspreuk" here refers to a typological or allegorical interpretation of scripture common in certain 17th-century theological circles.</note> of the Old and New Testaments. On the occasion of three treatises regarding the Mystery of the Trinity—which he regarded as the source of a threefold symbolic doctrine of the Holy Histories—he earned the most bitter hatred from everyone. As a result, he was forbidden from the Lord’s Supper, although without any demonstration of error or proof of truth. After he had used the waters at Aachen to drive away a nearly constant headache, he withdrew to Drenthe as if to a Patmos <note>Patmos is the island where the Apostle John was exiled; the author uses it here as a metaphor for a place of lonely exile.</note>. There, the High-Born Land-Steward of Drenthe and Coevorden, the Baron of Pallandt, loathing this "Theological Hatred," ordered Deusingius to be invited back to the Holy Supper and received in the presence of the Synod. Returning from there to Groningen, he was brotherly received by the ministers of the French Congregation. He passed away on January 3, 1722. (Bockz. van Breemen, Vol. V, p. 925). The famous compiler extracted these matters from the letters of Deusingius himself, written not long before his death, adding the following judgment on page 936: *Should anyone think that in those types of studies (Biblical-Typological) he might have exceeded moderation, all will nevertheless confess this: that there was in him such a great power in the Scriptures as was never found in a man of his order, and very rarely even among theologians.*

*On the number of the Name of the Beast, 666* <note>original: "De numero Nominis Bestiæ 666"</note>. Bockz. van Breemen, Vol. I, Part 1, p. 155.

*Exegesis of Psalm 19* <note>original: "Exegesis Psalmi XIX"</note>. Breemer Bockz, Vol. II, Part V, p. 773.

*Mystical Commentary on the Decalogue and a Mystical explanation of both the History of the Woman with the Issue of Blood and the daughter of Jairus, and the Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus the beggar.* Leeuwarden, 1700.

*The Mystery of the Six Days of Creation* <note>original: "Mysterium Hexaemeri Creationis"</note>. Manuscript.

*Mystical-Prophetic Commentary on all of CHRIST’S*

### MELCHIOR DURINGER.
Professor in Church History and Chronology at Bern, to be counted among the learned, the godly, and the unfortunate. He was born in the year 1647 in the month of April, promoted to the Holy Ministry in 1667, to the above-mentioned Professorships in 1701. Melancholic <note>original Dutch: "zwaargeeftig," implying a heavy or depressive temperament</note>, unmarried, solitary, charitable, one who gave what he had left over from his maintenance to the poor. Upon the outbreak of a fire on the first of January 1723, having fallen from the third floor, he ended his life an hour later, after some blood had run from his Ear and Mouth, aged 76 years. A Friend has placed the following Epitaph for him:

->This Monument, which you see, Traveler,<-
->Has not from white Marble, but from Sincerity<-
->for himself erected<-
->MELCHIOR DURINGER<-
->Minister of the Divine Word, and of the Holy Language<-
->as also of Ecclesiastical History<-

<column-break/>

->In the Academy at Bern, Extraordinary Professor.<-
->If you ask after his character, all that pure Virtue<-
->Can grant to mortals, he possessed,<-
->By piety of Manners, Godliness, Chastity, beloved everywhere.<-
->If after Learning, all that the Arts have difficult, what secrets the cycles of time contain,<-
->what obscurities the languages of the East contain<-
->he has by tireless labor and persistence explained to himself.<-
->Finally he, by an unfortunate death, not without the greatest longing of the good,<-
->By a very heavy fall, while wishing to escape violent flames on the third floor<-
->having fallen from above, died Jan. 1.<-
->1723.<-
->After he, for 76 years for GOD, for the Fatherland, and for the Pupils who love the Muses, had lived happily, yet often for himself unhappily.<-

*Chronology, in which is reviewed the series of times from the creation of the World until these our times. Basel, by Jac. Werenfels 1704. Quarto.* <note>original: "Chronologia, in qua recensetur temporum series..."</note>

*Historical-Chronological Reflections on Passages of Holy Scripture: 1 Peter 1:10, 11, 12; Job 2:20; Acts 7 and 13. Respondent was Joh. Jac. Erhard. At Bern by Nic. Em. Haller and Company 1711. Quarto.* <note>original: "Reflexiones Historico-Chronologicæ..."</note>

### SAINT EPIPHANIUS.
A Palestinian from Eleutheropolis, skilled in the Hebrew, Syriac, Egyptian, Greek, and partly Latin languages, chosen bishop of Constantia (which was formerly Salamis) on the Island of Cyprus since the year after Christ’s Birth 367. Where he lived with such fame of Holiness that before the year of Christ 647, a Temple was dedicated by the Cypriots in the name of Epiphanius, as appears from the 94th Question of Anastasius Sinaita. He died on a journey near or over a hundred years old in the year after Christ 403. Fabricius: *Library of the Greeks*, Book V, Chapter 2, page 414.

Among his works are available:
*On Weights and Measures, a book on Weights and Measures.* <note>original Greek: Περὶ μέτρων καὶ Σταθμῶν.</note>

*On the twelve Gems which were on the Garment of Aaron, Greek and Latin Book. Jola Hierotarantino [being the] Translator, with a Supplement by Conrad Gessner. Also available from the same author is "On all kinds of fossils," at Zurich by Jac. Gesner 1568. Octavo. Also available: "On Matthias Hiller’s Book on the twelve Gems on the Breastplate of the High Priest": at Tübingen 1698. Quarto. And in his Hermeneutic Syntagma 1711. Quarto.* <note>original: "De duodecim Gemmis, quæ erant in Veste Aaronis... De omni rerum fossilium genere."</note>

# OF THE AUTHORS.

### MICHAEL ERNESTUS ETTMULLER
Doctor of Medicine and Professor of Anatomy and Surgery at the University of Leipzig.
*Whether Poisonous Plants existed before the Fall of the First Parents?* <note>original: "An Plantæ Venenatæ ante Lapsum Protoplastorum extiterint?" The "Protoplasts" refers to Adam and Eve, the first-formed humans.</note> *Ephemerides of the Academy of Natural Curiosities, Century VII, Appendix, page 209.*

->EUSEBIUS.<-
Not the son, nor the sister’s son, nor the slave, but the friend, brother, or relative of Eusebius of Nicomedia; he was the Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine from the year of our Lord 315 until 339 or 340, when he died at over seventy years of age. A man beloved by the Emperor Constantine, to whom he was also distantly related by blood; he was the most learned man of his century, according to the judgment of Basil *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, "trustworthy because of his great experience" <note>original Greek: "dia polupeiian ἀξίπιστος"</note>, and according to Nicephorus Gregoras, *History*, Book XIX, page 592, "the first among the learned men of that time" <note>original Greek: "τῶν τότε λογίων πρῶτος"</note>. See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 4, page 30. 
Among his unpublished works found in Fabricius, page 104:
*Fragment on Measures and Weights* <note>original: "Fragmentum de Mensuris & Ponderibus"</note>, from the manuscripts of Isaac Vossius, no. 179.
*On the Death of Herod* <note>original: "De Morte Herodis"</note>, a manuscript in the Basel Library.

->EUSTATIUS.<-
Called "the Antiochene," from Syda in Pamphylia; a Confessor and dignified defender of the Catholic Faith against the Arians <note>The Arians were a group in the early Church who held distinct views on the nature of the Trinity</note>, and Bishop of Beroea in Syria. He was present at the Council of Nicaea in the year of our Lord 325, and was appointed by that same council as Bishop of Antioch in place of Paulinus. Later, having been attacked by the Arians with various slanders, he was deposed from his bishopric at the Synod of Antioch around the year 328. He died in exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace around the year 360. Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 21, page 166.
*A diagnostic (or critical) discourse against Origen regarding the observation of the belly-speaker in 1 Samuel 28* <note>original Greek: "Κατὰ Ὠριγένους διαγνωστικὸς (αἰ διαγνωστικὸς) εἰς τὸ τῆς ἐγγαστριμύθου θεώρημα". This refers to a debate over the Witch of Endor, who was described as a ventriloquist or "belly-speaker" in early translations.</note>. Allatius translated and published this in Lyons, 1629, in quarto. Reprinted in the English *Critici Sacri*, Volume VIII, and in Volume XXVII of the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyons 1677.

->EUSTATIUS.<-
A certain other man, not the Antiochene.
*Commentary* <note>original Greek: "Ὑπόμνημα"</note>, or an explanation of the *Six-Day Work* <note>The "Six-Day Work" or Hexaemeron refers to the biblical creation story.</note>, or rather a chronicle, beginning with the explanation of the Six-Day Work and extending the Sacred History until the time of the Judges. Labbeus, in his *Library of Manuscripts*, page 77, extends it to the times of Alexander the Great, but this addition has not seen the light of day, nor has the Latin translation by Johannes Mariana. It was published in Greek and Latin with the translation by Leo Allatius at Lyons, 1629, in quarto. In Latin, it appears in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyons 1677. See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 21, page 169.

### WOLFGANGUS FRANZIUS
Professor of Holy Theology at Wittenberg and Preacher in the Court Church there. Born in Plauen in Voigtland, 1564. He laid the foundations of his studies at Frankfurt an der Oder. At Wittenberg, he was made Professor of History. Teacher of Theology in 1598. Superintendent at Kemberg in 1601. Recalled to Wittenberg to the Theological Professorship and Provostship in 1605. He was stricken by a stroke in 1620, and a second in 1628, from which he died.
*Sacred History of Animals, in which the principal properties of most animals are briefly adapted for parabolic use* <note>original Greek: "εἰκολογικον", meaning for the sake of illustration or likeness</note>, *with commentaries or supplements of observations from more recent Natural History, of similarities, emblems, and hieroglyphs for the use of both civil and ecclesiastical oratory; the work of Johannes Cyprianus, Doctor of Sacred Theology and public Professor at the University of Leipzig. Including necessary indices for all genres, and among them the "Homiletic Guide" for the benefit of ministers of the word and students of Theology.* <note>original: "Historia Animalium Sacra... Accedunt Indices... Hodegus Homileticus..."</note> Frankfurt and Leipzig: by Godfr. Leschius, 1712. Previous editions are Wittenberg 1624 (octavo), 1653 (quarto), and Amsterdam 1643 (duodecimo) by the Janszoons.

### GEORGIUS LUDOVICUS GOLDNER

### MELCHIOR DURINGER.
Professor of Church History and Chronology at Bern; to be counted among the learned, the godly, and the unfortunate. He was born in the year 1647 in the month of April, promoted to the Holy Ministry in 1667, and to the aforementioned Professorships in 1701. He was of a serious disposition, unmarried, solitary, and charitable, distributing what remained of his support to the poor. During a fire that broke out on the first of January 1723, he fell from the third floor and ended his life one hour later, after some blood had flowed from his ear and mouth, aged 76 years. ->If you ask of his learning, all that the difficult<-

->cycles of time,<-

### ST. EPIPHANIUS.
A Palestinian from Eleutheropolis, skilled in the Hebrew, Syrian, Egyptian, Greek, and partly Latin languages; chosen Bishop of Constantia (which was of old Salamis) on the Island of Cyprus since the year after Christ's birth 367. There he lived with such renown for holiness that before the year after Christ 647, a temple was dedicated in the name of Epiphanius by the Cypriots, as appears from the 94th question of Anastasius Sinaita. He died on a journey, near or over one hundred years old, in the year after Christ 403. Fabricius, *Library of the Greeks*, Book V, Chapter 2, page 414.

Among his works available are:
*Περὶ μέτρων καὶ Σταθμῶν, a book on Weights and Measures.*

*A Greek and Latin Book on the twelve Gems that were on Aaron’s robe. Translated by Jola Hierotarantino with a corollary by Conrad Gessner. Also available by the same: On every type of fossil, at Zurich by Jac. Gesner 1568. 8vo. Also available regarding Matthias Hiller’s Book on the twelve gems in the breastplate of the High Priest: at Tubingen 1698. 4to, and in his Hermeneutic Collection 1711. 4to.*

# OF THE AUTHORS.

### MICHAEL ERNESTUS ETTMULLER
Doctor of Medicine and Professor of Anatomy and Surgery at the University of Leipzig.
*Whether Poisonous Plants existed before the Fall of the First Parents?* <note>original Latin: "An Plantæ Venenatæ ante Lapsum Protoplastorum extiterint?" This refers to the theological question of whether harmful nature existed before the biblical Fall of Man.</note> *Academic Ephemerides of Curious Nature, Century VII, Appendix page 209.*

->EUSEBIUS.<-
Not the son, nor the sister’s son, nor the slave, but the friend, brother, or relative of Eusebius of Nicomedia; Bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, from the year of our Lord 315 until 339 or 340, when he died at over seventy years of age. A man beloved by Emperor Constantine, to whom he was also distantly related by blood; the most learned of his century, according to the judgment of Basil on the Holy Spirit, chapter 29, <unclear>trustworthy</unclear> <note>original Greek: "ἀξίπιστος," meaning worthy of belief or credible</note> through much experience; and according to Nicephorus Gregoras, Book XIX of his *History*, page 592, <unclear>the first among the learned of that time</unclear>. <note>original Greek: "τῶν τότε λογίων πρῶτος."</note> Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 4, page 30.
Among his unpublished works found in Fabricius, page 104:
*Fragment on Measures and Weights*, manuscript of Isaac Vossius, number 179.
*On the Death of Herod*, manuscript in the Basel Library.

->EUSTATIUS.<-
Called the Antiochian, from Syda in Pamphylia; a Confessor <note>A "Confessor" is a title for a saint who suffered for the faith but was not martyred.</note> and dignified defender of the Catholic <note>Here "Catholic" refers to the universal, orthodox Christian faith against the Arian heresy.</note> Faith against the Arians, Bishop of Berrhoea in Syria. He was present at the Council of Nicaea in the year of our Lord 325, and was appointed Bishop of Antioch in place of Paulinus by that same council. Later, having been attacked by the Arians with various slanders, he was deposed from his bishopric at the Council of Antioch around the year 328; he died in exile at Trajanopolis in Thrace around the year 360. Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 21, page 166.
<unclear>A discerning discourse against Origen regarding the vision of the ventriloquist</unclear>, <note>original Greek: "Κατὰ Ὠριγένους διαγνωστικὸς (αἰ διαγνωστικὸς) εἰς τὸ τῆς ἐγγαστριμύθου θεώρημα." This refers to the biblical story of the Witch of Endor in 1 Samuel 28.</note> a debate against Origen regarding the woman with a familiar spirit in 1 Samuel 28. Allatius translated and published it in Lyon, 1629, in quarto. Reprinted in the English *Critici Sacri*, Volume VIII, and in Volume XXVII of the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, 1677.

->EUSTATIUS.<-
A certain person, not the Antiochian.
<unclear>Commentary</unclear>, <note>original Greek: "Ὑπόμνημα."</note> An explanation of the Six Days’ Work <note>The "Six Days' Work" (Hexameron) refers to the biblical narrative of Creation.</note>, or rather a chronicle, beginning from the explanation of the Six Days’ Work and extending the Sacred History to the times of the Judges. Labbeus, in the *Library of Manuscripts*, page 77, extends it to the times of Alexander the Great, but this addition has not been published, nor has the Latin translation by Johannes Mariana. It was published in Greek and Latin with the translation of Leo Allatius in Lyon, 1629, in quarto. In Latin in the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, 1677. See Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 21, page 169.

### CONRADUS FRIDERICUS FEUERLIN

*Inaugural Philosophical Dissertation on Miracles.* The presiding chair was Joh. Henr. Müller, Professor of Physics and Mathematics. Altdorf: published by Jod. Wil. Kohles, 1714, in quarto.

### WOLFGANGUS FRANZIUS
Professor of Holy Theology at Wittenberg, Preacher in the Court Church there. Born in Plauen in Vogtland, 1564. He laid the foundations of his scholarly studies at Frankfurt an der Oder. Made Professor of History at Wittenberg; Teacher of Theology in 1598. Chief Church Superintendent at Kembergen in 1601. Recalled to Wittenberg to the Theological Professorship and Provostship in 1605. Stricken by a stroke in 1620, and a second time in 1628, from which he died.
*Sacred History of Animals, in which the principal properties of most animals are briefly adapted for <unclear>illustrative</unclear> use,* <note>original Greek: "εικολογικον" (eikologikon), referring to the use of images or icons for moral or theological teaching.</note> *with commentaries or supplemental observations from more recent Natural History, Similes, Emblems, and Hieroglyphics for both civil and ecclesiastical oratorical use; the work of Joannes Cyprianus, Doctor of Sacred Theology and public Professor at the University of Leipzig. Included are necessary indices of all kinds, and among them the Homiletical Guide for the benefit of Ministers of the Word and students of Theology.* Frankfurt and Leipzig: published by Godfr. Leschius, 1712. Previous editions were in Wittenberg, 1624 (octavo) and 1653 (quarto), and Amsterdam, 1643 (duodecimo) by the Janszoons.

# LIST OF NAMES

### Le GRAND,
Prior of Neuville-les-Dames and of Prevessin.
He added several treatises to the *Historical Description of a Voyage to Abyssinia* by Father Jerome Lobo, a Jesuit. The sixth treatise, on page 257, was titled: *Of the Red Sea*, and *Of the Navigation of the Fleets of Solomon*. The entire work was printed in Paris and The Hague by P. Gosse and J. Neaulme, 1728, in quarto.
The title of the seventh treatise, on page 266, is: *Of the Queen of Sheba*. <note>original French: "de la Reine de Saba"</note>

### ZACHARIAS GRAPIUS.
Professor of Theology at Rostock.
*Dissertation examining certain tenets of a very recent writing under the title of Geological Questions, VIII, Section III.* <note>original Latin: "Diff. quæ examinat placita quædam Scripti Recentissimi sub titulo Geologiæ Quæst. VIII. §. III."</note> Published at Rostock, 1700 and 1709.

### GREGORY OF NYSSA. <note>Gregorius Nyssenus</note>
Brother of Basil the Great; younger, yet nearly equal in knowledge and learning. For this reason, he was called by Suidas <term>most learned in every peak of education</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐλλογιμώτατος ἐν πάσῃ παιδείας ἀκμάσεως"</note>; and for the pleasantness and beauty of his writing style, <term>sweetest, bright, and dripping with the flowers of delight</term> <note>original Greek: "γλυκύτατος, λαμπρὸς καὶ ἡδονῆς ἀνθῶν ἀποστάζων"</note> by Casaubon; and because of the respect he earned in the Church through his merits, he was called <term>the father of the fathers, and the light-bearer of the Nyssenes, a man second only to his brother in both speech and conduct</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁ τῶν πατέρων πατὴρ, καὶ ὁ τῶν Νυσσαίων φωστήρ, ἀνὴρ μετὰ τὸν ἀδελφὸν δεύτερος ἔντε λόγοις καὶ τρόποις"</note>. He served in the office of Orator as a Reader when he was about 40 years old. He was ordained Bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia by his brother Basil around the beginning of the year of our Lord 372. Later, experiencing the hatred of the Arians <note>A group following Arianism, which disputed the nature of the Trinity</note>, he was deposed from his station and was only restored by Gratian after the death of Emperor Valens in the year 378. He was present at the second General Council of the Church at Constantinople in the year 381, and at another there in the year 394. Nothing certain is known of his death. *Greek Book-hall: Book V, Chapter 20, page 143.*
<term>An Apologetic on the Six-Day Creation</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἀπολογητικὸς περὶ τῆς ἑξαημέρου." This refers to the "Hexaemeron," or the six days of the biblical creation.</note>. A defending explanation of the six days of creation, addressed to Peter, Bishop of Sebaste, his brother. Laurentius Sifanius being the translator, it is found in the Latin translation of the works of Nyssenus, at Basel, 1562, in folio. The translation by Peter Francis Zini of Verona, at Venice 1553 and 1574 in octavo, is preserved in the Greek-Latin printings.
<term>On the Making of Man</term> <note>original Greek: "Περὶ κατασκευῆς ἀνθρώπου"</note>, a book to the same brother Peter; Suidas calls it <term>a wonderful volume</term> <note>original Greek: "τεῦχος θαυμάσιον"</note>. The translation by Dionysius the Small is in the Latin edition of the works at Basel, 1562, folio. It was also published at Cologne in 1537, 1551, and 1573, and at Paris in 1677, octavo, in the remains of Jean Mabillon. With Leunclavius as translator, at Basel 1567, octavo, from the bookstore of Johannes Oporinus.
*On the Words of Genesis 1:26: Let us make Man in our image and our likeness*, two sermons. These were translated by Peter Francis Zini; found in the Greek-Latin editions at Venice, 1553 and 1574, octavo.
*A Letter to Bishop Theodosius, on the Ventriloquist*, <note>original Latin/Greek hybrid: "de Engastrimytho." This refers to the Witch of Endor, often described as a ventriloquist in early theological texts.</note> to be found with the translation by Fronto Ducæus. At Ingolstadt, 1596, octavo.

### JACOBUS GRONOVIUS.
Born in Deventer, 1645. His father was Johann Frederik Gronovius, with whom he moved to Leiden. Learned in the liberal arts and in Law, from here he sailed to England, where, having examined the libraries of Oxford and Cambridge, he became known to Pococke, Pearson, Meric Casaubon, and others. In his twentieth year, he was offered a professorship at Deventer, which he declined, intending to visit other countries. The following year, he traveled with the Envoy of the States-General of the Netherlands,

<column-break/>

Paats, to Spain and Italy. There, through the mediation of Cardinal de' Medici and Magliabechi, he was appointed Professor at Pisa in Chimentello's place, becoming a colleague of Noris. Two years later, he traveled via Venice and Padua to Germany. In the year 1679, he was called to the Professorship at Leiden in Holland, to which was added the office of Geographer <note>original Dutch: "Wereldbeschryver," literally 'world-describer'</note> in the year 1702. He died in 1716 of grief over the untimely death of his youngest daughter. He left behind two sons, Doctors of Medicine and Law. He had sharp disputes with Feller, Perizonius, Isaac Vossius, Fabretti, Le Clerc, Küster, and others.
*Academic Exercises on the ruin and fall of Judas the betrayer* <note>original Latin: "Academicæ Exercitationes de pernicie & casu Judæ proditoris"</note>, held in the autumn of the year 1682 at Leiden by Daniel van Gaasbeek. 1683, quarto.

### STANISLAUS GREPSIUS.
*On the Multiple Hebrew Shekel and Talent, likewise on Hebrew measures of both dry and liquid goods. Preceded by an Epitome of Weights and Measures found among profane authors, chiefly taken from Budé.* <note>original Latin: "De Multiplici Siclo & Talento Hebraico... ex Budæo potissimum desumpta."</note> Found in Crenius’s *Dissertations on History, Criticism, and Philology*, Volume II, page 302.

### NICOLAUS GUIBERTUS.
Physician from Lorraine.
*Assertion regarding Murrhine, or those things expressed by the name murrhine, against certain people who argue less correctly about them; a small work in which many memorable things are brought forward concerning Myrrh, potions, ointments, and murrhine vessels, the drinking of myrrhed wine, as well as the Vinegar offered to CHRIST our Savior, and not a few other hidden matters; the errors of many are detected, and many passages of writers are both restored from corruption and clarified from obscurity.* <note>original Latin: "Assertio de Murrhinis... ac aliis non paucis reconditis adferuntur..." Murrhine refers to a rare material used for luxury vessels in the Roman era, often debated by scholars as to whether it was fluorite, porcelain, or glass.</note> Frankfurt, 1597, octavo.

### GEORG. HENRICUS HAEBERLIN,
Professor of Holy Theology and Superintendent at Tübingen.
*A Bundle of Myrrh from Song of Solomon 1:13, represented.* <note>original Latin: "Fasciculus Myrrhæ ex Hogel. I. 13. repræsentatus." The 'Hogel.' is an abbreviation for 'Hoogelied' or Song of Solomon.</note> Defended by Johann Wilhelm Bauman of Leudfidel in Franconia. At Tübingen, by Mart. Rommejus, 1690, quarto.

### BENEDICTUS HAHN.
*Dissertation on the Ghost of Endor* <note>original Latin: "Diss. de Spectro Endoreo"</note>, presided over by Jo. Ernest Gerhardi. Jena, 1722.

### JOHANNES van HAMM.
*Sacred Philological Exercises on the Inner Altar and its Mystery.* <note>original Latin: "Exercitationes Philologicæ Sacræ de Ara interiore ejusque Mysterio."</note> At Herborn, by Joh. Nic. Andreas, 1715, octavo.

### JAC. ALBERTUS HANSELMANN.
From Michelbach in Hohenlohe, Franconia.
*On the Magi who set out for Bethlehem with a star as their guide.* <note>original Latin: "De Magis stella duce Bethlehemum profectis."</note> The presiding officer was Joh. Herman van Elswich, ordinary Associate in Philosophy. Wittenberg, by Sam. Creusig, 1716, quarto.

### HERMANNUS van der HARDT.
Professor of Philosophy at the University of Helmstedt, Provost at Marie-berg; he had intended to publish his smaller works together under the title: *Enigmas of the Ancient World* <note>original Latin: "Ænigmatum prisci Orbis"</note>. But because of the inserted treatise *Jonah in the Whale* <note>original Latin: "Jona in Carcharia."</note>, which was forbidden by the Courts, he was assessed a fine of 100 Rijksthalers and all copies were confiscated. The author not only obeyed but also consumed eight folio volumes of his collections by fire, and sent some of the ash in eight chests to the Court. *Book-hall of Bremen, Vol. VII, 741.*
*On the Monument of Lot’s Wife* <note>original Latin: "De Monumento uxoris Lothi"</note> in *Ephemerides of Philology, Discourse IV.*
*Samson’s Foxes*. <note>original French: "Renards de Samson"</note>
*The Jawbone of an Ass*. <note>original French: "La Machoire d'Ane"</note>

### JOH. CHRIST. HARENBERG.
*Double miracle at Siloah, John 5:1-9.* in the *Bremen Book-hall, Vol. VII, page 82.*

# OF THE AUTHORS.

*Essay on investigating the antiquity of the water drawn at Siloam <note>Siloam: a rock-cut pool on the southern slope of the City of David in Jerusalem</note>, from an illustrated passage in Isaiah XXX. 29.* found on page 105.

*Observation on the harmful south wind to illustrate Psalm XCI. 6.* found on page 630.

*Description of the method of extracting gold and silver in Arabia and Ethiopia, from Job XXVII. 1–11.* Found in the *Bremen Book-Room* <note>original Dutch: "Breemer Boekz:", referring to the scholarly journal *Bibliotheca Bremensis*</note>, Class VIII. page 93.

*Observation on the words Adarkon, Darkemon, and Rekemon <note>original Hebrew: אדרכון, דרכמון, רכמון; ancient units of currency, specifically Persian darics</note> to illustrate the passages 1 Chronicles XXIX. 7, Ezra II. 69, Nehemiah VII. 70, 71, 72.* Also found there on page 623.

*The dew of Hermon descending upon the mountains of Zion from Psalm CXXXIII. 3.* Found there on page 970.

->JACOBUS HASAEUS,<-

Teacher of both Laws, Professor of Moral Philosophy in the Illustrious School at Bremen, died in his 72nd year of age on June 17, 1723. This untimely death was announced by his most excellent brother in the *Bremen Book-Room*, V. Class. page 386.

*Dissertation on the computation of the months of Paul’s journey, which he undertook from Jerusalem to Rome, to illustrate Acts XXVII. and XXVIII.* In the *Bremen Book-Room*, Class I. Volume I. page 17.

*Dissertation on the Tukkiyim <note>original Hebrew: תוكيים; usually translated as peacocks or parrots</note> which the fleet of Solomon and Hiram is recorded to have brought in 1 Kings X. 22. and 2 Chronicles IX. 21.* In the *Bremen Book-Room*, Class II. Volume III. page 468.

*Dissertation on the "whirring wings" <note>original Hebrew: צלצל כנפים; tsiltsal kenaphayim</note> and "clanging spears" <note>original Hebrew: צלצל קנים; tsiltsal kanim</note> to illustrate Job XL. 31. and Isaiah XVIII. 1.* In the *Bremen Book-Room*, Class V. Volume IV. page 563.

*Dissertation on the depopulations of the Jewish land by the Gazam, Arbe, Jeleb, and Chasil <note>original Hebrew terms for different stages or species of locusts mentioned in Joel</note>, to illustrate the prophecy of Joel I. 4, 11, 25, and in defense of the Greek version of the Alexandrian Translators <note>the Septuagint</note>.* In the *Bremen Book-Room*, Class VII. page 773.

->THEODORUS HASAEUS.<-

*Inquiry into the Leviathan of Job and the Whale of Jonah.* Bremen, at the expense of Johann Andreas Grimm. At the press of Hermann Brauer. 1723. Octavo.

->GOTTHARDUS HEIDEGGER.<-

Born in Zurich, August 4, 1664. Educated in the charity school <note>original: "Voedsterling School"</note>, admitted to the Holy Ministry since the year 1681; in 1687, he was chosen as Pastor at St. Margret in the Rhine Valley; at Rohrbach in 1697. Thereafter, Overseer of the students, in which office he died—after bloodletting for hemorrhoids, eventually suffering from dropsy—in the year 1711. A man worthy of a better fate and longer life due to his singular shrewdness of mind and deep learning.

*Sacred Recreations*, at Zurich 1711. Octavo. In the final part of which appear *A public discourse on the Nazirites in the Old Testament; Public Lectures on the Rapture and Purpose of Paul; Four Lectures on the Groaning Creation*, published at the expense of J. Finster.

->JOANNES HENRICUS HEIDEGGERUS.<-

Zurich theologian, highly renowned among the Reformed, owed more than all my praise to my godfather at Holy Baptism. Born July 1, 1633. His father was Hartmann Heidegger, Pastor at Ursweil; his mother Magdalena Wagner. Bereft of the former in 1643, and the latter in 1647. Sent abroad by the common council of the Church leaders, he went to Marburg in 1654, utilizing the housing, table, and instruction of Johannes Crocius. Moving to Heidelberg via Johann Heinrich Hottinger, the very famous Professor of Oriental Languages and Theology, he formed an unbreakable friendship with Ludwig Fabricius. Appointed Extraordinary Professor of the Hebrew language, admitted to the intimacy of Johann Freinsheim, and joined Hottinger in the school of wisdom. In 1659, called to Steinfurt to the theological

<column-break/>

professorships and Church History, he was consequently decorated with the honorary rank of Doctor, with Hottinger presiding. In 1660, having returned to his homeland, he entered into marriage with Elisabeth de Duno. In 1661, having undertaken a brief journey to the Netherlands, he became known to Perizonius, Gronovius, Graevius, Cocceius, and Comenius. In 1665, he bid farewell to the school at Steinfurt, which had been dispersed due to war; returning to his homeland, he accepted the call to teach Christian Ethics. In 1667, appointed to the Theological Professorship in place of Hottinger. In 1676 <note>Note: text says 1676, likely a chronological entry despite following 1667</note>, called to Leiden in Holland as Professor of Theology in place of Johannes Cocceius, he preferred to serve his homeland, with the government intervening. In 1671, he suffered the loss of his daughter Magdalena in her fourth year. In 1681, he was called to Groningen for the Theological Professorship. In 1693, he was nearly overwhelmed by the unforeseen death of his only daughter Elizabeth. Finally, he returned his soul to his Creator and Savior on January 18, 1698, having endured several misfortunes. He left behind two sons, Johannes Jacobus and Philippus, a Doctor of Medicine, who died in Paris in the year 1730.

*Heads of the Fathers* <note>original Hebrew: ראشي אבות; Roshe Avot</note>, *or the Sacred History of the Patriarchs.* This appeared in 1657, 1671, Utrecht 1683, and Zurich 1729, where in the 14th section he treats the *Longevity of the Patriarchs*; in the 17th, *Noah’s Ark*.

In the first volume of the *Select Treatises*, he deals in the 4th section with the *Last Supper of Christ*; in the 10th, with the *False Samuel summoned by the Witch of Endor*.

In the third volume of the Treatises: VII. on *Aaron's Calf*. VIII. on the *Punishment for Calf-worship and the reconciliation of the people*. XV. on the *Fig tree cursed by Christ*.

In the fourth volume of the Treatises: IV. on *Miracles in general*. VI. on the *Miracles of the Evangelical Church, First and Last*.

->PH. HEINIUS.<-

Professor in the school for students of the Reformed at Halle in Saxony.

*On the cause of the Animals brought to Adam. On the outer Altar of Moses. On the diameter of the Brazen Sea. On the name of Azazel.* There are others available besides these, which fall outside our scope, in the collection of various writings and the three bundles by the same author. At Halle in Magdeburg, from the bookstore of Rengers. 1717. Octavo.

->CHRISTOPHORUS HELVIG.<-

Doctor of Medicine, Professor at Greifswald.

*A specimen of Sacred Pharmacology regarding Antimony, Hemlock, and the Great Fish of Tobit (or the Catfish), taken from the three kingdoms of Nature.* The defender was Erich Gotlieb von Seelen, of Kedigen. At Greifswald by Daniel Benjamin Starck 1708. Quarto.

He promised a description of holy:
> Minerals.
> Plants.
> Animals.

->ANDREAS HELVIGIUS.<-

*Chronological Forerunner, or two Dissertations: 1. on the truth of the common Christian Era. 2. on the Feast in John V: whether it was Passover, and how many Passovers of Christ's Ministry are to be counted.* Rostock 1634. Quarto.

**HERBERT**, Bishop of Hereford in England.
*Some Animadversions upon a Book entitled, the Theory of the Earth. 1685. 8vo.* <note>Herbert Croft (1603–1691) was an English clergyman who wrote this critique of Thomas Burnet's famous "Sacred Theory of the Earth."</note>

**JOHANNES HERBINIUS**, from Brieg in Silesia.
*Dissertations on the ADMIRABLE CATARACTS OF THE WORLD <note>original: "de ADMIRANDIS MUNDI CATARACTIS"</note>, both above and below ground, and their Principle, the circulation of the Elements, where on the same occasion the true and genuine cause of the Ebb and Flow of the Sea is asserted, as well as the true site and location of the terrestrial and original Paradise in Palestine is restored, shown in a Chorographic Table <note>A chorographic table is a map depicting a specific region or district</note>, and defended against the Utopians, Indians, Mesopotamians, and others. Amsterdam: by Janusz van Waasberge 1678. 4to.*

**CHRIST. AUG. HEUMANNUS.**
He taught the liberal arts and philosophy at Jena, from where he was called in the year 1708 to be the inspector of the Theological Seminary in Eisenach, and thereafter to Göttingen, where he conducts himself with distinction as the Director of the Seminary and applies himself with particular diligence to serve the learned world.
*Dissertation on the Fate of Lot's Wife. 1706.* <note>original: "de Fato Uxoris Lothi"</note>

**MATTHÆUS HILLER.**
Professor of Oriental Languages at Tübingen, and Councilor to the Duke of Württemberg and Abbot at Königsbronn, etc.
*Hierophyticon, or a Commentary on Passages of Sacred Scripture that mention Plants <note>original: "Hierophyticon sive Commentarius in Loca Scripturæ Sacræ, quæ Plantarum faciunt mentionem"</note>, divided into two Parts, of which the former concerns Trees and the latter concerns Herbs. Supplemented by a Preface by Salomon Pfister, Professor at Bebenhausen, containing the Life, merits, and Books of the Blessed Author, both published and in Manuscript. At Utrecht by Jac. Broedelet 1725. 4to.*
*Treatise on the Gems in the Breastplate of the High Priest of the Hebrews.*
*Hebraic Questions on Plants mentioned in Holy Scripture, Decades I and II. 1716.* <note>A "Decade" in this context refers to a group of ten scholarly questions or essays.</note>

**JOH. WILHELM HILLIGER.**
*Balaam and his speaking Ass, from Numbers XXII. 21–33.* <note>original: "Bileamus, ejusque Asina loquens"</note> The defender <note>The "defender" or "respondent" was the student who publicly argued the thesis written by the professor</note> was Joh: Krücken of Hamburg. At Wittenberg by Christian Schröter 1702. 4to.

**PAULUS CHRIST. HILSCHER.**
Master of Holy Theology and Teacher at Old-Dresden.
*On the mystical Triangle, Square, Pentagon, and Hexagon <note>original Greek: "Τριγώνῳ, τετραγώνῳ, πενταγώνῳ & ἑξαγώνῳ"</note> in the Article of the Holy Trinity and CHRIST.* In the Leipzig Miscellany, Part II, by the heirs of Lankisius 1716. 8vo.

**ST. HIPPOLYTUS.**
The sweetest and clearest Teacher of the Church, according to Chrysostom in his sermon on the False Prophets, Part VI, page 401; a student of St. Irenaeus. Stephanus le Moyne states that he was Bishop of the Roman Port <note>Portus Romae</note>, a famous merchant city in Arabia, as he also maintains that he was an Arabian by descent, and taught from the time of Alexander Severus until that of Philip the Arab, who began to reign in the year of Christ 244. The Martyrologies celebrate his martyrdom on the 22nd of August, he having been, as they say, drowned in water.
*On the Ventriloquist <note>original Greek: "’Εις τὴν ἐγγαστρίμυθον"; this refers to the Medium or "Witch" of Endor in 1 Samuel 28</note>.* Concerning Saul and the Sorceress. From Fabricius's *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 1, pages 203, 209. Among the lost writings.
*On the things after the Hexaemeron <note>original Greek: "’Εις τὰ μετὰ τὴν ἑξαήμερον"; the Hexaemeron refers to the six days of Creation</note>.* Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 22. Among the lost works.

**JOH. ESAIAS HOECHSTETTER** of Weißenburg.
*Inaugural Dissertation in which it is demonstrated that the Waters above the Heavens <note>original: "Aquas supra Cœlestes"</note>, Genesis I. 6–7, are nothing other than the Waters of the Planets.* Presided over by Georg Paulus Rötenbeccius, Professor of Rhetoric and Politics at Altdorf, by Henr: Meyer 1707. 4to.

<column-break/>

**SAMUEL CHRISTOPH. HOLLMAN**
Ordinary Philosopher, Assistant, and Professor at the University of Wittenberg.
*Philosophical Dissertation on the obligation of the Christian Astronomer toward the Holy Scripture.* The defender was Joh. Phil. Gross of Thurm from Meissen, 1725, 4to, by the Widow Gerdes.
*Philosophical Commentary on Miracles and the genuine Criteria for them, and on the opinions of certain others regarding the same. 1728.*

**HOOPER.**
Bishop of Bath and Wells.
*An enquiry into the state of the antient Measures, the Attic, the Roman, and especially the Jewish. with an Appendix concerning our old English Money and Measures of content. London 1721. 8vo.*

**JOANNES HOPKINSON**, Englishman.
*Synopsis of Paradise, or a description of Paradise <note>original: "Synopsis Paradisi, sive Paradisi descriptio"</note>, taken from various writers of different languages and ages, with a Chorographic Table of the same.* Found in Crenius's *Historical, Critical, and Philological Dissertations*, Fascicle II, page 1.

**SAMUEL HORTINUS,**
Of Bern, Son of Samuel Hortinus, Minister at Oberweil.
*Philosophical-Theological Dissertation on Miracles.* Presided over by Dr. Samuel Scheurer, Professor of Holy Theology at Bern. At the Printing House of the Illustrious Commonwealth, 1728.

**HOSIUS, or OSIUS.**
For over 60 years Bishop of Corduba; having been present at many Church Councils, and finally having presided over the Council of Nicaea in 323 and the Council of Serdica in 347, he eventually yielded at that hour to the Arians who held the upper hand under Constantius. He departed this life at over one hundred years old in the year of our Lord 361.
*On the interpretation of the Sacerdotal Garments <note>original: "De interpretatione Vestium sacerdotalium"</note> which are in the Old Testament; a work elaborated with excellent sense and wit.* Isidore of Seville, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 1. Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, chapter 24, page 399.

**JOHANNES JACOBUS HOTTINGERUS.**
Born 1652 at the beginning of December, his father being **Johannes Henricus Hottingerus**, public Professor of Oriental Languages, Church History, and Rhetoric at the University of Zurich; his mother Anna Huldrich, only daughter of Henrik Huldrich, Deacon in the Holy Ghost Church. He laid the first foundations of his literary studies at Heidelberg, where his most worthy father was called in 1655 by the Elector Karl Ludwig to the Theological Professorship and the oversight of the seminary of wisdom. His father returning to Zurich and being declared Professor of Theology in 1661, the son also continued the course of his studies there. In August 1670, being a traveling companion to **Antonius Klingler**, he visited Basel; in 1671, the Roman Cantons; in Basel from August 1672 to December 5, 1673, he resided with **Lucas Gernler** and received instruction from **Rudolf Wetstein** and **Joh. Zuingerus**. In 1673, he had intended to go to the University of Marburg, but due to the war disturbances then troubling Germany, he judged it more advisable to change his intention and return to Basel. From here, in February 1675, he traveled to Geneva with his companion **Godfried Ursinus of Danzig** (who, intending to travel to Paris, drowned between Geneva and Lyon); there he became known to **Philippus Mestrezat**, **Ludwig Tronchinus**, **Francis Turretin**, **Francis Burlamach**, **Benedictus Calandrinus**, and **Reinhartus Vitriarius**. Returning from there to Zurich on January 12, 1676, he gave an account of his studies.

# OF THE AUTHORS.

<note>This entry concludes the biography of Johannes Jacobus Gesnerus, whose name began on the previous page.</note> ...admitted to the rank of Proclaimers of God’s Word in the following March, 1677. Called to the congregation at Stallikon, he entered the state of marriage with *Elizabeth Lavatera*, daughter of *Johannes Lavaterus*, Professor of Philosophy, and *Elizabeth Oeria*. By her, he fathered several children, of whom those remaining are *Johannes Jacobus*, Deacon of the Main Church; *Anna Elisabeth*, wife of *Joh. Jacobus Gesnerus*, Investigator and Bailiff; and *Joh. Henricus*, a merchant and Captain. In the year 1686, on the 1st of June, he was promoted to the office of Pleban <note>A 'Pleban' was a senior secular priest or pastor of a city’s principal church.</note> of the Zurich Main Church, and in 1698 to the Professor of Divinity. Then, on the 1st of March 1721, he was deprived of his very beloved better half, and on the 20th of May 1701 of his son *Johannes*. On the 14th of August 1729, he suffered a stroke in his left eye, but was afterwards, by God’s grace, so happily delivered from it that, at the beginning of the year 1730, he was able to resume both the public lectures and disputations as well as private teaching exercises. He was appointed to succeed *Johannes Henricus Heideggerus* as Professor of Divinity, a position which he has filled with the greatest praise until now, by God’s grace, 1731.

*Theological Exercise on the Miracles of JESUS CHRIST* <note>original: "Exercit. Theol. de Miraculis JESU CHRISTI"</note>. Defended by: Henrik Murerus, Jac. Dæniker, Jac. Cellarius, Casp. Grimm, Jonas Kunzlin, Petrus Glaron, and Leonh: Luchsinger. Zurich, by David Gesner, 1713. 4to.

*The Latter Part, or Section IV, of the Theological Exercise on the Miracles of JESUS CHRIST, which is porismatic, asserting the truth of CHRIST'S Miracles and the falsehood and vanity of the Antichristian ones.* <note>original: "Exercitationis Theol. de Miraculis JESU CHRISTI Pars posterior... quæ porismatica est..." 'Porismatic' refers to a deductive or consequential argument.</note> Defenders were Jac. Hagenbuch, Henr. Wirz, Petrus Collerus, Lod. Breittingerus, Joh. Meisterus, Josef Gygerus, and Casp. Zulzberger. At the same place, 1716. 5.

*All Biblico-Chronological Dissertations, demonstrating—both from the signs of the time assigned to the arrival of the Messiah, especially in the 70 Weeks of Daniel, and from the history of the Holy Evangelists concerning John, CHRIST, and Paul—that JESUS was both born in the fullness of time and is the CHRIST, against the Jews; and the integrity of the Sacred Codex is also defended throughout. A triple Appendix is added: 1. On the first Samaritans and their deportation to Syria; 2. On the new inhabitants of Samaria sent from Assyria; 3. On the dispersion of the XII Tribes.* <note>original title starts with the Greek "Παντας" (All) and continues in Latin: "Dissertationum Biblico-Chronologicarum..."</note> Utrecht, 1723. 8vo. A preface on Sacred Chronology and its writers was provided by Fred. Adolph. Lampe, Teacher of Holy Divinity and Professor at the University of Utrecht.

# SOLOMON HOTTINGERUS.
Son of the Great *Johannes Henricus*, Professor of Physics at the Zurich School and Canon of the Chapter at Thuringen; a man to be held in the highest honor for many reasons—due to his piety, learning, and experience—including by me, his student. He was declared a Master of Medicine on March 19, 1672, at Basel, with *Johan Rudolf Burcardus* presiding. He passed away in 1713.

*Sacred Physics, or a Dissertation on Lightning, proposing its Nature in general according to its causes and effects.* <note>original: "Βροντολογια [Brontologia - the study of thunder] Physico-Sacra, seu Dissertatio de Fulmine..."</note> The respondents being four candidates in Philosophy. Zurich, 1698. 4to. Published by Bodmer.

--- *Special part, presenting the more powerful adjuncts of the Lightning-bolt: the Flash, the Thunder, and the Lightning Strike specifically.* <note>original: "...ειδικῶς [specifically] sistens."</note> Defenders: seven candidates in philosophy. At the same place, 1700. 4to.

*Specimen of Sacred Physiology.* <note>original: "Specimen Physiologiæ Sacræ."</note> Defenders: Huldrik Weker and Henr. Kölliker. Zurich, by Bodmer, 1704. 4to.

*General and Special Physics according to the History of Creation from Genesis I, presented in summary:* <note>original: "...κατ' ἐπιτομὴν [in summary] proposita"</note> Defender: Joh. Jac. Grobius. Zurich, by Gesner, 1706. 4to.

--- *Sacred-Physical Biography, or a Dissertation on life: its nature, essence, intervals or ages, especially also on the discomforts of the Old Man, according to the illustrious passage of Ecclesiastes XII. 3-8, and finally on Death, the opposite of life.* <note>original: "Biographia Physico-Sacra..."</note> Defenders: Felix Wyfsius, Joh. Rod Eberhard, Joh. Casp. Ringglin, Dieth. Meyer, Joh. Jac. van Birch, Casp. Fuelin, Huldr. Wyfsius, Casp. Schinzius, and Joh. Rod. Seeholzer. Zurich, by Gesner, 1706. 4to.

*The Book of Nature, presented from Psalm XIX, 1-7.* <note>original: "Liber Naturæ..."</note> Defenders: Joh. Casp. Sprynglin and Joh. Henr. Dentzler. Same place, by Dav. Gesner, 1711. 4to.

# JOHANNES CONRADUS HOTTINGERUS.
Son of *Johannes Conradus*, a very experienced apothecary, and nephew of the great *Joh. Hendrik*. He was a preacher at Höngg, where he passed away.

*The House of Mercy according to the Law of Moses, or a Philological Dissertation on the Pool of Bethesda, regarding the passage in John V. 2, 3, 4.* <note>original: "בית חסדא כדת משה [Beth Hesda kedat Moshe] seu Dissertatio Philolog. de Piscina Bethesda..."</note> Presiding: Dr. Joh. Bapt. Ottius, teacher at Zollicon and Professor of the Hebrew Language. Zurich, by Gesner, 1705. 4to.

# PETRUS DANIEL HUET.
Bishop of Avranches in France: formerly the tutor to the Dauphin <note>The heir apparent to the French throne.</note>, a very learned man, renowned for his writings.

*Commentary on the Voyages of Solomon.* <note>original: "Commentatio de Navigationibus Salomonis."</note>
*Treatise on the Site of Paradise.* <note>original: "Tractatus de situ Paradisi."</note> Paris, 1691.

# HENRICUS HULSIUS.
Born in Cronenburg in the Duchy of Berg; his father was *Antonius van Hilde* of the Berg region, preacher at Cronenburg for 11 years and at Elverfeld for 29 years; his mother was *Margaretha Steinberg*, daughter of *Petrus Steinberg*, a teacher at Mettmann. He was born on October 10, 1654. He laid the first foundations of his studies at the school in Elverfeld. In the year 1667, he was sent to Duisburg; here he primarily increased his knowledge of the views of *Descartes* and *Cocceius*, having utilized the instruction of *Jo. Henr. Hugenpooth*. In the year 1673, he went to Marburg. From there he departed for Leiden in Holland, and then to Harderwijk, where he was honored with the Doctoral Laurel on July 6, 1679. *Samuel van Dieft*, Teacher of Holy Divinity, was his promoter. In the year 1681 or 1682, the Chair of Divinity at Duisburg on the Rhine was offered to him. He lived unmarried until August 10, 1705, when he married *Anna Maria Werhd*, the daughter of *Kaspar Werhd*, an innkeeper in Amsterdam, who is said to have played the role of a Xantippe <note>Xantippe was the wife of the philosopher Socrates, traditionally remembered as a nagging and difficult woman.</note>. Having been delivered from her on September 12, 1720, he chose for his spouse on August 24, 1721, *Geertruid van Eiken*, a girl of 16 years, whom he—she having previously been his maidservant—appointed as the heir to all his goods, down to the last penny. He passed away on April 4, 1723, at 69 years of age. *Bremer Boekzaal, Class VII, page 898.*

*A Commentary on the prerogatives and goods of ancient Israel under the Old Testament, included in 15 Dissertations, which are followed by 17 sections of related material concerning the nobler matters of the Old Testament.* <note>original: "Commentarius in Israelis prisci prærogativas..."</note> Leiden, 1713. 4to. Among other treatises found therein are the following: *On the Scapegoat [Azazel]; On the Hair of Samson; On the Sacrifice of Isaac; On Jacob's struck and limping Thigh; On the 70 Weeks of Daniel; On the purification of Leprosy, menstruation, and impurity from the dead.*

# JOACHIMUS CHRISTIANUS JEHRING.
*Dissertation on the Region of Tarshish.* <note>original: "Dissert. de Regione Tarshisch."</note> Found in the *Bremer Boekzaal, Class VIII, page 78.*

### JOHANNES.

The Alexandrian, called "the Christian" by a multitude of writers, and named PHILOPONUS <note>meaning "lover of labor"</note> because of a wonderful application of effort; also called GRAMMATICUS, perhaps because he publicly taught grammar in Alexandria. The founder of the sect of the Tritheists <note>a heretical belief that the Trinity consists of three separate deities</note>, condemned in the Council of Constantinople in the year 781. *Greek Books, Vol. V, Book 37, Chap.*

*Seven Books of Explanations on the Mosaic Creation of the World <note>original: "Τῶν εἰς τὴν Μωϋσέως κοσμογονίαν ἐξηγητικῶν λόγοι ζ'"</note>, addressed to Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Published in Greek and Latin with the translation of Balthazar Corderius at Vienna, 1630. 4to.*

*Dispute on the Passover <note>original: "Disputatio de Paschate"</note>, [on the thirteenth, etc.] <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῇ τριςκαι. [epi tē triskai.]"</note>, stating that on the thirteenth day of the Moon, the day before the legal Passover, the spiritual Lord's Supper occurred, and that CHRIST and his disciples did not eat the Paschal lamb at that time. It is read in the books appended to the same work in Greek and Latin by Corderius. Under the title of "Johannes Damascenus on Unleavened Bread," it is found in the manuscript in the Coislin library, according to the testimony of Montfaucon.*

### JOHANNES LEMOVICENSIS.

### CHRISTIANUS JOHRENIUS.

JOLA. Of sacred Tarentum, see Epiphanius.

### ULRICUS JUNIUS.

Was born in Ulm of honorable parents; he laid his foundation at the school there and especially absorbed the principles of mathematics under Honoldus. Following this, he studied at Jena and subsequently at Leipzig, where he worked diligently on the improved Almanac and made himself so well-beloved that he was appointed extraordinary Professor of Mathematics, and later ordinary Professor and Royal Astronomer; he died in the year 1726.

*Errors of Astrologers concerning the Nativity Theme of CHRIST <note>original: "Errores Astirologorum circa Thema CHRISTI geneihliacum"</note>. Leipzig 1701. 4to.*

### ST. JUSTIN MARTYR.

A Samaritan, originally from Nablus in Palestinian Syria, or Shechem; son of Priscus, grandson of Bacchius; appears to have been born in the year of Christ 89. Experienced in every kind of philosophical instruction, he first heard the Stoic, then the Peripatetic, then the Pythagorean, and finally the follower of Plato. From there, set aflame with the desire

<column-break/>

to know the teachings of CHRIST by the discourses of a certain old man (perhaps Polycarp), he gave himself entirely to them and defended the Christian doctrines with mouth and pen against Jews and Heathens; finally accused by Crescens, a Cynic philosopher, he confirmed his faith with his blood, suffering martyrdom under Junius Rusticus, Prefect of the City, in the 74th year of his age, in the year of CHRIST 163, in the third year of the consulship of M. Aurelius Antoninus and L. Verus. *Fabric. Bibl. Græc. Book V, chap. 1, p. 51.*

*Among his writings that are lost, [the following] have come to light:*

*Memoirs on the Six Days of Creation <note>original: "Hypomnemata eis Hexaëmeron"</note>: from which Anastasius has taken excerpts and preserved them in the 7th Book of the Hexaëmeron <note>term: Hexaëmeron refers to theological treatises on the six days of creation described in Genesis</note>.*

### BERNHARDUS PETRUS KARLIUS,

*Consideration of the Responses of the Renowned Driessenius, Theologian of Groningen, to the Doubts concerning the Apocalyptic Chronology <note>original: "Chronotaxin Apocalypticam"</note> and the Millennial Kingdom of Christ (Apoc. XX), as if still to be expected, recently raised to him by the Noble and most Learned Man Hermann Deusing, Doctor of both Laws, a renowned and excellent scholar of Prophetic Theology.* In the Bremen Book-hall Class II. Vol. VI. p. 961.

*Discourse on the Miracle of the Sun or the Shadow returning ten lines through the degrees which it had already descended on the sundial of Ahaz, by which the promised restoration of health and the extension of life for 15 years was confirmed to the lethally ill Hezekiah, 2 Kings XX, 2 Chron. XXXII, and Isaiah XXXVIII; with a Supplement on the Miracle of the Sun and Moon commanded to stand still by Joshua, Josh. X.* In the Bremen Book-hall Cl. IV. Vol. IV. p. 635.

*A New Conjecture concerning the Scapegoat <note>original: "Hirco ἀποπομπαίῳ [apopompaiō]"</note>, sent away, on Leviticus XVI compared with Hebrews XIII:13.* In the Bremen Book-hall Cl. VI. Vol. II. p. 225.

### ATHANASIUS KIRCHER.

Was born in 1602 at Geisa, a place not far from Fulda. In his early years, his father—the Magistrate at Haselstein—taught him himself; he then sent him to the Jesuits at Fulda. Having miraculously survived two grave dangers, he vowed himself to this Order and entered it at Paderborn in 1618. He taught at Würzburg, but was little esteemed due to his slight physical stature and timid eyes. The war times of that period drove the Fathers and himself from one place to another, as far as France, where he stayed for a time with the Jesuits at Avignon. He finally arrived in Rome, partly through envy and partly through the fame of his excellent experience in explaining antiquities, during a dangerous storm. There he explained ancient monuments and successfully improved what was lacking, also working out many particulars in mathematical and optical matters, and finally had the honor of being the Imperial Mathematician; he died on November 30, 1680. He still lives in his writings and in the wonderment regarding

### GEORGIUS CASPARUS KIRCHMAIER.
Professor of Eloquence at Wittenberg, born in 1635 at Uffenheim in the Franconian Margraviate of Anspach. His father was *Georg Abel*, Bailiff <term>Schout: a local administrative and judicial official</term> of the ducal city and district. Having been sent to Wittenberg in 1655, he studied there under *Johannes Sperlingius* and *Augustus Buchnerus*. He was appointed Professor of Rhetoric there in 1661. Under the name of *Phosphorus* <note>meaning "The Light-Bringer" or "Morning Star"</note>, he shone as the discoverer of the "Morning Star" <note>likely a reference to his membership in the Academy of Nature Researchers</note> at the Academy of Nature Researchers. A man of very great fame, largely due to his familiar correspondence with *Bullialdus, Hevelius, Baecierus, Conringius, and Magliabecchi*—the most prominent men of his century. Shortly before his death, having undertaken a journey to the Netherlands, he became known to *Gronovius, Graevius, and Witsius*. He died, however, in the year 1700 of a high fever.

*Several Dissertations on the Basilisk, the Unicorn, the Phoenix, the Behemoth, the Leviathan, the Dragon, the Spider, the Tarantula, and the Bird of Paradise.* <note>original title: "De Basilisco, Unicornu, Phœnice..."</note> The second, enlarged edition. At Wittenberg, at the expense of the heirs of *Johannes Berger*, by *Michael Meyer*, 1669, octavo. The previous edition is attached to the *Description* by *Sperling*, at Leipzig, at the expense of *Johannes Berger*, 1661, octavo.

### JOHANNES JACOBUS LAVATER.
Of Zurich in Switzerland. Born on the 30th of October, 1657. His father was *Johannes Lavaterus*, a very famous Professor of Philosophy and Canon of the Thuringian Chapter; his mother was *Elisabeth Deria*, a grand-niece of *Ludwig Lavaterus*, the principal Minister of the Zurich Church. In the year 1677, on the 30th of May, he was ordained to the Holy Ministry. In 1684, he was appointed Professor of the Catechism in the College of Language and History. In 1695, the Chair of Ethics in the Carolinum College was added to his duties. Two years later, in 1697, he exchanged both these professorships for the Chair of Rhetoric and Eloquence in the College of Language and History, an office he served for 13 years. In the year 1710, on the 8th of September, he was made Professor of Theology at the Carolinum College, succeeding the very famous man *Johannes Casparus Wolfius*. In 1725, his strength having gradually declined for some time, he passed away very peacefully. From the year 1687, his wife was *Anna*, daughter of *Johannes Schaufelberger*, a councilman and twice a judge, by whom he left nine children.

*Theological Dissertation on the contemplation of the works of Nature, according to the guidance of Holy Scripture.* Defended by *Andreas Zimmerman*, accepted from *Johannes Jacobus Lavaterus*. Zurich, by *David Gesner*, 1713, quarto.
*Dissertation on the operative Providence of GOD in intelligent creatures, before and after their desertion by God, whereby the purpose He set for Himself in Creation never fails.* Ibid., 1714, quarto.

# LIST OF NAMES

### JOHANNES JACOBUS LAVATERUS.
Born to *Johannes Jacobus*, the prominent theologian, in the year 1694. Recorded on the List of Ministers of God’s Word on October 2, 1714. Thereafter, in the years 1718, 1719, 1720, and 1723, while holding the office of Extraordinary Professor at the Fatherly School <note>The Carolinum in Zürich, a predecessor to the university</note>, he conducted public lessons during Summer Fridays on the most memorable histories found in the Holy Scripture. These primarily concerned the Kings and the affairs of the Tyrians, Egyptians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, and Syrian-Macedonians, and finally the Roman governors in Syria and the procurators of Judea. These accounts were compared with the writings of secular authors, whose testimonies on these matters were partly clarified and partly confirmed, with many prophecies of the Prophets pertaining to these events being recounted throughout that work. In 1724, the associate professorship in the College of Human Sciences was conferred upon him, followed by the full professorship on May 24, 1725, which he commenced with a solemn oration regarding the *Principles of the Jewish Religion and Theology*.

### LEVINUS LEMNIUS.
Born at Zierikzee in Zeeland in 1505. Honored with the master’s laurel crown in medicine <note>An MD degree</note>. After his wife passed away, he chose the clerical life and died as a Canon in the year 1568. His son, *Wilhelm*, personal physician to Erik XIV, King of Sweden, suffered the loss of both property and life when the King was deposed from the royal throne.
> *A clear explanation of the herbs and trees which are commonly found in the Bible, from which the sacred Prophets drew their comparisons and adapted their allegories to things; in which narrative individual passages are explained where the Prophets, having observed the nature of plants, illustrate their sermons and support the divine oracles.* <note>original: "Herbarum atque Arborum, quæ in Bibliis paſſim obviæ ſunt..."</note> Published at Antwerp by Willem Simonsz: 1566, in octavo.
> *A clear explanation of the Similes and Parables which are drawn from herbs and trees in the Bible.* <note>original: "Similitudinum ac Parabolarum..."</note> Antwerp 1569, in octavo, by Willem Simonsz. Erfurt 1581 and 1584 by Esaias Mechler.
> *Similes and Parables — — — To which are added two books by Franciscus Rueus on certain Gems, especially those mentioned by John in the Apocalypse, and others whose use has become widespread among all in this age; and one book by Levinus Lemnius on Astrology.* <note>original: "Similitudinum ac Parabolarum - - - Accedunt Franciſci Ruei de Gemmis..."</note> Frankfurt 1591, by Joh. Weechel and Petrus Vischer.

### JOHN LENG
Doctor of Divinity, Rector of Beddington and Chaplain in ordinary to his Majesty.
> *The natural obligations to believe the principles of Religion and divine Revelation in XVI. Sermons, preached in the Church of S. Mary le Bow, London in the Years 1717. and 1718. at the Lecture founded by the honourable Robert Boyle Esquire.* London 1719.

### JACOBUS JEHUDA LEO, or LEONITIUS.
A Spaniard by descent, he later moved to Middelburg in Zeeland. A man skilled in many languages, he labored for several years, even to the point of exhaustion, to reconstruct the Temple of Jerusalem in a small-scale model based on the most ancient records.
> *Four Books on the Temple of Jerusalem, both the first, which King Solomon built, and the later one, which Vespasian destroyed. By the order and auspices of the Serene Prince Lord Augustus, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg, revised from Hebrew into Latin by Joh. Saubertus. Added to this edition are various figures taken from Hebrew monuments and very accurately engraved in copper.* <note>original: "De Templo Hierofolymitano... ex Hebræo Latine recenſiti à Joh. Saubertu"</note> At Helmstedt by Jac. Müller 1665, in quarto. The author first

Stam in 1643, under this title: *Portrait of the Temple of Solomon, in which is briefly described the structure of the Temple building, and of all its vessels and utensils: the model of which may be found after the same author as anyone may see. Composed by Jacob Judah Leon, Hebrew, inhabitant of Middelburg in the Province of Zeeland, in the year of the Creation of the World 5403.* <note>original: "Portrait du Temple de Salomon..."</note>

### JOHANNES LIGHTFOOT,
Doctor of Theology at the University of Cambridge and Master of St Catharine’s Hall; a man exceptionally skilled in the Oriental languages. He was born at Stoke-on-Trent in the County of Stafford in 1602. Sent in the year 1617 to Christ’s College in Cambridge. In the County of Derby at Repton, he was appointed to instruct the youth. He laid the first foundations of Rabbinic philology under Sir Rowland Cotton. From his travels in foreign lands, he was called back by a vocation to the ministry at Stone in the County of Stafford. Finally, he was added to the ministers of the Church of Westminster. At the end of the year 1643, he was called to the pastoral service of Munden in the County of Hertford, in which position he died in 1675 as a Canon of Ely. He was honored with the doctoral laurel in theology in 1652 and served as Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge University in 1655. He maintained correspondence with the most famous men of his century: *Buxtorf, Brian Walton, Castellus, Pocock, Samuel Petit, Poole*, and others.
> *On the Temple of Solomon after the captivity, especially how it stood in the days of our Savior, as well as on the service of the Temple, its vessels, utensils, and other matters of that same time, that is, the time of CHRIST.* <note>original: "De Templo Salomonis poſt captivitatem..."</note> In English, London 1650.

### MARTINUS LIPENIUS.
Sub-Rector of the school at Halle.
> *Solomon’s Navigation to Ophir Illustrated.* <note>original: "Navigatio Salomonis Ophiritica illuſtrata."</note> Wittenberg at the expense of Andreas Hartman, 1660, in duodecimo.

### MICHAEL FRIDERICUS LOCHNER,
of Hummelsheim,
Nuremberger, Chief Physician to his Sacred Imperial Majesty and physician to the Imperial Person, Nobleman of the Holy Roman Empire, Count Palatine <term>Paltsgraaf: a high-ranking title of nobility with judicial powers</term>, Director of the Leopoldine-Caroline Academy of Natural Scientists, Senior of the Medical Society at Nuremberg, and during his life, my most intimate friend. He was born at Fürth, not far from Nuremberg, on the day before March in the year 1662. His father was *Karl Frederik*, a very zealous minister of that place, and his mother was *Sabina Majera*, daughter of *Joh. Jakobus Majerus*, a Swiss by descent and merchant in Nuremberg. As a boy of six, he was sent to Nuremberg and raised with motherly love by the widow *Pühler*. Being taught in the Aegidian School, he progressed so much under *Johannes Seinsheimerus* that at twelve years old, he wrote a pure Latin oration and also composed Latin and Greek verses. From there, he was committed to the care of his uncle *Jacobus Hieronymus Lochner*, who was an assistant of the Royal Consistory in Wismar, a preacher in St. Nicholas Church, and later an assistant in the Duchies of Bremen and Verden (located at Stade) and ecclesiastical head at Bremen. In Wismar, he had as teachers *Urbanus Lehman* and *Michaël Freundius*; in Rostock, *Augustus Varenus*, where at the recommendation of *Jakob Stokmann*, he applied himself to medicine.

...which he added to his theological exercises. Traveling from there to Copenhagen, he became acquainted with *Olaus Borrichius, Casparus Bartholinus, and Oliger Jacobæus* <note>all famous Danish scientists and physicians</note>; at Kiel with *Morhofius, Christian Korthold, Joh. Daniel Major, and Joh. Nicolaus Pechlinus*. In the year 1679, he undertook a journey to the Netherlands, and having returned home in 1680, he went to Altdorf <note>a university town near Nuremberg</note>, studying under *Mauritius Hoffmann, Jacob Pancratius Bruno, Johannes Mauritius Hoffmann, and Joh. Christoph. Sturmius*. From there, he traveled through Switzerland to France. In Paris, having made friends with *Johannes Zellerus* (later a Professor at Tübingen), he became an intimate associate of *du Verney, Buffier, Petit, and Baudot* <note>leading French anatomists and scholars</note>. In the year 1683, he withdrew to Richelieu by way of Orleans, Blois, Tours, and Saumur for the sake of the French language; at Saumur, he befriended *Joh. Casp. Eisenfchmid*, who later became a Professor of Mathematics at the University of Strasbourg. Intending to sail to England, he was tossed about at sea for four or five weeks before finally coming ashore, though he immediately resumed his journey to the Netherlands. At Leiden, he became known to *Theodorus van Craanen, Paulus Hermannus, Lucas Schacht, and Nuck*; in Amsterdam to *Ruysch* <note>Frederik Ruysch, the world-famous anatomist known for his preservation techniques</note>. In the year 1684, passing through Utrecht, Cologne, and other cities along the Rhine, he traveled home and debated at Altdorf to obtain his doctoral degree. From there, he departed for Italy in the company of Count *Joh. Georg Volkamer*, and also became known at Padua to *Karel Patin, Dominicus de Marchettis, Antonius Molinetti, and Felix ab te Viali*. In 1685, he was decorated with the laurel wreath <note>awarded his doctorate</note> at Altdorf by *Joh. Maur. Hofmann*. Returning from there to Nuremberg, he practiced medicine there with very successful results, earning the title "Doctor of the Poor" from the needy. In the year 1712, as the Senior of the Medical Society, he took upon himself the care of the hospital, which responsibility he handed over to his son-in-law in 1719. Having been appointed as the administrator of the journals of the Natural Researchers <note>The *Ephemerides* of the Leopoldina Academy</note>, he primarily saw to it that they did not appear in print unless they were refined; so much so that his late-night labors smelled of the oil lamp <note>a metaphor meaning his work showed signs of great diligence and late hours</note>. He entered into marriage with *Anna Maria*, daughter of *Johannes Vierzigan*, a citizen of Nuremberg, in 1686, from which marriage were born *Joannes Fredericus, Ursula Dorothea, Sabina Felicitas, Anna Maria, Johannes Henricus*, and *Catharina Dorothea*. Three of these gave back their spirits to GOD in their childhood. *Johannes Henricus*, growing up pleasantly to the hope of his parents and the comfort of his relatives, was snatched from life in his 19th year in 1715 at the University of Wittenberg. In that same year, *Anna Maria* was married to *Christoph Ludov. Göckel*, a physician in Baden, Wolfstein, and Nuremberg. The same disease, which appears under the name of smallpox and had taken the brother, also consumed *Sabina Felicitas*. Our subject died of a very fierce, hot fever on October 15, 1720, in his 58th year. *Erhardus Reusch* has described the life of this very worthy man more extensively, inserted in the German Journals, the 9th and 10th Century; Appendix, page 571.

->JOBUS LUDOLPHUS.<-
<note>Known today as Hiob Ludolf, the founder of Ethiopian studies in Europe.</note>
Born at Erfurt in 1624, where his father was *Job, a city magistrate*, and his mother was *Judith Brand*. He mastered the foundations of learning at home, where he learned Latin, Greek, and Philosophy. In his 19th year <note>OCR 39 is likely 19</note>, he was admitted to the university and applied himself to medicine and also to the art of writing, particularly in the French, Spanish, Dutch, and Italian languages. In his 22nd year, he undertook the study of Law, and under *Elsnerus*, the Hebrew, Chaldean, Syriac, Samaritan, Arabic, Armenian, and Ethiopic languages. In 1645, he went to Leiden, where he received instruction from *L'Empereur* regarding *Jewish Jurisprudence*, from *Golius* in Arabic, and from *de Dieu* in Persian, as well as the English and Swedish languages. Whereupon he traveled further with *Thysius* to the peace negotiations at Münster, and from there to France, specifically to Caen to visit *Bochart*, who taught him the Oriental languages; Ludolf, in return, taught him the Ethiopic language. In Paris, he had access to *Puteanus, Saravius, and Drelincourt*; at Saumur to *Capellus and Benoit*. In the year 1654, he saw London and Oxford in England. At Leiden, he arranged the books of the deceased *L'Empereur*. At Utrecht, he lived in close confidence with *Voetius and Anna Maria van Schurman* <note>Schurman was the most learned woman of the age</note>. He traveled further with the Lord of *Rosenhan* and was also ordered by Queen *Christina* to travel to Rome to fetch manuscripts, where he became knowledgeable in the language of the Abyssinians <note>the Amharic and Ge'ez languages of Ethiopia</note>. He went via Paris to Sweden, where he also became knowledgeable in the Portuguese, Finnish, and Russian languages. He then left his patron, the Lord of *Rosenhan*, and came home via Denmark and Copenhagen; however, because his father had passed away, he turned to Nuremberg. His offices were many and weighty: the position of Secretary of Fiefs at Gotha offered to him he left to his nephew, and by order, he collected the remains and the armor of Duke *Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar*. In the year 1652, Duke *Ernest the Pious* sent him as Secretary of the Legation to Regensburg; in the year 1654, he appointed him as Governor <note>tutor</note> to his Princes, particularly Prince *Albrecht*. In the year 1659, he was made a Court Councilor; at Altdorf, he held a public debate on the *punishment of crimes* upon obtaining his Doctorate. He went as an envoy to Heidelberg and attended the election of Emperor *Leopoldus*. In this year, King *Charles Gustavus* requested that he travel with his natural son, *Gustavus Carlson*. After other duties, he traveled in the year 1673 with Prince *Albrecht* and went via Wolfenbüttel and Hamburg to Sweden, at which court he became the friend of the most prominent people. After his return, the new Duke *Frederick of Gotha* appointed him as Director of the Chamber, and while he was attending to the Prince's affairs in Berlin, his wife passed away, whereupon after a very great request, he obtained his discharge in 1678. However, he retained the title of Councilor, and Privy Councilor of the entire Ernestine line, along with an annual pension. He then chose to reside in Frankfurt, but could not avoid many state services; he was there in the year 1681 at the...

### JOHANNES LUNDIUS.

*The Ancient Jewish Sanctuaries, Divine Services, and Customs, presented in a detailed description of the entire Levitical Priesthood, in five distinct books.* It treats:
I. Of the Tabernacle, its construction, furnishings, and movement, both in the wilderness and in the land of Canaan, and where it finally remained.
II. Of the Temple, both the first and the second; of its construction, form, splendor, furnishings, etc., and its twofold destruction.

### THOMAS LYDIAT.
Born at Okerton in the Province of Oxford in 1572, his father *Christophorus* being a London merchant. He completed his literary studies at the school in Winchester and at the University of Oxford. Having become the Cosmographer <note>a scholar of geography, astronomy, and mapping</note> to Prince Henry, after the Prince's death, he became known to Archbishop **Usher** <note>James Ussher, famous for his biblical chronology</note>, with whom he traveled to Ireland and lived for two years at the college in Dublin. Returning from there, he was promoted to the rectory of Okerton. He was thrown into prison for a time for being a guarantor for a relative's debt which he was unable to pay, but was released through the help of Laud, Usher, and others, with the exception of Johannes Seldenus, who refused to contribute anything. During the Civil War, remaining loyal to the King, he suffered much in both body and property and fell into extreme poverty. He died at Okerton on April 3, 1646. A man who, in the judgment of Usher, was more skilled in matters of chronology than Joseph Scaliger <note>the most famous scholar of his age</note>.

<column-break/>

*Astronomical Lecture on the Nature of the Heavens and the condition of the Elements, and on the causes of the principal motions of the heavens and stars. Also a physiological inquiry into the origin of perennial cold and hot springs, and on that occasion, on the origin and causes of almost all subterranean things, as well as the tide and saltiness of the sea, and the universal flood. By which two short commentaries the constitution of the universe is sketched, such that the opinions accepted by many Peripatetic philosophers today concerning the immutable fifth essence of the heavens and the proportions and placement of the elements are refuted; while the natural history of the Holy Scriptures regarding the water above the heavens and the subterranean fire is confirmed according to the genuine, anciently accepted view.* London, published by John Bill, 1605, octavo.

### RABBI MOSES MAIMONIDES OR R. MOSHE BEN MAIMON.
A Jew among the most learned, he lived at the beginning of the 13th century, born in Córdoba, Spain. Due to his precocious and successful progress in studies under the paternal instruction of *R. Joseph*, he incurred the envy of those who were jealous of him; to flee them, he crossed over to Egypt, for which reason he was also called the *Egyptian Moses*. He taught in Alexandria and Damascus and was held in very high esteem by the Sultan of Egypt <note>Saladin</note>, whom he had cured of a serious illness. A man exceptionally skilled in the Hebrew, Arabic, Chaldean, Turkish, and Greek languages; also possessing a thorough knowledge of medicine, philosophy, and mathematics; deeply learned in Jewish theology and law, having an aversion to the fables of the Talmudists <note>scholars focused on the traditions of the Talmud</note>. He had drawn the principles of his philosophy from the writings of the Arabs and those of Aristotle, for which reason he was suspected by some Jews. On the occasion of his book *More Nevochim* <note>The Guide for the Perplexed</note>, he was placed on the list of heretics by a trio of Rabbis—*Solomon of Montpellier, Jonah, and David*—who were nonetheless themselves driven out of the synagogue by other Rabbis. It is said that he traveled from Egypt to Judea and died here at seventy years of age, being buried in Upper Galilee.

*Treatise on the Chosen House, or on the figure and form of the Temple Building, translated by Ludovicus de Compiegne de Veil.* To be found in the *Library of Philological History*, Volume VI, page 1.
*On the Apparatus of the Temple, its Instruments and Ministers.* Ibid, page 84.
*On the Manner of Entering the Temple.* Ibid, page 161.
*On Things Forbidden at the Altar.* Ibid, page 228.
*On the Manner of Performing Sacrifices.* Ibid, page 282.

*On the Manner of Performing Divine Service on the Solemn Day of Atonement.* Ibid, page 651.

*On Fasting. Translated by Lud. de Compiegne.* Ibid, page 759.
*On the Solemnity of Atonement.* Ibid, page 819.
*On the Solemnity of Passover.* Ibid, page 837.
