In the year 1658, he went to Leipzig, primarily making use of the instruction of *Johann Michael*. Having traveled through Germany from there, he departed for Italy in the year 1659. At Padua, he pursued Archaeology and Belles-Lettres <note>The humanities or "fine letters"</note> primarily under *Carlo Offredi*, and Medicine under *Franciscus Bonardo, Prosper Todeschi, Hieronymus Frimigelica, and Petrus de Marchettis*. Proceeding to a second marriage, he married *Margaretha Elizabeth*, daughter of *Hermannus Pincierus*, a jurist and eldest Canon of the Episcopal Chapter at Lübeck, by whom two daughters and a son survived their father. In the year 1667, he was provided for as Chief Physician by the most illustrious Widow of Anhalt-Zerbst, but he declined that office, as he did another illustrious one offered to him in Copenhagen. In the year 1683, on account of his *Cimbrian Work* <note>referring to his research on the Cimbrian Peninsula or Jutland</note>, he undertook a journey to Denmark and Sweden; having traveled through almost the entire Cimbrian Chersonese <note>The Jutland peninsula</note>, he was favored with many benefits in Copenhagen by the King of Denmark and in Stockholm by Charles XI, King of Sweden. Here, on July 22, attacked by an acute fever, with jaundice following it and a very stubborn constipation, he became so weakened that he died on August 3, having been declared an Assessor of the Courts in Pomerania by the King shortly before his death.

### JOHANNES HENRICUS MAJUS.
Born February 5, 1653, at Pforzheim in the Margraviate of Baden-Durlach, his father being *Johann Georg*, a preacher in his paternal city, and his mother *Margaretha Dorothea Uzinia*. In his eleventh year, he was sent to Durlach alongside his older brother *Jo. Burchard*, later Professor of the grammar school at Durlach and teacher in History and Eloquence at Kiel. He had for teachers *Joh. Fechtius, Flekhamer, and Jo. Gerhard Arnoldus*. Having departed for Wittenberg in the year 1671, he hung upon the words <note>original: "at van den mond," meaning he was a devoted student</note> of *Schurtzfleisch, Stolberg, Abraham Calovius, Jo. Georgius Crenius, and Jo. Meisnerus*. Traveling to Sweden, he came to *Esdras Edzardus*, and took it upon himself in Copenhagen to instruct the children of

<column-break/>

a certain court official. Having returned to Hamburg and been taken into the house of Edzard, he directed the studies of three sons for three years. Afterward, he taught Oriental Languages <note>Likely Hebrew, Aramaic, and Syriac</note> at Leipzig, and at Wittenberg, he refined the only son of Calovius in Oriental literature. Having traveled to Strasbourg, he heard *Sebastian Schmidt* and *Balthasar Bebel*. He was a court preacher here to the Illustrious Prince of Palatinate-Veldenz, *Leopold Ludwig*, but after a year, he was appointed by the Illustrious Margrave of Baden-Durlach as preacher in St. Stephen’s Church and Professor of the Holy Language <note>Hebrew</note> at Durlach. He entered into marriage with *Sabina Helena*, daughter of the very noble *Michael Praunius*, Doctor of Both Laws <note>Civil and Canon Law</note> and Court Councilor to his Highness; by her, he fathered four children, of whom the father was survived by *Maria Helena*, married to *Wilhelm Balthazar Wagnerus*, Minister of the Divine Word at Crumstadt, and *Joh. Henr. Majus*, Professor of Greek Antiquities and Oriental Languages at Giessen. He was called to Giessen in the year 1689 to the university teaching post in the Holy Languages; the dignity of Chief Court Preacher was also conferred upon him. He was so satisfied with these offices that he declined the office of General Superintendent in East Frisia, as well as that of Ecclesiastical Councilor and Overseer at Berlin, and likewise that of first theologian and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Kiel, which were offered to him. His first wife having died, he married in the year 1702 *Anna Clara Hoffman*, widow of *Antonius Raumburger*, Licentiate in Both Laws and city clerk at Frankfurt, by whom he had four children, all of whom, with the mother who died in 1716, preceded him in death. In the year 1717, he chose his third spouse, *Sophia Margaretha*, daughter of *Johann Christoph Holzhaussus*, a preacher at Frankfurt. After a preceding inflammation of the kidneys and an abscess having broken through, he died on the 13th Sunday after Trinity, 1719, in the 66½ year of his age. *Bremer Boekz. V. Cl. p. 298.*

### DANIEL GUILIELMUS MOLLERUS
Born in Pressburg <note>Modern-day Bratislava, Slovakia</note> in Hungary on May 26, 1642. His father was *Otto*, a goldsmith from Brunswick; his mother was *Rebecca Berghammerin* from Linz in Austria. While the plague was raging in his fatherland, he went to Trenčín in Bohemia and to Nagymagyar in Hungary to learn languages; afterward, he laid the foundations of the liberal arts and philosophy at the preparatory school in Pressburg. In the year 1661, he traveled through Austria, Moravia, Bohemia, and Saxony to reach Leipzig, and then Wittenberg, where he was a houseguest <note>original: "tafelgenoot"</note> of *Quenstedt* for several months. From there, he traveled to Copenhagen with the Saxon embassy; returning to Wittenberg, he completed his studies under the teachers *Kirchmayer*, *Baier*, *Walther*, and others. Departing from here for the Netherlands and England, he later traveled through Silesia, Poland, and Prussia, arriving in Strasbourg in 1666. There he heard the lecturers *Schmid*, *Bebel*, *Boeckler*, and *Scheid*; he also held lectures himself on logic, metaphysics, rhetoric, poetry, and chiromancy <note>Hand-reading or palmistry</note>. For a time, he was the supervisor of the three sons of *Moggius*, the Magistrate and head of the schools in Colmar. He also practiced chemistry <note>original: "Stofscheikunst"</note> for three months under the guidance of *Pieter du Pont*. After traveling through all of Switzerland, he returned to Strasbourg, and later reached Rome by way of France, Savoy, and Italy. In 1667, he was present there for the coronation of *Clement IX*. From Rome, he departed for Naples. Returning again to Rome, he was granted an audience with the Pope himself through the influence of Cardinal *Ernest, Landgrave of Hesse*. From there, via Venice, Trento, Augsburg, Ulm, Munich, Ingolstadt, and Regensburg, he returned to Pressburg in November 1670. After traveling through Hungary, he was promoted to the Sub-rectorate at the school of his fatherland. When persecution broke out, he was sent on behalf of the city of Pressburg to the Imperial Court. From Vienna, he came to Nuremberg by way of Moravia, Bohemia, and the Upper Palatinate. Having detoured to Frankfurt for the sake of *Spener* <note>Philipp Jakob Spener, the "Father of Pietism"</note>, and being called to the office of Court Preacher at *Birkenfeld* on Spener's recommendation, he declined the opportunity because he would have had to follow the army. Returning to Nuremberg in November 1674, he was appointed Professor of History and Metaphysics, a position he preferred over an invitation to become Co-rector at Brzeg in Silesia with the promise of succeeding to the Rectorate. In 1675, he married *Anna Sibylla Braun*, who passed away on August 15, 1691. In October 1692, he celebrated his second marriage to *Helena Sibylla*, daughter of the great *Joh. Christoph Wagenseil*. I myself was present at this stately and honorable wedding. He was a man of manifold learning, of very abundant reading, and a living example of piety and sincerity. His final fate was brought on by a very painful urinary condition <note>original: "koudepis," likely referring to strangury or bladder stones</note>, followed by a wasting of the fluids, internal heat, consumption, and after consumption, death; on February 25, 1712.

*History of the Magi Worshipping CHRIST.* The defender was *Joh. Christoph Mayer* of Nuremberg. Altdorf, by Henr. Mayer. 1688. Quarto.

*Dissertation on Moses the Philosopher.* The defender was *Georg Jacob Schwindel*, of Nuremberg. Altdorf. 1707. Quarto.

*Oration on the Babylonian Confusion of Tongues*, delivered at Wittenberg.

<header>OF THE AUTHORS.</header>

# FRANCIS MONCAEJUS.
->from Vreudenthal.<-

*A most accurately considered and explained history of two divine appearances: that of the Burning Bush, and the next, which occurred to Moses in the inn as he returned to Egypt. A specimen of a larger work long striving for the light and soon (1699) to break forth, which shall be titled and themed "On Divine Appearances."* <note>original: "Apparitionum divinarum duarum... Historia accuratissimè considerata & explicata..."</note> Found in the *Library of Philological History*, Volume IX, page 257.

# STEPHAN MORINUS.

Minister of the Divine Word and Professor at Amsterdam, born in Caen in Normandy in 1625. He laid the foundations of his education there and also at Sedan. He served as a Minister in Caen and was an assistant to Bochart <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a renowned French Protestant biblical scholar and geographer</note>. Because of his religion, he fled to the Netherlands in the year 1685. He was appointed French Minister and Professor of Oriental Languages in Amsterdam and passed away on May 5, 1700.

*Dissertation on the Hours of the Saving Passion of JESUS CHRIST our LORD* <note>original: "Diss: de Horis salvificæ Passionis..."</note>, at Leiden, 1686, Quarto.

*Description of Paradise according to the mind of Bochart.* <note>original: "Descriptio Paradisi ad mentem Bocharti."</note>

# HADRIAN MORLANDUS.

*On Paradise.* <note>original: "De Paradiso."</note> In the first part of the *Miscellaneous Dissertations*, Utrecht, 1706.

# HENRY MULLER.

Born in Lübeck in 1631, he laid his foundations in Oriental Philology and Philosophy at Rostock. From there he went to Greifswald in the year 1647 and stayed for three years. In Leipzig, he benefited from the instruction of Carpzov, Hülseman, and Geier; in Wittenberg, from Calovius and Meisner. Returning to Rostock in 1653, he was made Archdeacon of St. Mary's Church, and six years later, Professor of the Greek Language. In 1660, he was honored with the doctoral laurel <note>received his doctorate</note> at Helmstädt. In 1662, he was called to the dignity of Superintendent and the pastorate of St. Mary's Church in Hamburg, and shortly thereafter to the Professorship of Theology. Having declined several other calls, he finally accepted the dignity of Superintendent at Lübeck in 1671, where he died four years later.

*History of the Passion, Crucifixion, and Burial of our Lord JESUS CHRIST, illustrated with Theological-Historical-Critical Notes.* <note>original: "Historia Passionis, crucifixionis & Sepulturæ Domini nostri..."</note>

# ANDREW MULLER.

Surnamed Greiffenhagen, a very famous man of letters, born in Greiffenhagen in 1630. At the age of 16, he wrote Hebrew, Greek, and Latin verses. Having completed his studies at Rostock, Greifswald, and Wittenberg, he was called to the Rectorship at Königsberg, and later to the pastorate at Treptow. Leaving that post, he traveled to London on the advice of Walton and Castellus <note>Brian Walton and Edmund Castell, editors of the London Polyglot Bible</note>, where he assisted these men in the work of the *Polyglot Bible* <note>A Bible containing the text in several ancient languages in parallel columns</note> and the Lexicon for ten years. A proof of his singular focus on the work was that he did not even look out his window to see the solemn entry of Charles II. Having returned to Germany, he obtained the pastorate at Bernau in the Middle March and finally became Provost at Berlin in 1667. Resigning this position of his own accord, he departed for Stettin on February 11, 1685, so that he might devote himself entirely to Oriental languages, especially Chinese. Falling into a very painful illness, in a state of delirium he sacrificed his very best manuscripts—among which was perhaps his "Chinese Key" <note>A legendary lost work intended to simplify the learning of the Chinese language</note>—to Vulcan <note>Meaning he burned them</note>. He passed away on October 26, 1694, and he gifted his Chinese printing equipment to the Library of Berlin in grateful recognition of favors received.

*Disquisition on the Passion Eclipse.* <note>original: "De Eclipsi Passionali Disquisitio."</note>

<column-break/>

# JOHANNES MULLER, of Nuremberg.

*Elisha, a Prophet at the sound of Music. 2 Kings 3:15.* <note>original: "Eliseus ad Musices sonum Propheta."</note> The presiding officer was Dr. Johann Andreas Schmidt, Abbot of Marienthal, Doctor of Theology and Professor. At Helmstädt by Georg Wolfgang Hamm, 1715, Quarto.

# NICOLAUS MULLER,
->Professor of Medicine and Mathematics.<-

*The Luni-Solar Year of the Jews and the purely Lunar Year of the Turk-Arabs. Each recently derived from its own sources and connected to the Roman Year by an easy method.* <note>original: "Judæorum Annus Lunæ solaris & Turc-Arabum Annus merè Lunaris..."</note> Groningen, by Johannes Sas, 1630, in folio <note>A large book format</note>.

# ANDREW HERMAN MUNTER,
->From Olterrode in the territory of Hanover.<-

*Disputation on the Crossing of the Israelites through the Jordan.* <note>original: "Disp. de Transitu Israëllitarum per Jordanem."</note> The presiding officer was Dr. Johann Georg Abicht, Professor at Leipzig, by Brandenburger, 1712, Quarto.

# JOHANNES MUSAEUS.

*On the Numbness of Teeth from the strange taste of Sour Grapes.* <note>original: "De Stupore Dentium ex gustu Omphacis alieno."</note> <note>A reference to the biblical proverb in Ezekiel 18:2 regarding the teeth being set on edge</note>

# JOHANN GEORGIUS NEBELIUS,
->Teacher at<-

*Sketch of the Philosophy of Abraham.* <note>original: "Sciagraphia Philosophiæ Abrami."</note> The presiding officer was Dr. Johann Heinrich Majus, Theologian at Giessen. Giessen, 1707.

# CASPAR NEUMANN.

Born in Breslau on September 14, 1648. His father was the City Receiver; his mother was Anna Maria Vierlingen. In place of the art of pharmacy, he turned to his studies after his father's death, which he pursued diligently at the school of St. Mary Magdalene and at Jena. There, Schilter accepted him as a member of the Society of Inquirers, where he gained great acclaim. That university recommended him to Ernest the Pious <note>Duke of Saxe-Gotha</note> to be a traveling preacher for his son, Prince Christian. Upon his return, Duke Frederick appointed him Minister in the Altenburg Court Church. In 1689, he became Deacon of the Church of St. Mary Magdalene in Breslau, and thereafter Head Pastor and Assessor of the Consistory in the year 1697. He was an Overseer and Preacher in St. Elizabeth's Church, and also a Professor in both schools—a learned, pious, and polite man. He died on January 27, 1715.

*Two Physical-Sacred Difficulties: concerning the Gems called Urim and Thummim, and concerning the Food of besieged Samaria.* <note>original: "Biga Difficultatum Physico-Sacrarum..."</note> Breslau, 1707, Quarto.

# NICEPHORUS GREGORAS,

From Byzantium, a brave opponent of the Palamites <note>Followers of Gregory Palamas in a 14th-century theological dispute</note>, condemned at the Synod of Constantinople in the year 1351 by the Patriarch Callistus and other followers of Akindynos. He grew old in the monastery and later passed away in the year of Christ 1359. See Fabricius, *Greek Bibliography*, Book V, chapter 30, page 400. Among his writings are available:

*On the Measure of Noah's Ark. From Origen.* <note>original: "De Mensura Arcæ Noæ. Uit Origenes."</note> In the Baroccian Codex 48. 19.

*To the Logothete concerning the Great Fish, and other Living Creatures.* <note>original: "Ad Logothetam de Magno Pisce..."</note> Possevin in the *Sacred Apparatus*.

# PAUL HENRY NICOLAI.

*On the Symmetry of the Molten Sea of Solomon, for the purpose of vindicating 1 Kings 7:23 from a charge of non-geometry.* <note>original: "De Symmetria Maris Ænei Salomonis..."</note> The defender was Johann Heinrich Stüntzel. Wittenberg, 1717, Quarto.

# BERNHARD NIEUWENTYDT,
->Doctor of Medicine, Mayor of the City of Purmerend in North Holland.<-

*The right use of world-contemplations, for the conviction of atheists and unbelievers.* <note>A famous work of natural theology using scientific observations to prove God's existence</note> Amsterdam, 1717, Quarto.

# A. NORRELIUS, a Swede.

*A brief treatise on the Sacred Birds Arbeh, Chagab, Solam, and Chargol, Leviticus 11:21, 22.* <note>original: "Schediasma de Avibus Sacris..." these Hebrew terms refer to types of locusts or leaping insects permitted for food</note> In the *Bremen Bibliography*, Class III, page 36.

# LIST OF NAMES

JOHANNES OLDERMANN.
*Dissertation on Ophir and Tarshish.* <note>original: "Differt. de Ophir & Tharfis." Ophir and Tarshish are biblical locations famous for their wealth and gold.</note> Helmstedt 1714. Quarto.

CONRADUS OLDIUS
*Dissertation on the dwelling, food, and clothing of John.* <note>original: "Diff: de domicilio, victu & amictu Johannis." Referring to John the Baptist.</note> To be found in Crenius's *Fasciculus V. Philological and Historical Exercises.*

### ORIGEN
An Alexandrian, wondrously experienced in Philosophy and all Human Learning. He was born around the year of CHRIST 186, in the 6th year of the Emperor Commodus. His father was Leonidas, who underwent Martyrdom in the year of CHRIST 202. After he had explained the secular and sacred Scriptures in his fatherland since his eighteenth year of age, he resigned from his teaching position in grammar and succeeded his teacher Clement of Alexandria in the office of Catechist, or public Minister of Inquiry, until around the year of CHRIST 231. At age 46, driven out of Alexandria by the hatred of Bishop Demetrius, he stayed for some time thereafter in Caesarea, where around the year of CHRIST 228 he was ordained as an Elder (*Presbyter*) by Alexander and Theoctistus, Bishops of that region. Around the year of CHRIST 218, Julia Mamaea, mother of the Emperor Alexander Severus, summoned him to Antioch, desiring to be instructed by him, since which time he also became known through letters to Philip the Arab and his spouse Severa. Meanwhile, plagued in many ways by a pressing persecution under Maximus and greatly under Decius, and forced to flee to many places, he finally passed away in Tyre in the year of our Lord 253, in the 70th year of his age, a little before the death of Gallus and Volusianus. A man, according to the judgment of Athanasius cited by Socrates in Book VI, 13, of his histories, called *Wonderful and most industrious*, <note>original Greek: "Thaumafios kai Philoponootatos"</note> for which reason he was also called *The Adamantine, The Labor-Lover, The Brazen-Gutted, The Arranger, The Compendium.* <note>original Latin/Greek: "Adamantius, Philoponus, Chalcenterus, Suntakteys, Suntakteyrion." These nicknames refer to Origen's legendary stamina for work and study.</note> Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, Chapter 1, page 213.

Among the works of Origen currently available are:
*Homily on 1 Kings 28 regarding the Ventriloquist.* <note>original: "Homilia in 1. Reg. XXVIII. de Engaftrimytho." This refers to the story of the Witch of Endor.</note> This came to light with the translation of Leo Allatius at the end of *Eustathius on the Hexaemeron* at Lyon, 1629. Quarto. Reprinted in the *Critica Sacra* in London, 1660. Folio. Part VIII.

*Interpretation of Hebrew Names of Holy Scripture and Measures.* <note>original: "Hebraicorum Nominum S. Scripturæ & Menfurarum interpretatio."</note> This was first published in Greek by Joh. Martianay with his own translation and that translated by Jerome, in Part II of the works of Jerome in Paris, 1699. Folio. See Fabricius, page 223.

JOHANNES BAPTISTA OTTIUS.

Halma 1702. Octavo.

Casp. Haferung, Doctor and Professor of Theology: at Wittenberg by Gerdes. 1716. Quarto.

Class I. Volume II. page 60.

PHILIPPUS OUZEEL.
Teacher of Medicine and Theology, and Professor of the latter at Frankfurt on the Oder. Born in Danzig on October 7, 1671. His father was Michael Ouzeel, his mother Esther van Haysteen. Tost about through many lands due to the too-early passing of his father and uncle, he finally came to Bremen, utilizing the help of Alersius, Schwelingius, and Haseus; departing from here in the year 1691, he was well-acquainted with learned men in Groningen, Franeker, and Leiden. In the year 1697 he crossed over to England; in 1698 he came home again; in 1706 he went to the Netherlands again, and was made a Doctor of Medicine on July 18, 1709; in 1711 appointed as Minister in Leiden for the High German Congregation; in 1717 called to Frankfurt as Professor of Theology and service as a Reformed Minister. In the year 1719 he entered into a marriage with Anna Christina Ring. Leaving no children behind, he died of a wasting illness after constant short-winded sweats, being also tormented by passing blood, on April 16, 1724. *Bremen Library* Class VIII. page 900.
*Inaugural Dissertation on the Skin Leprosy of the Hebrews.* <note>original: "Diff. Inaug. de Lepra Cutis Hebræorum."</note> Franeker: 1709.

JOH. PASCHIUS, of Ratzeburg in Saxony.

His father was Antonius, first Schoolmaster at Damme, later Professor of Theology...

# OF THE AUTHORS.

<note>This section continues the biography of Jacobus Perizonius, a famous Dutch classical scholar.</note> erudition at Deventer. He primarily dedicated himself to humanistic learning at Leiden in Holland under *Rykius*. Before this, he made use of the instruction of *Gysbertus Cuperus* at Deventer, and of *Johannes Georgius Graevius* at Utrecht. From Delft, where he taught in private, he was called in the year 1680 to the Professorship of Eloquence and History at Franeker; from there in 1693 to Leiden in Holland to the Professorship of History, Eloquence, and the Greek Language, where he passed away on April 6, 1715. By his last will, he bequeathed to the University the sum of 20,000 guilders, as well as his manuscripts and other books.

*Dissertation on the Death of Judas from the word <unclear>to hang oneself</unclear> <note>original: "απαγξασθαι"</note>, in which the passages of Matthew 27:5 and Acts 1:18 are explained and reconciled, and those things which were noted regarding Aelian’s Various History V. 8. are defended.* At Leiden by Joh. du Vivie and Izaak Severinus. 1702. Octavo.

### PHILO.
A Jew, whose fatherland was Alexandria; <unclear>a man famous in all things</unclear> <note>original: "ανηρ τα παντα ενδοξος"</note>, according to Josephus in *Antiquities* XVIII. 10. From a noble and priestly lineage, brother of Alexander Lysimachus, the Alabarch of Alexandria <note>An "Alabarch" was a high-ranking Jewish magistrate or official in Roman Alexandria, often responsible for customs or taxes.</note>, that is, Master of the Scripture and of the Assessments. Having reached many years of age, he was the Head of the embassy of his countrymen to the Roman Emperor Caligula (Cajus) around the year of CHRIST 40. Following Eusebius, Jerome relates in the *Catalog of Ecclesiastical Writers* chapter II that when he had come to Rome for the second time, he had spoken with the Apostle Peter and enjoyed his friendship. However, it seems unbelievable to Basnage that Peter would have come to Rome before the death of Claudius. *Annals* Volume 1, page 499. Fabricius, *Greek Library* IV. Book 4. chapter page 104.

*On the Confusion of Tongues on Genesis XI. 1. page 319.*
*On the Tabernacle.* Is lost.
*On the Animals fit for Sacrifice, and on the kinds of sacrificial animals* page 835.

### HENRICUS PIPPING.
Preacher and Professor at Leipzig, Professor of Holy Theology and Chief Court Preacher at Dresden.
*On Saul cured by Music.* <note>original: "De Saulo per Musicam curato."</note>

### GEORGIUS PISIDES.
Called Pisides after his fatherland <note>Pisidia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>, Deacon of the Great Church at Constantinople, Seal-bearer and Referendary in the Chancellery; whom some mistakenly take for Georgius, who at the end of the ninth century became Archbishop of Nicomedia from being Seal-bearer of Constantinople. Pisides lived around the year of CHRIST 630.

*On the Work of the Creation of the World, an Iambic poem in 1880 verses.*
This work was published in Greek at Rome in 1590, octavo, under the false name of Cyril of Alexandria, under this title: <unclear>Of our father among the saints, Cyril, Patriarch of Alexandria, on the properties of animals and plants, in iambic verses.</unclear> <note>original: "του εν αγιοις πατρος ημων κυριλλου πατριαρχου Αλεξανδρειας περι ζωοοον ιδιοτητος και φυτοων διαστιχοων ιαμβικοων"</note>. But *Frederik Morell* had already published it under the name of Georgius Pisides at Paris in 1585, 5. <note>likely "in quarto" or "in 12mo"</note>, which edition was reprinted at Heidelberg by Commelin in 1596, octavo; it also appears in the collection of Greek Poets at Geneva 1614, in folio, and in the Appendix of the Greek Church Fathers by Bignon at Paris 1624, in folio. Fabricius, *Greek Library* Book V, chapter 16, page 691.

<column-break/>

### PLINY the Elder.
Born in *Verona*, lived in the first century under *Vespasian and Titus*, in whose glowing favor he stood because of his good qualities. Some modern writers do not wish to clear him of ungodliness <note>meaning atheism or naturalism</note>, or at least feel that his customs paved the way for it. He is said to have been suffocated by the smoke and flame of Mount *Vesuvius* in the year 79, when he had approached too close to it in order to observe it.
*Natural History in 37 Books*, edited by *Father Hardouin* at Paris 1685. 5 volumes in Folio.

### HIERONYMUS PRADUS.
A Spaniard from Baeza, enrolled in the Society of the Jesuits in 1572; passed away at Rome in 1592. He taught Theology in his fatherland and at Cordoba. However, his interpretations of *Ezekiel* were completed by *John Baptista Villalpandus*, a Jesuit.

*Explanations of Ezekiel and the Apparatus of the City and Temple, illustrated with commentaries and images. A work divided into three Volumes.*
Vol. I. *Rome, printed by Aloysius Zannetti. 1596. folio.*
Vol. II. *On the Last Vision of Ezekiel by John Baptista Villalpandus, in which the form of the Temple and its vessels is expressed both by commentaries and by many copperplate descriptions. Rome, printed by Ildefonsus Ciacconius, published by Carolus Vullietus, 1604. folio.*
Vol. III. *Apparatus of the City and Temple of Jerusalem, Part I and II. Rome, by the same, 1604. folio.*

### OTTO PHILIPPUS PRAUN,
Of Kempten; Physician-in-Chief to the Reverend Prince, and City Physician there.
*Physico-Anatomical Analysis of Ecclesiastes Chapter 12, in which a living image of the Old Man and of Death is delineated, and illustrated with new Anatomical findings.* The manuscript was shared with the author by his High-Reverence. I have also made use of it to adorn "Spiritual Physics."

### ABRAHAMUS PUNGELER,
Of Düren; Theologian at Herborn. Born May 31, 1679; admitted to the Holy Ministry March 31, 1700. Declared Teacher of Holy Theology May 31, 1701; called to the dignity of Philosophical Professor at the University of Herborn February 27, 1703; to the extraordinary Theological Professorship in 1705; to the ordinary in April 28, 1706; and to the primary one, which is called the Caufeniaan chair, as well as in Church History in 1709. *Bremen Book-Hall*, Class V, page 165.
*Three Dissertations on the History of Creation. Franeker 1701. Quarto.*

### CASPARUS QUESTEL,
Jurist, Councilor to the illustrious Duke of Holstein, serving both the Court and the Consistory of Plön.
*Historical Account of the High Antiquity etc.* Plön 1703.

### JOHAN NICOLAUS QUISTORP.
Teacher of Holy Theology and Professor at Rostock.
*Academic Program, in which he rouses his academic citizens to pious meditations on the sight of our Savior and only King JESUS CHRIST, sweating drops of blood.*

### PAULUS RABE.
Professor of the Greek Language at the University of Königsberg.

# N A M E   L I S T

<margin>Philological Exercise on the Clothing of John the Baptist regarding Matthew 3:4 and Mark 1:6. <note>original: "Exercit. Philol. de Amictu Joannis Baptistæ"</note> The Defender was Christoph Conrad Falk. Königsberg, published by Reusner, quarto, 1693.</margin>
->JO. CHRISTIANUS RABE,<-
->Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine.<-
*On the Spirit of Infirmity, or the Soul of Sicknesses.* <note>original: "De Pneumati atheneias, of van de Zieie der Ziektens." The Greek term "pneuma astheneias" refers to a spirit of weakness, often cited in Luke 13:11.</note> Through which he indicates his Medical and Philosophical Schools.

->JOHANNES RAJUS.<-
<note>Known in English as John Ray (1627–1705), a foundational figure in modern taxonomy and natural history.</note>
Among the most excellent writers who lived in the previous century and investigated and described Natural History, especially the Plant and Animal Kingdoms; an Englishman by nationality. At Cambridge, he completed his studies and received his academic honors, as well as the dignity of the Holy Ministry; however, because he did not conform to the customs of the Episcopal Church, he was excluded from the holy offices. <note>Ray was a non-conformist who resigned his fellowship rather than sign the Act of Uniformity in 1662.</note> Having departed for Italy and other countries of Europe with the Counts *Francis Willoughby* and *Philip Skippon*, he was everywhere a very precise observer of Natural Description; he passed away in 1705 or 1706.
*Three Physico-Theological Discourses concerning: 1. The primitive Chaos and the Creation of the world. 2. The general Deluge, its causes and effects. 3. The dissolution of the world, and future conflagration.* London 1693, octavo; 1697, octavo; 1713, octavo. Expanded in High German, Hamburg 1698, octavo.
*The Existence and the Wisdom of GOD, manifested in the Works of Creation.* <note>original: "L'existence & la Sagesse de DIEU, manifestées dans les Oeuvres de la Creation."</note> Utrecht 1714, octavo. Translated from the English.

->HADRIANUS RELANDUS.<-
<note>Adriaan Reland (1676–1718) was a famed Dutch Orientalist and cartographer.</note>
Born July 7, 1676, in De Rijp in North Holland, his father *Johannes* being a minister there; he followed him to Alkmaar and Amsterdam. Here, under *Francius, de Bie, and Surenhuysen*, he progressed so well that in his 14th year he went to the University of Utrecht, where, having first laid the foundations in Hebrew and Rabbinical studies, he learned the Arabic language under *Henry Syke*. In the year 1696, he went to Leiden. From there, he was called to Lingen for the Professorship in Philosophy and Oriental Languages, which he declined. He was accepted by the Earl of Portland as a tutor for his son. He was declared Professor of Philosophy at Harderwijk in 1699, and immediately thereafter Professor of Oriental Languages at the University of Utrecht, with the King of England promoting this; there, having declined calls to Franeker and Leiden, he passed away on February 5, 1718, from smallpox, leaving behind a son and two daughters.
*Palestine illustrated from Ancient Monuments, Volume II.* <note>original: "Palæstina ex Monumentis Veteribus illustrata"</note> Utrecht, by Willem Broedelet. 1714, quarto. Nuremberg: 1716.

*First Part of Miscellaneous Dissertations. 1. On the Site of the Terrestrial Paradise. 2. On the Red Sea. 3. On Mount Gerizim. 4. On Ophir. 5. On the Cabiri gods. 6. On the ancient Indian Language.* <note>original: "Dissertationum Miscellanearum Pars Prima..."</note> In the same place, 1706, octavo.

->SAMUEL REYHER.<-
Distinguished Predecessor, Professor of Law and Mathematics at the University of Kiel, Councilor to Saxe-Gotha; born April 19, 1635, at Schleusingen in the County of Henneberg. His father was *Andreas*, Rector of the schools at Schleusingen, Lüneburg, and Gotha. At Leipzig in 1654, he heard *Jacobus Thomasius, Philippus Müllerus, and Amadeus Eckholt*. The patron of his studies was *Andreas Winckler*, a councilor and merchant, who made him his traveling companion on his journey to the Netherlands. At Leiden, he heard *Jacob Golius, Nicolaus Goldman, and Frans van Schooten*. Having returned to Gotha and being appointed to instruct the Prince, he was again stirred by the desire to travel to the Netherlands, but stayed in Rinteln because the Plague forbade him from proceeding further. From there, he was called to the Professorship in Mathematics at Kiel in 1665; to that of extraordinary Professor of Law in 1673; to the ordinary post over the Institutes in 1683; and to the Professorship over the Codex in 1692; he passed away on November 22, 1714.

Or: Biblical Wisdom, which is collected from the five Books of Moses, the remaining Holy and Prophetic Books of the Old Testament, and the Evangelical and Apostolic writings of the New Testament; therein is presented a clear explanation of many dark places in Holy Scripture, proven through Mathematical sciences, along with an interpretation of several types found in the Old Testament, and their confirmation through those of the New Testament.* <note>original German: "Biblische Weißheit, welche aus den fünff Büchern Mosis..."</note> At Lüneburg, by Joh. Georg Lipper, 1712, folio. A work begun but not completed.

He was born at Leipzig on December 9, 1652; his father was *Andreas*, Professor of Poetry and later of Physics, and Dean of the University; his mother was *Catharina Elisabeth*, daughter of *Tileman Olearius*, Archdeacon at Halle by Saint Ulrich. ### OF THE AUTHORS.

...[his fa]ther’s side was, in German, *Andreas Bachman*, a Councilor at Halle. In his youth, he was a very brave soldier against the Turks and the Spaniards in *Hungary* and the *Netherlands*. According to the custom of the age, the father of our subject changed his name to *Rivinus*. <note>The name "Bachman" translates to "Man of the Brook"; "Rivinus" is the Latinized version derived from *rivus* (brook).</note> His paternal grandmother was *Dorothea Krebs*, widow of *Jeremias de Compascuis*. His father having been taken from him on April 4, 1656, our *Rivinus* laid the foundations of his scholarship under *Jakob Thomasius, Christian Friedrich Frankenstein, Joachim Feller, Valentin Alberti, Adam Rechenberg*, and others. He was declared a Master of Philosophy on January 15, 1671, while *Johannes Ittig* was Dean. Subsequently, for his instructors in Medical Science, he studied under *Michael Ettmüller, Gottfried Welschius,* and *Johannes Bohnius*. At the University of Helmstedt, on the advice of *Hermann Conringius*, he received the doctoral laurel wreath on October 15, 1676. Returning from there to his native university in 1677, he applied himself to Law and obtained the position of Teacher of Medicine at Leipzig. On July 9, 1688, he was admitted into the Medical Faculty; on March 31, 1691, he obtained the public office to teach Physics (Natural Science), and on April 20, he was entrusted with the oversight of the Medicinal Herb Garden. On February 12, 1701, he was appointed Professor of Pathology and Senior of the Medical Society. Added to this, on February 13, was the dignity of both Fellow in the College of the *Majorum Principum* and Decemvir <note>A member of a ten-man administrative council.</note> of the University on April 23; and on December 13, 1719, the public office of Physician and the Deanship of the Medical Society.

He entered into four marriages: the 1st on October 22, 1677, with *Catharina Sophia de Lange*, who became the mother of *Johanna Catharina* on December 14, 1678, but she died four days after her mother (who had passed on December 20). The 2nd on September 6, 1681, with *Anna Sophia Pinker*, by whom he saw a daughter, *Kristina Sophia*, born far too prematurely and surviving barely three days, followed by the mother in childbed on June 11. The 3rd on September 15, 1685, with *Johanna Margaretha Kuhlewein*, who gave birth to *Johanna Elizabeth* on June 19, 1686, but after barely a year had passed, she left him a widower again on September 14; the little daughter also died shortly thereafter on January 1, 1687. The 4th on February 25, 1690, with *Katharyne Elisabeth Winkler*, by whom he had *Johanna Catharina* on November 11, who was married on July 19, 1710, to *Rudolf Lodewyk Langguth*, Court Commissioner to the most Illustrious King of Poland and Elector of Saxony; by her he saw three grandsons and one granddaughter, though they were deprived of their father and mother. After this daughter, *Winkler* bore him two sons: *Johannes Augustus* on December 18, 1691, and *Augustus* on January 27, 1693, who died on March 19. 

Saddened after so many unfortunate occurrences and weakened in strength, in his old age he was tormented by gravel in the bladder and kidneys <note>Kidney stones.</note>, compounded by a very severe inflammation of the side (*pleurisy*); he ended his life on December 30, 1723, aged 72 years. On January 3, 1724, he was interred in the Pauline burial grounds without a funeral procession, as he had commanded, yet he was nonetheless honored by the University with a publicly posted eulogy. Not long after, his surviving son *Johannes Augustus*, Doctor of Medicine and heir in all things to his father’s virtues, followed him, passing away on May 10, 1725; so that *Quirinus Augustus* now lives on only in his nephews and his learned writings.

*Of the true Age of the World, as well as of our Savior, as clearly proven from the precise agreement of Astronomy with both Sacred and Secular History.* <note>original German: "Vom wahren Alter so wohl der Welt..."</note> Leipzig, published by Philip Wilhelm Stock, 1721, quarto.

->DIONYSIUS ANDREAS ROELL,<-

->R O E S E R.<-

->MICHAEL ROTHARDUS.<-
*Samuel Restored.* <note>original Latin: "Samuel redivivus."</note> In the *Critica Sacra*, Part VI, page 310, of the Frankfurt edition.

->OLAUS RUDBECK,<-
From Uppsala, son of *Olaus*, nephew of *Johannes*, Bishop of the Diocese of Västerås.
*Biblical Ichthyology, Part I: On the Bird Selau, mentioned in Numbers 11:31. In which it is demonstrated with manifest arguments, against Bochart and Ludolf, that it was not a feathered bird, nor a locust, but rather a species of fish; with a short analogy between the Hebrew and ancient Gothic languages added.* <note>original Latin: "Ichthyologiæ Biblicæ Pars I. de Ave Selau..." Rudbeck’s theory that the biblical "quails" were actually fish was highly controversial.</note> Uppsala, 1705, quarto.
*Biblical Ichthyology, Part Two: On the Fullers' Soap (Borith), proving with many significant arguments and reasons that it was not a plant, much less lye or soap, but rather purple dye, from Jeremiah 2:22 and Malachi 3:2.* <note>original Latin: "Ichthyologiæ Biblicæ Pars altera, de Borith Fullonum..."</note> Uppsala, 1722, quarto.

->FRANCISCUS RUEUS,<-
Physician of Lille.
*Two Books on several Gems, especially those mentioned by St. John in the Apocalypse, and others whose use is now widespread among all people: No less useful to Theologians than to Philosophers.* <note>original Latin: "De Gemmis aliquot..."</note> To be found in the book of *Gesnerus* regarding all sorts of things excavated from the earth. Zurich, published by Jacob Gesner, 1568, octavo.

->CLAUDIUS SALMASIUS,<-
Universal man of letters and critic among the most famous, born in 1588 in Burgundy. His father was *Benignus*, Lord of *Saumaise-le-Duc* (a village in Auxois) and a councilor in the Parliament of Dijon; his mother was a Reformed Protestant. *Claudius* had a very precocious mind, which at ten years old sang Latin and Greek verses. Having completed his studies at Paris and Heidelberg, he was called to Leiden in Holland to succeed *Scaliger* as an honorary Professor. Upon his departure for France, Cardinal *Richelieu* offered him an annual salary if he would remain in the Kingdom and write the history of his life. Also summoned by the Queen of Sweden, he stayed an entire summer in Stockholm. Having returned to the Netherlands to take the waters at Spa, he died there two days after his arrival on September 3, 1652. He had earned the hatred of the learned world because he could suffer almost no one to be above him, and he did not spare the greatest men of learning: *Lipsius, Scaliger, Heinsius, Sirmondus, Spanhemius, Grotius, Blondellus, Amyraut, Bochart*.
*On the Cross of Christ, etc. see Bartholinus.*

->JOH. CASPARUS SANTOROCCIUS.<-
Professor at the University of Marburg.
*Certain thoughts on the ASTONISHING MIRACLE OF TONGUES, which occurred in a wonderful manner in Acts 2; wherein it is more accurately investigated, in the form of an Academic Dissertation, whether and how the Apostles alone received the gifts of various tongues at the fulfillment of the day of Pentecost?* <note>original Latin: "Cogitata quædam de STUPENDO LINGUARUM MIRACULO..."</note> Marburg, 1718, octavo.

# LIST OF NAMES

JOHANNES SAUBERTUS,
->Professor at Helmstedt.<-

*A Thorough Report on the German Translation of the Treatise of Jacob Judah Leon regarding Solomon’s Temple recently published in Hanover, as well as against the Untruths committed in said translation.* <note>Original Latin title: *Grundlicher Bericht uber die neulichst zu Hannover ausgegangene Teutsche Dolmetschung des Tractats Jacobi Jehuda Leonis von den Tempel Salomonis...* Jacob Judah Leon (1602–1675) was a famous Jewish scholar known for his detailed models of the Temple.</note> Helmstedt, published by Jacob Müller, 1665. Octavo. *See Leo.*

HENRICUS SCHARBAU,
->Preacher in the Castle Church at Lübeck.<-

*On the Plants included under the Term Pnoëys and those that Respire, for the illustration of the passage in Acts 17:25.* <note>Original: *De Plantis ab Voce Pnoëys comprehensis & respirantibus*. The term *Pnoëys* is a Greek-derived word for "breath" or "wind."</note> In the *Leipzig Miscellany*, Volume V. Leipzig, published by the heirs of Lankisius, 1712. Octavo.

SAMUEL SCHELGVIG.

Born in Lissa, March 1, 1643. His father was Samuel, a preacher at Guraa and Sondewald; he studied at Glogau, Breslau, and Wittenberg; 1667, Assistant Rector and Professor at Thorn; in the year 1673, Professor of <term>First Philosophy and Ethics</term> <note>Original Latin: *Philosophia primæ & Practicæ*.</note> at Danzig; in the year 1675, Extraordinary Professor of Theology. 1681, Preacher in St. Catherine’s Church; 1685, in place of Strauchius, Preacher in the Holy Trinity Church and Rector; also having become a Teacher of Holy Theology in the same year, he turned down <term>Calls</term> <note>Formal invitations to take a prestigious academic or ecclesiastical position.</note> to Stockholm, Riga, Dorpat, Greifswald, Wittenberg, etc. He died in 1715.

*On the Miracle at Siloam, John 5:1–9. Dissertation II.* Danzig, 1681. Quarto.

*A Philological and Theological Exercise on the Statue of Salt from Genesis 19.* The <term>Respondent</term> <note>The student who publicly defended the thesis under the professor's supervision.</note> was *Joh. Laur. Fischer.* Danzig, 1680.

JOHANN GEORGIUS SCHELHORN.

Born in Memmingen, where he laid his academic foundations; in 1712, he departed for Jena; 1714, to Altdorf. He became a teacher and Keeper of the Public Library, as well as a Vicar of the Holy Service in his birth city. He is the author of the *Literary Pleasantries* <note>Original Latin title: *Amanitates literariæ*.</note>.

*An Observation on the "Fish-Spears" of Job 40:26.* <note>Original Hebrew: צלצל דגים (*Tsiltsal Dagim*). This refers to a difficult passage in Job (sometimes numbered 41:7 in English bibles) regarding harpoons or spears used for hunting aquatic creatures.</note> In the *Bremen Library*, Class IV, Part III, page 572.

JOHANN JACOB SCHEUCHZER.

The author of this present SACRED PHYSICS, was born on August 4, 1672. His father, *Johannes Jacobus*, the City Physician of Zurich, fell asleep godly of a burning fever in the 42nd year of his age, most painfully mourned by all upright men, his surviving widow, mother, sons, and daughters. His mother, *Barbara Fesin*, is by God's singular grace still alive in the 77th year of her age, being a daughter of *Johannes Fesius*, a Minister of the Divine Word and Director of the Carolinum School. I laid the foundations of the sciences under worthy and faithful teachers: *Rodolphus Hospitalerus, Henricus Nüzlinus, Rodolphus Hospinianus, Jacobus Huldricus*, and my aforementioned and dearly beloved maternal grandfather. Under the Professors *Rodolphus Hofmeisterus* the Elder, *Jacobus Lavaterus, Henricus Hottingerus, Henricus Frisius* in the so-called preparatory school of *Human Wisdom*. But in the higher schools under *Joannes Henr. Heideggerus, Joann. Casp. Wolphius, Joann. Lavaterus, Joann. Henr. Suicerus, Rodolph. Ottius, Henr. Lavaterus, Joann. Herrlibergerus*, and—whom I must name first—*Salomon Hottingerus*. To these I must add myself, seeing as I taught myself most of my literary exercises, having handled them according to my own thoughtful perception. On April 9, 1692, I ventured among foreigners in the company of *Jacob Cramer* (afterwards Professor of Oriental Languages and Theology at Herborn) and *Jacob Reutlinger* (currently a Canon in the Chapter

<column-break/>

of Thuringia): I came to Altdorf, where my patrons and instructors were *Wagenseilius, Maurit. Hofmannus* (father and son), *Pancratius Bruno*, and *Jo. Christoph. Sturmius*. In July of the year 1693, I went from Altdorf to the Netherlands, and heard *Jacob Vallan* and *Joh. Munniks* at Utrecht, and was made a Doctor of Medicine on January 26, 1694, by the aforementioned *Vallan*. Thereafter I toured the Netherlands; took my way through Friesland, Hamburg, the Brandenburg lands, Lower and Upper Saxony, Bohemia, Bavaria, and Franconia, and arrived home quite happily. I also completed my first Alpine journey in this year. In the year 1695, I visited Nuremberg and Altdorf once more, with the intention of advancing further in Mathematics under *Sturm* and *Eimmart*. When I returned home from there, I was accepted among the City Physicians and was assured by the Most Honorable Council in my hope for a Professorship in Mathematics. After this, on November 9, 1697, I entered the state of marriage with my heart’s beloved spouse, *Susanna Vogelius*, daughter of *Kaspar Vogelius* (one of the <term>Council of Two Hundred</term>) and *Margaretha Ottin*. Through God’s goodness, three of our sons are still living: *Johann Jacob*, in the military service of Their High Mightinesses the Lords States General <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note>; *Johannes*, a Minister of the Divine Word at Suamendingen; and *David*, who has learned the art of copper engraving. I cannot think of my fourth son without great sadness, as he died in the year 1729 in London, in the house of my great patron and benefactor, the well-born Knight *Hans Sloane* <note>Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753), whose massive collection formed the core of the British Museum.</note>, whom the learned world sensibly misses. I add no further matters concerning myself here, lest I should seem as if I were of a mind to praise myself, intending only to list the samples of my labor which pertain to this present subject.

*The Sacred Physics of Job, or Job’s Natural Science compared with that of today.* Zurich, 1721. Quarto.

*Herbal of the Flood.* <note>Original: *Herbarium Diluvianum*.</note> Second edition, twice as extensive as the first. At Leiden, at the expense of *Pieter vander Aa*, 1723. Folio. The first came to light at my own expense in Zurich, published by Conrad Gesner, 1709.

*The Complaints and Defenses of the Fishes.* Zurich, published by Gesner, 1708. Quarto. <note>A satirical work where fossilized fish complain about being ignored by mankind.</note>

*Oration on the Use of Mathematics in Theology.* Zurich, at the expense of *Joh. Finstler*, from the press of Hardmeyer, 1711. Quarto.

*Museum of the Flood*, published by Bodmer at Zurich, 1716. Octavo.

*Oration on the Miracles of Christ’s Passion.* Manuscript.

*A Specimen of Sacred Physics concerning Locusts.* Respondents: *Joh. Henr. Maagius* and *Joh. Jac. Cellarius.* Zurich, published by Heidegger and Rahn, 1724. Quarto.

*Man as a Witness of the Flood and a Seer of God.* <note>Original: *Homo Diluvii testis & Theoskopos*. This refers to Scheuchzer's famous (and mistaken) identification of a giant salamander fossil as a human who perished in the biblical Flood.</note> Respondents: 13 Candidates in Philosophy. Zurich, published by Henr. Byrgklin, 1726. Quarto.

*Specimen of a Biblical-Physical Work on Exodus 20:1–7.* Defenders were *Franc. Kauffman* and *Joann. Casp. Hessius.* From the same press, 1727. Quarto.

PHILIPPUS CASIMIRUS SCHLOSSER.

### JOH. GEORG. SEIDEL.
*Dissertation on Saul illuminated after being deprived of the light of his eyes for three days, concerning Acts 9*. <note>Refers to the conversion of St. Paul on the road to Damascus.</note> Jena, 1702.

### JOH. JACOBUS SEIFERHELD,
->from Halle in Swabia.<-

*Philological Defense of the passage in Judges 15:15 concerning the Jawbone of an Ass, in which the unfair false interpretation of the Halle observer is refuted, and the version of Blessed Luther is defended*. <note>Original Latin title: *Vindiciæ Philologicæ Loci Jud. XV. 15. de Maxilla Asini...* This relates to Samson’s feat of strength.</note> Tübingen, by Job Frankius, 1716, in quarto.

### JOH. PHILIPPUS SESEMANN.
->from Naumburg.<-

*Dissertation on the Stone Knives used in the circumcision re-instituted by Joshua, Joshua 5:2*. The chairman was Dr. Joh. Georg Abicht, Professor. Leipzig, by Brandenburger, 1712, in quarto.

### SEVERIANUS.
Bishop of Gabala, a native Syrian, an eloquent and learned man, to whom John Chrysostom showed much friendship, for whom he obtained the Emperor's favor, and to whom he even entrusted his congregation during a journey to Ephesus. <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an important Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople.</note> However, because Severianus was not faithful to him and drew the listeners entirely away from him, they became enemies, and Chrysostom rebuked him, eventually driving him out of Constantinople. He passed away, after further deeds, during the time of Theodosius the Younger, whom he had baptized, in the year of Christ 408. *Fabricius, Greek Library, Book V, Chapter 34, page 267.*

From his sermons, the 14th on Genesis 6, *on the Creation of the World*, <note>Greek: *eis Kosmopoiian*.</note> was published in Greek among the writings of St. Chrysostom, Volume VII, page 587, by Henry Savile; and in Greek and Latin by Frant. Combefis in the *Addition to the Library of the Fathers*, Volume 1, page 211. Paris, 1672, in folio.

### JOHANNES SIMON.
->Adjunct of the Philosophical Faculty, Rector of the School at Wittenberg.<-

*The Variegated Offspring of Sheep produced by the work of the Patriarch Jacob, considered in its natural causes*. <note>Refers to Genesis 30, where Jacob used peeled branches to breed spotted or speckled sheep from Laban's flock.</note> The defender being Johannes Ernestes Weber, of Dresden; at Wittenberg by Matth. Henckel, 1675, in quarto.

### CHRISTIANUS FRIDERICUS SINNER,
->from Leipzig, Teacher at Weisbach.<-

*On the Nakedness of the First Parents, concerning Genesis 2:25*. To be found in the *Leipzig Miscellany*, Volume 1: at Leipzig by the heirs of Lankisius, 1716, in octavo.

### JUSTUS SOEFFING.
*History of the Creation of the World with Chronological and Theological Notes*. Rudolstadt, 1667, in quarto.

### CHRISTOPH. SONNTAG,
->Doctor of Holy Theology and Professor at the University of Altdorf.<-

Born at Weida in Vogtland in 1654. Declared Master at Jena in 1674. In that same year, appointed as overseer to the sons of the Count of Ronou and Biberstein; two years later, a preacher at Oppurg; 1685, Superintendent at Schleusingen; 1690, Professor of Theology and Overseer of the University of Altdorf, having first been honored with the title of Doctor at Jena. He was particularly skilled in Greek, a language he had also taught at Altdorf; I have even heard him deliver orations in Greek. He passed away in 1717.

*Dissertation on Shittim Wood*. <note>Shittim (acacia) wood was used to build the Ark of the Covenant.</note>

<column-break/>

### GODOFREDUS SPROTTA.
*Dissertation on the Longevity of the Patriarchs*. <note>Refers to the long lifespans of biblical figures such as Methuselah.</note> Leipzig, 1668.

### JOHANNES STENGEL.
Born at Mercklingen, in the territory of Ulm, 1694, where his father Johannes was a preacher and his mother was the daughter of the learned school governor at Ulm, Guilielmus Diezius. He studied at Ulm and Altdorf, where he became a Master and held lectures; he died as a candidate for the Holy Ministry at Ulm in 1729.

*Observations on the Biblical Juniper to illustrate three passages of Scripture: 1 Kings 19:4, 5; Job 30:4; Psalm 120:4. In the Bremen Book-room, Class VII, page 856.*

### CHRISTIANUS VAN STOOKEN.
->Court Preacher to the Most Illustrious Bishop of Lübeck and Superintendent.<-

*Inaugural Disputation on the Flowering Rod of Aaron*. <note>Refers to the miracle in Numbers 17.</note> The chairman was Christian Koitholt, Doctor of Holy Theology and Professor. Wittenberg, 1685.

### JOH. MAURITIUS STHOR.
*The Apples of Sodom to illustrate Wisdom 10:7. Leipzig, 1695, in quarto.* <note>The "Apples of Sodom" were legendary fruits that looked tempting but supposedly dissolved into smoke and ash when tasted.</note>

### ÆGIDIUS STRAUCHIUS,
Licentiate in Holy Theology, Professor of Mathematics, born at Wittenberg on February 21, 1632, to Johannes, a legal scholar, who was taken from him when he was barely seven years old. At Leipzig, he applied himself to humanistic studies, Oriental languages, and philosophy, as well as theology. Having returned to Wittenberg at the end of 1650, he was made a Master of Arts on April 28, 1651; two years later, an adjunct of the Philosophical Faculty, and for 16 years an associate and extraordinary Professor in the lower mathematics. On October 13, 1662, he was declared a teacher of theology; in 1664, Professor of History; and in 1666, associate of the Theological Faculty. Called to the Rectorship at Stettin, to the High Professorship at Eperies, and to the Rectorship at Danzig in 1669, along with the office of Professor of Theology and the ministry, which call he accepted. However, difficulties arose from the disputes which he heatedly maintained with the Catholics and the Reformed, such that he preferred to choose the call to Hamburg, and later the theological professorship offered to him at the University of Greifswald. When he intended to assume this position, he was taken prisoner at Küstrin by the Elector of Brandenburg, but was released through the intercession of the Kings of Sweden and Poland and the people of Hamburg. He then traveled to Danzig, where he behaved somewhat more cautiously regarding the disputes, and ended his life in 1682.

*Historical-Chronological Dissertation on the Sacred Calculation of the 70 Weeks of Daniel*. Defended by Petrus Gödtkens of Hamburg. Wittenberg, 1660; found in the *Historical, Critical, and Philological Dissertations, Volume I, page 393.*

*On the Birth of the World*. Wittenberg, 1652, in quarto.

*On the Time of the Flood*. Wittenberg, 1653, in quarto.

*On the Year of Abraham's Birth, his calling, and the 430 years of the Israelites' stay in Egypt, from Exodus 12:40*. Wittenberg, 1653, in quarto.

*On the Passover of the Crucifixion*, which immediately followed the same... <note>Original Latin: *De Paschatos Staurosimou*. This refers to theological debates regarding the timing of the Last Supper and the Crucifixion in relation to the Jewish Passover.</note>

### LEONH. CHRISTOPH. STURMIUS,
Son of Johann Christoph. <note>Leonhard Christoph Sturm (1669–1719) was a prominent German philosopher and architect who sought to reconcile biblical descriptions with architectural theory.</note>

*Architectural Outline of the Temple of Jerusalem from the sources of the Holy Scriptures themselves, especially from Ezekiel's final vision; prepared in an architectural manner, yet so that those ignorant of architecture may also read it; further illustrated here and there with modest observations on Villalpando and figures engraved in copper.* <note>Original Latin title starts: *Sciagraphia Templi Hierofolymitani...* Juan Bautista Villalpando was a famous Jesuit whose massive work on the Temple was the standard reference Sturm was critiquing.</note> At Leipzig by Joh. Willem Kruger 1694, in quarto. Against this book was published:

*Epistolary Critique addressed to a friend residing at the Academy of Strasbourg, sent from Tübingen, concerning the Architectural Outline of the Temple of Jerusalem delineated a few weeks prior from the sources of the Holy Scriptures themselves, especially from Ezekiel's final vision.* <note>Original Latin title starts: *Epicriſis Epiſtolica...*</note> Strasbourg, in quarto.

*A specimen of Mathematics applied to the Interpretation of Holy Scripture, in which the Bronze Sea, or the Colossal Fountain of Solomon, is explained by means of Arithmetic, Geometry, Stereometry, Civil Architecture, Mechanics, Geography, and the arts of Hydraulics, Sculpture, and Casting, so that it might not only be perfectly reconstructed, but also...* <note>Original Latin title starts: *Matheſis ad Sacræ Scripturæ...* The "Bronze Sea" or "Molten Sea" was a large basin in the Temple of Solomon described in 1 Kings 7.</note>

1. *The most vexing doubts regarding its movement are dispelled by a genuine demonstration.*
2. *Other matters hitherto suppressed in silence are brought forward and solidly resolved.*
3. *Various opinions of authors are partly reconciled and partly dismissed using a selective and modest method of critique.*
4. *Remnants of Jewish Antiquity are placed in a new light, while others are newly discovered.*
5. *Both Philology and Mathematics are enhanced by new observations.*
6. *The Solomonic prerogatives are asserted above the magnificence of all other Kings.*
7. *Finally, the Typical significance of the Bronze Sea is more certainly determined.*

*All illustrated with copper plates, skillfully engraved in copper.* Nuremberg, at the author's expense by Joh. Leonh. Buggel. 1710, in octavo.

*Understandable Explanation of Holy Scripture, etc.* <note>Original German: *Verſtandliche Erklarung Heil. Schrift enz.*</note>

### THEODORE, surnamed Mopsuestia,
Born of illustrious and wealthy parents in Antioch, brother of Polychronius, Bishop of Apamea, and a close friend of John Chrysostom. Following the example of the latter, he embraced the monastic life while still very young around the year 369. In the episcopal dignity of Mopsuestia, a city in Cilicia, he succeeded Olympus around the year 394. He died in 429. <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia was a leading representative of the Antiochene school of hermeneutics, which favored literal rather than allegorical interpretation of the Bible.</note>

*On the Hexaëmeron, or Commentary on the Creation*, <note>Original Greek: *In Hexaëmeron of hermeyneian teys ktiſeoos*.</note> an explanation of the six-day Creation, a work divided into seven parts. *Photius* makes mention of it in Code 38. Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Book V, chapter 33, pages 153, 159.

### THYMUS.
*Dissertation on the Bronze Basin.* <note>Original Latin: *Diſſertatio de Labro Æneo*. This refers to the washing basin used by priests in the Tabernacle.</note>

### MICHAEL CHRISTIANUS TIEROFF.
*Disputation on the Statue of Salt.* <note>Original Latin: *Diſp. de Statua Salis*. Refers to the story of Lot’s wife in Genesis 19.</note> Jena 1657, in quarto.

### SALOMON van TILL,
Born 1644 in Weesp, a small town two hours from Amsterdam. He laid the foundations of his studies in Alkmaar and Utrecht, under Burman, Voetius, and others; and in Leiden under Heidanus and Cocceius. In his 21st year, he was called as a Minister to Helder and Huisduinen in North Holland, thereafter to De Rijp, to Medemblik, and as Teacher at Dordrecht. Here he became Professor of Holy Histories and Sacred Literature in 1702. He was made Professor of Holy Theology at Leiden, where he died on October 31, 1713. <note>The OCR says 1731, but historically Salomon van Till died in 1713. This may be a typo in the original text or transcription.</note>

<column-break/>

*Dissertation on the Location of Paradise, subjoined to the illustrated Malachi.* <note>Original Latin: *Diſſ. de Situ Paradiſi, Malachiæ illuſtrato ſubjuncta*.</note> Leiden 1701.
*Commentary on the Tabernacle of Moses* — *Sacred Zoology.* <note>Original Latin: *Commentarius de Tabernaculo Moſis* and *Zoologia Sacra*.</note>

### M. AUGUSTUS TITTELIUS.
*On the Camel passing through the eye of a needle, regarding Matthew 19:24. In the Leipzig Miscellany, Part V, by the heirs of Lanckisius 1717, in octavo.* <note>Original Latin: *De Camelo per foramen acus tranſeunte...*</note>

### JOHANNES TOLANDUS.
The natural son <note>Meaning illegitimate son.</note> of a Roman Catholic priest, born under an unlucky star in the year 1671 in Ireland, and raised in the Roman Catholic religion. In his 15th year, he read the Greek and Latin writers, primarily Livy. In his 16th year, he converted to the Non-Conformists. He laid the foundations of his studies at the seminary in Red-Castle, near Londonderry; from there he went in 1687 to the University of Glasgow, and later to Edinburgh, where he took the title of Master in 1690. From here he traveled to England and the Netherlands, having received instruction from Friedrich Spanheim. Having returned to England in 1695, he sought to undermine the foundations of the Christian religion and to mock it in public social circles and revelries, to which he was inclined. As a promoter of the sect of the Tolandists, he was banished by public Acts of Parliament. As his religious affairs went poorly, he joined the Republicans and published the writings of Milton, and later also those of Harrington. In the year 1702, he traveled to Hanover, Berlin, and Holland, where he died on March 21, 1722. <note>John Toland (1670–1722) was a controversial rationalist philosopher and freethinker whose book *Christianity Not Mysterious* sparked a major outcry.</note>

*Hodegus, one of four dissertations in the Tetradymus, in which he wishes to prove that the column of Cloud and Fire was a portable fire, and nothing miraculous.* <note>Original Latin title starts: *Hodegus, una ex quatuor...* Toland argued that the pillar of fire was merely a brazier carried at the head of the caravan.</note> London 1720. Against which appeared:

*Hodegus confuted in a plain demonstration, that the Pillar of a Cloud and Fire was not a Fire of human preparation but the most miraculous presence of God.* London 1721, in octavo.

The English title of Toland's treatise is:

*Hodegus, or the Pillar of Cloud and Fire, that guided the Israelites in the Wilderness, not miraculous, but as faithfully related in Exodus and equally practiced by other Nations, and in those places not only useful, but necessary.*

### LUCAS TOZZI.
*Physical Questions drawn from Holy Scripture.* <note>Original Latin: *Quæſtiones Phyſicæ ex Sacris Literis depromptæ*.</note>

### ABDIAS TREW.
Professor of Physics and Mathematics at Altdorf. He was born in Ansbach in 1597. He took the degree of Master at Wittenberg in 1621; thereafter he was a Deacon at Merckelbach and Rector of the school at Ansbach. Leaving this post on account of his numerous family, being the father of 21 children, he obtained the Professorship of Mathematics at the University of Altdorf in 1636, and in 1650, the Professorship of Physics. He died in 1669.

*A Theological-Philosophical Examination of the Anti-Biblical Hyper-sophistry of those who: 1. Deny the Mosaical waters above the heavens, as Matthias Flacius did and sought to defend before certain modern philosophers. 2. Make the universal flood a local one, as Isaac Vossius does. 3. Attribute the motion of the Sun and other stars to the Earth, as most modern astronomers do following Nicolaus Copernicus.* <note>Original Latin title starts: *Examen Theologico Philoſophicum...* This work shows the 17th-century resistance to the Copernican system and the "local flood" theory based on a literal reading of Genesis.</note> Nuremberg 1667, in quarto, by Phil. Miltenberger.

### ADAMUS TRIBBECHOVIUS.
Born in Lübeck on August 11, 1641. His father was Justus, an official of the student school in Lübeck; his mother was Anna, daughter of Adam Helmius, an elder in the Lübeck church service.

# OF THE AUTHORS.

He arrived at the Academy in Rostock in 1659. From there, he went to the universities of Wittenberg, Leipzig, and Helmstedt, where he continued his studies under *Calixtus, Balthazar Cellarius, Conringius,* and *Schaderus*. He declined invitations to become the Co-Rector at Lübeck and the Rector at Worms. In the year 1662, accompanied by *Antonius Henricus*—the only son of *David Gloxinius*, Burgomaster of Lübeck—he departed for Giessen, where he obtained the wealthy Schabbelian scholarship. In 1664, he was called to Kiel to serve as the Extraordinary Professor of Ethics, and in that same year, he was appointed Ordinary Professor of History. In 1672, he was raised to the dignity of Ecclesiastical Councilor at Gotha, and in 1677, he became the General Superintendent of the church there. Having been tormented by <term>melancholy</term><note>The original Dutch *zwaargeestigheid* refers to a state of severe depression or "black bile," a common diagnosis for scholars of the era.</note> for many years, he passed away on August 17, 1687. He was united in marriage in 1675 to *Sophia Elisabeth*, daughter of *Thomas von Auffen*, a Ducal Overseer, by whom he became the father of several children. See the *Life of Tribbechovius* <note>Justus Tribbechovius (1631–1687) was a German Lutheran theologian.</note> placed before the *Treatise on Scholastic Teachers* by *Tentzelius*.

*The Truth of the Creation of the World, as described by Moses, shown in the Traditions of the Heathen and the most ancient monuments of profane antiquity to convince Atheists*. <note>Original Latin: *Veritas Creationis Mundi, prout a Mose descripta est...*</note> The respondent was Bartholdus Johannes Brammer. Kiel, 1668. Found in *Dist: Hist. Crit. Philolog. Fascic.* page 227.

### LAURENTIUS BENEDICTUS TRIBEL,
->of Gotha.<-

*Philological Disputation on the Magi arriving after Jesus was presented in the Temple*. <note>Original Latin: *Disp. Philol. de Magis post Jesum in Templo repraesentatum advenientibus*.</note> The respondent was Georg Friedrich Schmidt of Gotha. Jena, published by Paulus Ehrich, 1715, in quarto.

### CHRISTIAN GOTTLIEB TROPPANEGER.
*Dissertation on the Dietetic Medicine of Holy Scripture*. <note>Original Latin: *Diss. de Diaetetica Sacrae Scripturae Medicina*.</note> The chairperson was Dr. Friedrich Hoffman. Halle, 1718.

### JOHANNES TSEETSI, Hungarian.
*Aphorisms, in which the Antiquities of the Ancient Hebrews are very briefly presented, published for the use of Scholastic Youth*. <note>Original Latin: *Aphorismi, in quibus Antiquitates Veterum Hebraeorum brevissime exhibentur...*</note> Bern, at the press of the Commonwealth, 1726, in octavo.

### EDWARD TYSON, Physician.
*On Pygmies, Satyrs, Cynocephali & Sphinxes, a commentary to illustrate the passages in Isaiah 13:21 and 34:14*. <note>Original Latin: *De Pygmaeis, Satyris, Cynocephalis & Sphingibus...* Tyson was a pioneer of comparative anatomy; he argued that "pygmies" in the Bible and ancient texts were actually apes.</note> The Latin translation was prepared by *Augustus Tittelius* of Hanover.

### JEAN FOY VAILLANT, the Elder.
*Dissertation on THE YEAR OF JESUS CHRIST discovered through ancient Medals*. <note>Original French: *Dissertation sur L'ANNEE DE JESUS CHRIST decouverte par les Medailles antiques*.</note> *Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions*. Volume IV, page 181.

### LUCILIUS, alias GIULIO CESARE VANINI.
Born at Taurisano in Apulia in 1585; he applied his fine intellect to Aristotelian Philosophy, traveled back and forth through Europe, and reasoned philosophically with great boldness. In France, he particularly drew much attention, and in November 1619, he was publicly burned at Toulouse as a scandalous <term>atheist</term>, after his tongue had first been cut out.

*DEFENSE OF THE MOSAIC AND CHRISTIAN LAW against Physicists, Astronomers & Politicians* <note>Original Latin: *APOLOGIA PRO MOSAICA ET CHRISTIANA LEGE...*</note> is cited in his *Amphitheatrum*, page 38.

### GEORG VECHNER,
Born at Freistadt in Silesia, 1590. His father was Georgius, a minister there. In Frankfurt in 1618, he was crowned with the laurel of a Doctor of Theology and obtained a professorship at the school in Beuthen, Lower Silesia. In 1646, he was a preacher at the church in Brzeg, as well as Superintendent of the nearby churches and director of the school. He passed away at the end of the year 1678.

<column-break/>

*Treatise on the Thorn of Paul* <note>Original Latin: *Tractatus de Palo Pauli*. This refers to "the thorn in the flesh" mentioned in 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note> 1678.

### PAULUS VERMEHREN, of Lübeck.

Theol: de Lapide septem oculorum...*</note> Under the chairmanship of Dr. Johann Schmidius, Doctor of Holy Theology and Professor at Leipzig; at the house of Immanuel Titius, 1716, in quarto.

### PETER VERNANTES, Englishman,
->Minister of the Divine Word.<-

### GERARD OF SAINT-VICTOR.
Lived around the year 1140.
*On the Temple of Solomon*. <note>Original Latin: *De Templo Salomonis*.</note>

### JUAN BAUTISTA VILLALPANDO,
Jesuit, Spaniard from Cordoba, wrote in the year 1596 a commentary on the last 22 chapters of *Ezekiel*. He was the colleague and successor in that distinguished work of *Pradus*, whom you may consult. He died in 1608, aged 56 years. See *Pradus*.

### CAMPEGIUS VITRINGA the Elder.
Born on May 16, 1659, at Leeuwarden in Friesland. His father was *Horatius*, Secretary or second Clerk of the High Court of Friesland, and later successor to his brother *Martinus* as a magistrate in Leeuwarden; his mother was *Albertina de Haan*. As a youth of 16 years, he could translate the original text of both Testaments upon opening the book. In 1675, he was sent to the University of Franeker, where he advanced under *Joh. Terentius, Nic. Blanchardus, Joh. Marckius,* and *Herman Witsius*; at Leiden under *Friedrich Spanheim* the Younger, *Christoph Wittichius, Stephanus Le Moyne,* and *Antonius Hulsius*. There he was honored with the degree of Doctor of Theology, with *Hulsius* being his promoter on July 9, 1679. Returning home, he was recorded among the <term>candidates for the ministry</term> in 1680. He was appointed Professor of Oriental Languages on August 19, 1680. In the autumn of 1681, he married *Wilhelmina van Hell*, daughter of *Simon van Hell*, a minister at Haarlem, who was the mother of five children: *Simon, two named Horatius, Campegius,* and *Joanna Margaretha*. Of these, the son *Campegius*, a Doctor of Holy Theology, was appointed to assist his father in the Theological Professorship while his father was still living. The father was called to the chair at Groningen on July 18, 1682; appointed Professor of Church History on May 6, 1693; and on August 22, 1698, was appointed successor to *Witsius*. Stricken by a severe stroke on March 31, 1723, he passed away in his 63rd year. *Bremen Library, Vol. VI, part 1, page 735*.

*On the Struggle of Jacob with the Angel, regarding Genesis 22:24-32*.
*First Theological Disputation*, in the *Bremen Library*, Vol. I, Part VI, p. 773.
. . . . . . *Disputation II*. In the *Bremen Library*, Vol. II, Part 1, p. 5.
*Disputation on the Wily Serpent*. Franeker.
*Introduction to the True Meaning of Ezekiel’s Temple, in Dutch*. Franeker, 1687, in octavo.
*The True Interpretation of Ezekiel’s Temple defended against J. H. Cocceius*. Haarlem, 1693, in octavo.
*Outline of Sacred History & Chronology from the Creation of the World to the Century of CHRIST’S birth. Including a Map of Prophetic Doctrine*. Franeker, 1708, in octavo.

### JOHANN DANIEL UNSELT, of Danzig.
*Philological-Physical Disputation on the Illustrious Passage of Genesis 1:2, regarding the Chaos of the World*. <note>Original Latin: *Disp. Philologico Physica ad Illustrem Locum Gen. I. 2. de Chao Mundi*.</note> The chairperson was Master Christian Bernhard Bücher, Assistant of the Faculty of Philosophy. Wittenberg, at the widow Gerdes.

### JOH. HENRICUS URSINUS,
Chief Superintendent of the Church in Regensburg. Born in Speyer in 1608. His father was Johannes, a Public Notary and Attorney; his mother was Anna Maria Lazig. In the year 1626, he was sent to the University in Strasbourg. When his father's city was taken by the Spaniards in 1632, he endured many miseries as an exile. In Mainz, he was appointed the first Rector of the Lutheran Seminary; in 1633, a teacher at Wyngarten; in 1634, Co-Rector at Speyer; in 1635, a preacher in the Augustinian Church. In 1643, he became the regular teacher in St. George’s Church, and in that same year, he was called to Regensburg to the dignity of Chief Superintendent, which he held gloriously until the final year of his life in 1666.
*Biblical Arboretum, in which trees and shrubs occurring throughout Holy Scripture are explained and illustrated with philological, philosophical, and theological notes.* <note>Original Latin: *Arboretum Biblicum...*</note> Nuremberg, at the expense of Joh. Tauber, printed by Christoph Gerardi, 1663. Octavo.

### MATTHIAS WASMUTH,
Born in Kiel on June 29, 1625; his father’s name was Georgius. At the University of Wittenberg, he studied under *Buchnerus, Scharffius, Sperlingius, Sennertus, Calovius,* and *Meisnerus.* In the Netherlands, he studied under *Golius, Coccejus,* and *Gentius.* In Basel, under *Buxtorf.* Returning to his fatherland, he was elected Professor of <term>Apologetics</term> <note>Original Dutch: *Bewyskunde*, the study of proofs for the faith.</note> at Rostock; and in the year 1665, when the University of Kiel was founded, he became Professor of Oriental Languages there, and in 1675, of Holy Theology. He died on November 18, 1688, while working on his astronomical study of the seventy weeks of Daniel.
*Letter on the MATHEMATICAL DEMONSTRATION of the YEAR OF THE DELUGE and its days expressed in Holy Scripture, from his own new Celestial Tables demonstrating all the years of the whole world: intended as an experiment and precursor to his own Astronomico-Chronological work.* <note>Original Latin: *Epistola de ANNI DILUVIANI...*</note> Included in the *Mosaic Mathematics* of Reyherus, pages 98–124.

### GEORGIUS WOLFGANGUS WEDELI
Born in Golßen in Lower Lusatia in 1645. His father, *Johan Georg*, was the first minister there and later the <term>Ephorus</term> <note>A regional overseer or superintendent in the Lutheran church.</note> at Spremberg; his mother was *Eva Röklin*. He learned the fundamentals at Spremberg and Golßen. He progressed further at the Schulpforta school, then came to Jena, where *Prætorius, Posner,* and *Weigel*, but especially *Guil. Rolfincius, Mobius, Schenckius,* and *Friderici*, equipped him even further. He wished to travel to other lands, but because his father died, he remained there another five years. Finally, he departed with *Oehlitius* for the March, Silesia, and visited Frankfurt, Wittenberg, and Leipzig. In his 21st year, he became a Doctor of Medicine at Jena; shortly thereafter, he was appointed Provincial Physician of Gotha by Duke *Ernst* the Pious. Meanwhile, he traveled to Holland. In the year 1672, he became Professor of Medicine at Jena, and finally, he was named Lord of the Estate in Schwarza, Imperial Count Palatine, Councilor and Chief Physician to the Illustrious Dukes of Saxony, and Public Professor of Theoretical Medicine. Among the multitude of his learned medical writings, many are named in his *Century of Medico-Philological Exercises*, which were produced to explain the <term>Sacred Pages</term> <note>Original Dutch: *Gewyde Bladeren*, meaning the Holy Scriptures.</note> using literary and medical principles. This work presents various readings, experiments, and very fine explanations, published in Jena at the expense of *Jo. Bielke* in 1701. Quarto. ### HERMANNUS WITSIUS. Professor of Theology.

An excellent theologian, learned and temperate. Born on February 12, 1636, in Enkhuizen in West Friesland, his father being *Nicolaus*, the mayor there. He acquired the principles of languages, philosophy, and theology from his uncle *Petrus Gerhardi*; his further progress he owed to the Universities of Utrecht, Leiden, and Groningen. He primarily acknowledged that he owed the core of inward Christianity to *Justus van den Bogaart*. <note>Justus van den Bogaart was a Dutch minister known for his influence on the "Nadere Reformatie" or Dutch Further Reformation, emphasizing personal piety.</note> In the year 1656, he was admitted to the rank of ministers, and at age 21 called as a minister to Westwoud and Binnewylend; he served the same office in Leeuwarden. In the year 1675, he accepted the theological professorship at Franeker, having first been made a Doctor; in 1680, a similar appointment at Utrecht. In 1685, he was a traveling companion to the Dutch Embassy to King *James II* in England, on which occasion he became known to the Archbishop and other illustrious men. In 1698, called to the theological professorship at Leiden, he went there, where he passed away on October 22, 1708, in his 73rd year.

*Sacred Miscellany, in Four Books.* <note>Original Latin: *Miscellaneorum Sacrorum Libri IV.*</note> *In which the prophets and prophecy, the mysteries of the Levitical Tabernacle, the comparison of the priesthood of Aaron and Christ, the Sanhedrins of the Hebrews, the four beasts of Daniel, the worship of Moloch, this age and the future one, the meaning of the Apocalyptic Epistles, and the schism of the Donatists are diligently and extensively discussed.
