# NATURAL HISTORY.

Q

...the literal sense of Holy Scripture: *dust shalt thou eat all the days of thy life*. But how shall one best understand this expression? For as soon as one examines Nature itself, one finds that a punishment of this kind, regarding a Snake, almost vanishes into smoke—or at least seems quite improper to bear the name of a punishment. All who know the nature of Snakes even slightly know well that it is a creature <note>original: "Ongediert," often meaning vermin or small creature</note> that uses all kinds of edible things for its food; daily experience sufficiently teaches that Snakes eat all kinds of fruits, bread, bran, meat, and many other strange foods—in a word, whatever they encounter. Although it often happens that while eating such foods they also swallow some dust or sand, this certainly should not seem very strange, as this is common to all other animals no less than to Snakes. Although the Earth, especially when considered on its own and apart from all other surrounding or nearby bodies, is not a nutritious food, one must nevertheless admit that when considered together with the unknown and hidden particles enclosed within it, it is the general Mother and Producer of all kinds of nutritious foods, and the fertile Nourisher of the plants of the earth. Consequently, if a Snake should happen to swallow some Earth, it swallows at the same time some nutritious slime or fatness, which serves above all as special food and cultivation for plants. Likewise, it occasionally gets many seeds that are hidden in the Earth, as well as a multitude of small roots, fibers, and countless invisible little animals into its body, through which it receives sufficient food for the maintenance of its life; far from having to exist solely on the simple eating of Dust and Earth. Furthermore, one cannot deny that there are many more Dust- and Earth-eaters among the creatures than the Snake alone, such as, among others, the Earthworms, maggots, Scorpions, Moles, and many others like them, who likewise seek their food in the dark bowels of the Earth. In what way, then, does one wish to maintain that the eating of Dust and Earth is a specifically assigned punishment for the Snake?

From what has just been said above about the Snake, and further from its cunning, from the conversation it had with *Eve*, from its unfounded and ridiculous summons before the Court of Justice, and finally from the heavy curse that the Creator, according to Holy Scripture, is said to have pronounced over it, one

<column-break/>

can sufficiently see and conclude that all these qualities and characteristics are of such a nature that one could hardly attribute them to a natural Snake without appearing to have strayed from the right path of fairness. Rather, they belong to that symbolic and so-called *Old Serpent*, that malicious and Hellish brood, that wicked and destructive Animal—I mean the evil Spirit, who under that name was cursed and suppressed by GOD. He was humbled into the abyss because of his former well-being, which was first Heavenly and Blessed, but is now exchanged for Hellish darkness and an eternal banishment from GOD’S Presence: humbled in Understanding and Will, with which he formerly considered nothing but Divine and Heavenly matters, whereas now on the contrary he thinks of Earthly and loathsome things: humbled in all his other Spiritual and exalted qualities; being stripped of the Truth, Wisdom, and Holiness with which he was previously adorned and clothed; humbled, yes, entirely submerged in the muddy pool of corruption, worthy even to be punished and humbled for his actions, by which it is to be understood that all power and ability have been taken from him. REVELATION <note>original: "APOC." for Apocalypse</note> XII. 9. One finds more such expressions of humiliation in Holy Scripture, first with the penitent Harper <note>A traditional reference to King David, credited with writing the Psalms and playing the harp.</note> *David*, PSALM XLIV. 26. *Our soul is bowed down to the dust; our belly cleaves to the Earth.* Add to this what one reads in the Lamentations of the Prophet *Jeremiah*: *Let him put his mouth in the dust*: Ch. III. v. 29. by which a deep humiliation must be understood. From this it also appears that such low humiliation should not be viewed so much as an assigned punishment, but rather as a symbolic way of speaking, since it takes place no less in Religious and virtue-seeking Souls than in Godless and punishable sinners. Furthermore, the ancient custom of the Heathens themselves—who used to drag defeated Enemies shackled behind their Triumphal Chariots <term>Zeegewagens: ornate chariots used in Roman victory processions</term> and trample those wretched outcasts into the dust and sand with their feet—seems to indicate clearly enough that such oppression is much more a punishment for unfortunate and defeated Warriors than for irrational and innocent Animals. Of this, the rich and diligent Antiquity has left us an eternal gift: a countless multitude of glorious Commemorative Medals <note>Refers to Roman coins or "medallions" celebrating military victories</note> of the Roman Emperors, upon which one can still see such histories very artistically depicted today.

They sufficiently convince us that such expressions of humiliation should not be regarded so much as an assigned punishment—especially regarding a mindless and innocent animal like a Snake—but rather as a figurative or symbolic way of speaking.

Q 2
<meta>catchword: harm-</meta>

...plants, which are of a singular nature and distinct from all other types of vegetation; or does the Holy Scripture intend by this only to signify the *Thorns* or sharp points themselves, with which the trunks, stalks, branches, flowers, and fruits of such plants are covered? For my part, I will freely admit—since in this matter everyone is free to follow their own judgment—that in place of the aforementioned word *Thorns*, I would above all choose those *thorny* or *prickly plants* which are so harmful and troublesome to the industrious farmer, because through their unstoppable spreading they ruin almost all fields, choke the good and useful crops, and are hardly fit for any other use than simply to be burned.

The word *Thistles*, which most closely corresponds to the Hebrew root word *Dardar* <note>original: "Dardar"</note>, was formerly used as a proper name for certain prickly plants. This is evident from ancient writers, namely *Dioscorides* (Book 4, Chapter 15) <note>original: "Dioscorides L. IV. C. 15."</note>, where this writer mentions two kinds of plants of that name: the first he calls *Earth-thistles* <note>original: "Aard-diſtelen"</note>, *whose leaves are not unlike those of the Purslane, though slightly thinner, having their runners stretched flat on the ground, and surrounded on the leaves with sharp and very hard points.* One can see these so-called Earth-thistles depicted with sharp and prickly leaves in the works of J.B. <note>likely Jean Bauhin, a famous 16th-century botanist</note>. Figure 1 shows this plant with its fruit or prickly seed-pod. The second sort of *Thistle* mentioned by *Dioscorides* is of a different nature, known by him under the name *Water-thistles* <note>original: "Water-diſtelen"</note>, because they grow in the water: they thrust their green crowns above the flood, but keep their sharp barbs hidden beneath it. *They have broad leaves and long stems, which are slightly thicker at the top than the bottom; their fruits are hairy and prickly, and produce a certain hard seed, which does not differ from the other.* These Water-thistles are, according to *Tournefort* <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort, an influential French botanist</note>, nothing more than a common water-weed that generally grows in rivers or brooks. See Figure 2. It deserves the name *Thistle* more than the previous one, because it has three sharp points. Moreover, it is not probable that the sacred writer intended to signify this or a similar water-plant by the aforementioned word *Dardar* (otherwise called *Thistles*), since it is used as a healing medicine for health and serves as a good and nutritious food for both humans and animals

<column-break/>

alike. What is more, the *Thracians*, who live near the banks of the river called the *Strymon* <note>original: "Strymon"</note>, use this very plant to fatten their horses, and even bake bread from it. The botanists <term>Kruydkundigen|Botanists, or those who study the properties of herbs</term> understand by the word *Thistle* a completely different plant, namely the so-called *Wild Caltrop* <note>original Latin: "Tribulus Sylveſtris"</note> among the Latins, in Dutch called *Wild Thistle* <note>original: "Wilde Diſtel"</note>, and by the Germans *Kletten-Korfel*; this plant has a large flower and is depicted in Figure A: alongside which several others of a similar but distinct nature can be seen. But what then is the reason that we translate the Hebrew root word *Dardar* in our language as *Thistle*? By which word people not only in this country, but even throughout the whole world, understand a prickly but very healthy plant? Although the same is expressed differently according to the specific nature of the languages or tongues spoken in each country. Why not rather use the word for stinging *Nettles*, or at least some other kind of lowly and disregarded wild *Weed*, whose power is unknown and which is esteemed as useless, in place of *Thistles*? All the more so because these latter are almost everywhere, especially by the Latins, called *Carduus Benedictus* <note>original Latin: "Carduus Benedictus"</note>, which is to say, *Blessed Thistle*, and for that reason are used with a desired effect as a very suitable remedy for human well-being and the restoration of weakened health, far from being regarded anywhere as a sign of punishment or curse, much less as a disadvantageous or unlucky plant. Thus, it is well to think that the Holy Scripture did not have *Thistles* in mind in this place.

Unless one wished to count as a punishment that which fertile Nature, through God's singular arrangement and favor, brings forth for the preservation of the human body; but such an opinion seems to conflict with all reason. In this way, the greatest difficulty lies particularly in this: that in this case one does not know how best to conduct oneself with respect to the Bible, and what finally is to be understood by the above-written content, since at least something, whatever it may be, is to be understood from it. To speak frankly, it seems to me that nothing else is signified by it than the excessive and consequently...

# SPIRITUAL

...harmful overgrowth of the aforementioned *Thorns* and *Thistles*, which typically oppress other more esteemed plants of the earth through their troublesome propagation and hinder their growth. Alternatively, one can also understand this as a powerful expression of the barrenness and infertility of the uncultivated Earth, which outside the Earthly Paradise possibly produced more *Thorns* and *Thistles* or other weeds than good and tasty plants. Whatever the case may be, it is nonetheless certain that all thorny and prickly plants, of whatever nature or shape they might be—each after its kind—are no less useful and beneficial for human use than all other good herbs. Consequently, they should not be regarded as unnecessary or contemptible outcasts of the Earth, since through the benevolence of the Creator, the Earth brings forth only good and useful plants. Evidence of this can be found in Rose, Bramble, and Gooseberry bushes, and many other similar plants that are covered with thorns and sharp points. Furthermore, it should be noted that because thorns are healing parts of such plants and are absolutely necessary to their entire created nature, they were undoubtedly created by GOD from the beginning of the world—that is to say, within the first six days of Creation—along with their own and all other plants, and not after the fall of the first Man, as many imagine. Meanwhile, anyone can clearly see that in this case, the Divine sentence pronounced against *Adam* and *Eva*—*the Earth shall bring forth Thorns and Thistles for you*—is not in the least violated or contradicted. For one might count it as a sufficient punishment, if you will, that the Earth possibly brought forth such a large and immoderate multitude of such troublesome and hindering plants at that time that they became unbearable to Man. Their abundant encroachment hindered the necessary growth of other plants, which these two newly-exiled Outcasts perhaps had more desire for; all the more because *Adam*, accompanied only by his wife *Eva*, found himself unable to overcome this unavoidable nuisance. He could only root out this prickly and uncomfortable Weed, if one may call it so, with great effort and labor, in the sweat of his brow. Just as today—

<column-break/>

—many a farmer and lover of agriculture is sufficiently convinced to his sorrow that all kinds of weeds are generally much more successful and prolific in their propagation than other plants. From this, the ancient and daily proverb, *Weeds do not perish* <note>original: "Onkruyd vergaat niet"; a common Dutch idiom similar to "ill weeds grow apace," suggesting that bad things are difficult to get rid of</note>, seems to have taken its origin, and not without reason.

Furthermore, no one should imagine that this great multitude of Thorny Plants finally arose in later times—that is, after or during the general Deluge <note>The Great Flood of Noah</note>—since the Divine curse must certainly have been fulfilled long before, indeed at the very time of its pronouncement. The nature-loving Reader will undoubtedly be convinced of this as soon as he has attentively considered the *Mistletoe leaf* <note>original: "Misselblad"; likely referring to a specific fossilized leaf specimen mentioned in the accompanying illustrations</note> depicted in the adjacent Plate Fig. 13, which was found printed and hardened in stone.

Likewise, the other part of the aforementioned verse, *you shall eat the Herb of the Field*, must be interpreted in such a way that it does not seem contrary to the use of plants even in the state of Innocence <note>The period before the Fall of Man</note> (*Gen. I. v 29*) and at that same time provide for Man's well-being and nourishment. *Adam* had until now lived in all freedom and glory in the Earthly Paradise—that delightful place of pleasure provided and planted by GOD Himself with all kinds of tasty and beautiful fruits—without having to exert any effort or labor to tend, care for, or cultivate them. Now, on the contrary, his former way of life is unhappily reshaped, and his glory turned into slavery. He is forced to undergo the heavy punishment of his crime with pain and sorrow, and to atone for the transgression of GOD’S command through an eternal exile from that incomparable Garden of delights all the days of his life. He who used to satisfy his appetite through the use of all kinds of earth and tree fruits is now condemned to eat the unsavory *Herb of the field* for the preservation of his life. A sad change for our common Father, who previously was fed in abundance by GOD Himself through Nature, but must now seek his food as a needy exile outside of Paradise—which he must, moreover, provide, plant, and gather with the bitter labor of his body and in the sweat of his brow!

# NATURAL HISTORY.

### PLATE XXXII.

*And the LORD GOD made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins, and clothed them.* Gen. III. v. 21.

---

> *The naked creature is here by GOD’S hand clothed,*
> *And the first pair adorned with rough beasts' hides;*
> *When they left Eden’s Court for their apple-bite,*
> *Through which all mortal seed awaited the death-knell.*
> *How great, how wonderful is GOD’S mercy*
> *To still raise up the fallen human!*
> *By covering his nakedness and preparing the first garment,*
> *Before storm, or heat, or cold comes to battle him.*
> *Every nation still clothes itself according to its nature,*
> *Indeed, even the lifeless seems wrapped in a garment;*
> *The Tree is preserved by the Bark, the Fruit by the Leaf,*
> *Through which the DEITY shows her endless power.* <note>The author uses "her" (haar) because the Dutch word for Godhead/Deity, 'Godheid', is grammatically feminine.</note>
> *But the monster FASHION has stifled useful habit;*
> *Bringing Splendor and Pride back in its place,*
> *And robbed the Earth-dweller of first Simplicity,*
> *To live according to the wanton command of Frivolity.*
> *The necessity of Nature requires no Flourish or Pomp,*
> *But Covering, to turn back the violence of Air and Wind:*
> *Learn then from Adam’s Garment, O humans all!*
> *How you must honor GOD your CREATOR through Humility.*

Clothing serves humans as a remedy for their shame, for the covering of their nakedness, and as a shield and protection against the manifold—indeed constant, boisterous, and fickle—changes of the air, which have been caused since the fall of the first pair in place of the previous well-ordered moderation. Previously, a few fig-leaves joined together were enough for the protection of Modesty, for which they alone served, and not to protect the body against the influences of the air; but after the Fall, nakedness required far more to be able to guard oneself against the uncomfortable workings of the Elements <term>Hoofdstoffen: literally 'main substances,' referring here to the classical elements like air and weather</term>, and to withstand the violence of the Sun's rays as well as that of the harsh winds. But in this case, Nature seems sufficiently satisfied with the hide or skin of some animal, especially if it is woolly or rough. From this, the LORD GOD, according to the testimony of Holy Scripture, made the first garments to cover the naked Adam and Eve. In former times, one saw the ancient Greek heroes covered with the hides of lions, tigers, and wild boars; even in later times they wore these out of splendor, flung over their weapons like cloaks, also covering their heads with the flayed hide of a lion’s or tiger’s head,

<column-break/>

to show themselves all the more terrifying to their enemies. The ancient High Germans went clothed in their tunics <note>original: "Paltrokken" — a type of long, heavy coat or gown</note> of variegated skins, without any splendor or finery, just as today the Tartars, Lapps, Finns, and Livonians, and the majority of the Hungarians, Poles, and Muscovites <note>The residents of the Grand Duchy of Moscow or Russia</note> are accustomed to cover themselves with the skins of beasts; although tyrannical Fashion has also become common among the latter, though not to be compared with that of the Western part of Europe. The Batavians, Sicambri, Pannonians, Suebi, and Goths used to arm themselves against the cold of the air and the wetness of the ground with nothing but animal skins, so that one would often have taken them for bears or lions themselves, unless a little of the uncovered face had shown the contrary; I say rightly "a little," for the ears and mouth being covered, only the eyes remained free to serve as guides for the body. Truly this clothing was more comfortable and useful for the body than our modern style with all its flourish and fuss, for the narrow and contracted air-pores of the skins block the penetrating cold from without, and preserve within the evaporating heat of the body,

<header>S P I R I T U A L</header>

body, so that they are at one time intended for two particular functions. <note>The author refers to the dual purpose of clothing: modesty and protection.</note> Furthermore, if someone is concerned with durability, there is nothing better than skins, as such coats can often be left to one's grand-nephews as an inheritance.

Nature itself sufficiently shows us the traces of this simple clothing. First, regarding Man, who has bare skin for the protection of his body—though not enough to cover himself against the accidents and changes of the air—whereas animals can protect and warm themselves with their own shaggy skins. Even vermin mostly have their horns and shells to cover themselves. Indeed, plants have their leaves to preserve and warm the flowers and fruits against the attacking harsh winds; trees have their bark for protection; yes, even the fish have their scales mostly as a covering; thus, necessity requires no finery or adornment. 

Consequently, if we look at the matter rightly, every nation can sufficiently manufacture its own clothes according to the temperateness of the climate under which it is located. The Northern Lands have their Badgers, Bears, and Foxes to clothe the inhabitants with their pelts against the sharp cold; the glowing Western lands <note>Likely referring to the West Indies or the Americas</note> produce birds with whose plumage the wild inhabitants adorn themselves more than they cover themselves; others are again situated under such a scorched climate that they can endure no clothes, except only as much as is necessary to cover their shame. From this, it is easy to prove that every household can be its own Tailor and Furrier, if only the ridiculous *Fashion* is excluded. The Emperor Augustus had, according to the testimony of Suetonius in his *Lives of the Caesars* Chapter 33, <note>original: "C. 33." refers to Suetonius's biography of Augustus</note> the following saying: *A costly and well-appointed garment is the banner of Pride and a breeding ground for Luxury.*

Since the weakness of our body

<column-break/>

has passed into a most delicate sensitivity, and our ingenuity has allowed itself to be carried away by all sorts of new inventions, all good use has also become an abuse under the name of *Fashion*; Simplicity has changed into Discomfort, Peace into Pride and Excess, and Humility has been trampled by an imagined Vanity. Since that time, men have demanded various things from various bodies, such as the innards of plants, <note>Likely referring to plant fibers like flax, hemp, or cotton</note> the wool of Sheep, the silk of Worms, and even from Spiders. <note>In the early 18th century, there were famous but largely unsuccessful experiments to harvest spider silk for textiles.</note> Every nation competes for splendor in clothing, to the extent that one spies on and apes the other, and everyone thereby wants to be the greatest, yes, some even go so far that through this cowardly imitation they become slaves to one another. One sees entire States, men and women, as if over a matter of great importance, struggling and quarreling for the prize of who is best dressed. Thus have *Adam's* conceited descendants deviated from the first Simplicity from time to time and from step to step.

In my opinion, it is not probable that anyone could say with certainty that *Adam* offered a sacrifice to GOD before the Fall; however, such is to be suspected, and even seems possible to be derived from Holy Scripture, as it would otherwise be a mere riddle how those animal skins, from which the LORD made coats for *Adam* and his wife, had come into Paradise: unless one wished to assume that GOD Himself had killed these animals and removed the hide; since it seems impossible that coats of skins would be made without animals having been slaughtered beforehand. It is likewise quite conceivable that people ate the meat of slaughtered animals before the Great Flood: all the more so because in former times, as well as today, it has been a common custom that those who served the Altar or slaughtered the sacrificial cattle lived from the Altar—that is, from the sacrifice.

> In what a dismal state would the mortal Race
> Ever sigh, had our GOD given us no garments!
> Now the Sunlight would burn us, then the Cold make us shiver,
> One would dread the day, one would fear the night.
> But the Garment and Covering which covers us, and that we wear,
> Prevents us from complaining of Heat or fierce Cold.

# NATURAL SCIENCE.

### PRINT PLATE XXXIII.

*And ABEL also brought of the firstlings of his sheep, and of their fat: and the LORD had respect unto ABEL and to his offering.*
*But unto CAIN and to his offering He had no respect: then CAIN was very wroth, and his countenance fell.* Genesis IV. v. 4, 5.

> As soon as Envy came into the World,
> Murder and Homicide and Violence took possession
> Of CAIN’S cruel mind: the Earth was by Fratricide
> Defiled, as soon as Hate had the first Peace disturbed.

Today, O alas! upon the wild theater of this World, the first and indeed the most lamentable of all Tragedies is performed. Scarcely have we, to our collective regret and heartache, seen the most shameful Fall of our first Ancestors—when the two Noblest of all Creatures of the Earth allowed themselves to be carried so far by *Pride* and *Lust* through the cunning of a Serpent that, having forgotten GOD’S strict command, they listened to the deceptive coaxing of a mindless Animal and, like blind and thoughtless mortals, followed its ruinous advice and solicitation out of curiosity—or shortly thereafter, two other and indeed the heaviest and most dangerous Passions appear that could ever dominate Man’s mind: two most intimate Friends, but at the same time most bitter Enemies, namely *Wrath* and *Envy*.

Scarcely had the Firstborn of the general Father noticed that the Sacrifice, which he offered to the LORD from the Fruits of the Field, was not pleasing to GOD; while he saw with inward spite and heartache that, on the contrary, the Offering of his Brother *Abel* did please the Almighty, or he was immediately, says Holy Scripture, inflamed by *Wrath*.

One may rightly say that it is no less a folly to want to follow the mad and lawless impulses of Man’s degenerate and corrupted Nature in everything, than to give free rein to an untamed, young, and spirited Horse. Where *Wrath* has the upper hand, there, to speak by way of parable, the entire rigging of the ship is immediately loosened; all sails are set; one suddenly lets the weak and rudderless Ship of oppressed and exiled Reason, for the sake of the boisterous waves of the troubled Sea of our

<column-break/>

unbridled passions, drift so far away that this powerless and abandoned Vessel, tossed violently back and forth by the choppy winds of a reckless fury, runs the extreme danger of finally being dashed to pieces against one or another hidden Rock. The necessary equilibrium—to explain the matter more through <term>Natural Science<note>The Dutch "Natuurkundiger" implies a physical or physiological explanation based on the laws of nature as understood in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note></term>—which exists between the nervous Fluids and the Blood, is entirely removed: the so-called <term>Vital Spirits<note>Historical medical term for subtle substances believed to flow through the nerves to transmit sensation and movement.</note></term> run, like a breached River or a plunging Stream that knocks down, destroys, and drags along everything it meets in its course, out of the Back of the Head—that is, from the posterior part of the Cranium—toward the Heart. Because of this, it happens that this most important and supreme organ of the Body, being much more powerfully contracted and disturbed than usual, drives the blood with quite uncommon violence toward the outermost parts of the small veins. From this arises that visible redness with which the face is usually covered when one is angry; the eyes seem to burn like fire in the head: one foams at the mouth with foulness, the lips tremble, the entire head is swollen—in a word, all the limbs of the Body, having fallen into disorder through *Wrath* and being troubled by internal irregular movements, make themselves ready for battle and want to attack the enemy immediately. Everything is in turmoil; every limb seems eager to risk the first blow. If anyone has the curiosity to see this mad and desperate passion—I mean *Wrath*—painted with more vivid and natural colors, let them read the educational writings of that ancient and excellent *Philosopher* and Teacher *Seneca*, *On Anger* <note>original Latin title: "de Ira"</note>, which he wrote regarding the *Nature*, *Causes*, and *Remedy of Wrath*,

<margin>Chapter I, which has left behind a singular instruction for posterity.</margin> It generally happens with the internal movements of the human mind just as it does with the Muses of *Apollo* and the raging Priestesses of *Bacchus* <note>A reference to the Maenads, followers of the god of wine, known for their ecstatic frenzy.</note>, who each wish to have their turn. Thus one sees that almost all people are different, not only because of their nationality, but even because of their character and particular disposition, so that even those who are related by blood are subject to the same fate. Let the pious and religious *Abel* be a witness to this in regard to his brother *Cain*. That good-natured and God-fearing youth is peaceful, composed, quiet of mind, still in behavior, friendly, lovely, and, what is visible and remarkable, youthful and blushing of face: whereas, on the contrary, the other is troubled, malicious, confused in thought, debauched, and hideous of sight; one sees his countenance constantly changing, now turning red with rage, then turning pale again through Hate and Envy; he swells with vengefulness, and loses the use of his senses through fury. One might not unfairly call such continuous madness a drunkenness of the soul. The miserable body is entirely flooded by the heated blood, which has violently run outside its usual boundaries, because the immoderate movement of the Heart has gained the upper hand. Thus it is that the stiff and agitated nerves play the master and, for that time, claim the honor of victory. This is evident from the contraction of the wrinkled skin and from the slower flow of the blood, which is weakened not a little because the blood tries to force itself through the smallest veins with too great a violence. Meanwhile, the Heart is burdened and oppressed by distress, and can hardly expel the disturbed life-fluids, but sighs and pants from exhaustion. A man who is possessed by Hate and Envy is tormented and unsettled day and night: his sleep is constantly broken, because his rest is repeatedly disturbed by malicious thoughts: moreover, his appetite fails him, the body wastes away, the face turns pale, the jawbones protrude, and the wrinkled skin barely covers the parched bones.

->*Lean HATE and ENVY are in the malicious being*<-
->*Of an envious man to be silently read:*<-

According to the literal expression of the sacred Writer, with which he wishes to indicate the immoderation of this violent passion, *CAIN was very wroth and his countenance fell*, so that even from his troubled face, the Hate and Envy with which his mind was internally possessed could be sufficiently perceived. It happens more often that envious and jealous people consume their own flesh and blood, just as rust eats away at iron. *Envy*, says *Antisthenes* <note>A Greek philosopher and pupil of Socrates.</note>, *is as harmful to the envious as rust is to steel*. The *Spanish* wish to express the same through their proverb: *To iron the rust, and envy to the base man.* <note>original: "Al hierro el orin, y la embidia al ruin."</note> That is as much as to say,

->*As Rust wears down the iron,*<-
->*So man dies through Hate and Envy.*<-

When one looks closely at the matter, one must confess that it is almost impossible for the weak and delicate constitution of our body to be powerful enough to withstand so many enemies that strike man unawares. How is it possible that all those thin and small veins, which are already significantly weakened and impaired by excessive fury, can hold back the fierce and irregular stream of the disturbed life-spirits? All the more so, because those delicate blood vessels, which were previously sufficiently dilated, are in this case far too much contracted and constricted, whereby the usual secretion <term>Scheiding: the physiological process of separating nutrients or waste within the body</term> in the extremities is entirely hindered and the healthy adhesion of the nutritious juices is prevented. Thus it happens that a certain sharpness arises in the blood, which causes many dangerous blockages, from which finally a long-lasting and deadly consumption <note>In this context, "teering" refers to a wasting disease or "atrophy of the spirit" that manifests as physical decline.</note> arises, which incessantly plagues the miserable follower of his unbridled passions until the end of his life, and drags him to the grave before his time, so to speak, through a most dismal and stubborn obsession with Envy and Vengefulness. Thus the degenerate fratricide becomes a cruel and unnatural murderer of himself.

# SPIRITUAL <note>original: "GEESTELYKE" — This likely refers to "Spiritual Matters" or "Religious Philosophy," given the context of the book's themes.</note>

<margin>

It usually happens with the inner movements of the human mind just as it does with the Muses of *Apollo* and the raving priestesses of *Bacchus*, each of whom wishes to have their turn. Thus one sees that almost all people are different, not only because of their nationality, but even because of their inner character and particular nature, so that even those who are related by blood are subject to the same fate. Witness to this are the Pious and Religious *Abel* in relation to his brother *Cain*. That good-natured and God-fearing youth is peaceful, composed, quiet of mind, still in behavior, friendly, lovely, and—what is visible and remarkable—youthful and blushing of face: whereas, on the contrary, the other is disturbed, malicious, confused in thought, erratic, and hideous of sight; one sees his countenance constantly changing; then he turns red with anger, then he pales again through Hatred and Envy; he swells with vengefulness, and loses the use of his senses through rage. One might not unfairly call such continuous frenzy a drunkenness of the soul. The wretched body is completely flooded by the heated blood, which has violently run beyond its usual limits, because the immoderate movement of the Heart has gained the upper hand. Thus it is that the stiff and agitated nerves play the master and, for that time, claim the honor of victory. This is evident from the contraction of the wrinkled skin and from the slower flow of the blood, which is weakened not a little because the blood tries to force its way through the very smallest veins with too great a violence. Meanwhile, the Heart is burdened and oppressed by driving out the vital fluids <note>The author refers here to the "vital spirits" or humors, which early modern science believed governed health and personality.</note>, but sighs and pants from exhaustion. A person who is consumed by Hatred and Envy is tormented and unsettled day and night: his sleep is constantly broken, because his rest is repeatedly disturbed by malicious thoughts: moreover, his appetite fails him, the body decays, the face turns pale, the jawbones protrude, and the wrinkled skin barely covers the parched bones.

->*Lean HATRED and ENVY are silently to be read*<-
->*In the malicious being of an envious person:*<-

->*His burning eyes are betrayers of his heart,*<-
->*His gaunt bones reveal what pains him internally.*<-

According to the literal expression of the Sacred Writer <note>A reference to the author of the Book of Genesis.</note>, with which he intends to convey the immoderation of this violent passion, *CAIN was very angry and his countenance fell*, so that even from his disturbed face, one could sufficiently perceive the Hatred and Envy with which his mind was inwardly possessed. It happens more often that envious and jealous people consume their own flesh and blood, just as rust eats away at iron. *Envy*, says *Antisthenes*, a Greek writer, *is as harmful to the envious as rust is to steel*. The Spaniards wish to convey the same through their proverb: *Rust to iron, and envy to the wicked.* <note>original Spanish: "Al hierro el orin, y la embidia al ruin."</note> That is as much as to say,

->*Just as Rust wears down the iron,*<-
->*So Man dies through Hatred and Envy.*<-

When one looks closely into the matter, one must confess that it is almost impossible for the weak and delicate constitution of our body to be powerful enough to withstand so many enemies that strike Man unawares. How is it possible that all those thin and tiny veins, which are already significantly weakened and injured by excessive fury, can hold back the fierce and irregular stream of the disturbed vital spirits? <term>Vital spirits (levensgeesten)</term> <note>In historical medicine, these were "refined" substances in the blood thought to carry out the functions of the soul and brain.</note> Even more so, because those delicate blood vessels, which were previously sufficiently dilated, are in this case too much contracted and constricted, whereby the usual separation in the extremities is entirely hindered and the healthy attachment of the nutritious juices is prevented. Thus it happens that a certain sharpness arises in the blood, which causes many dangerous blockages, from which finally a long-lasting and deadly consumption <note>wasting disease</note> proceeds, which incessantly plagues the wretched follower of his unbridled passions until the end of his life, and drags him to the grave before his time, so to speak, by a most distressing and stubborn obsession with Envy and Vengefulness. Thus the degenerate Fratricide becomes a cruel and unnatural murderer of himself.

### PRINT PLATE XXXIV. XXXV.

->*Make for yourself an Ark of $^1$ Gopher wood; with $^2$ rooms you shall make this Ark, and you shall pitch it inside and out with pitch.* **Genesis VI. v. 14.**<-

---

It was the corruption of all flesh, which had filled the Earth with malice, that gave cause to 그hat terrible threat of the LORD: *behold, I shall destroy them, that is, all the degenerate and corrupt descendants of Adam, along with the Earth.* Yet the gracious All-Preserver <note>A title for God emphasizing His role in maintaining creation.</note> seems unable to completely overlook His immeasurable Loving-kindness toward Mankind. Therefore, He deigns to give good courage to the despondent Noah, who was seized by a deadly terror, by promising him a firm assurance of his and his children’s preservation. Although it would have been equally possible for the Most High to preserve Noah’s lineage amidst the general waves of the Deluge through a supernatural miracle—just as He in later times kept the innocent Daniel unharmed among the hungry Lions, and his three companions in the burning Oven—yet it pleased GOD to make effective an uncommon and until then unknown means, which He had drawn from the rich treasury of Nature, willing that the same should be worked out and completed not only by those of Noah’s lineage, but also through the help of others. 

This rare and Divine Remedy was the so-called *Ark*, which GOD the LORD commanded *Noah* to build, and which is called by *Hesychius* <note>An ancient Greek grammarian and lexicographer.</note>, an ancient Greek writer, a wooden pen, or a small timbered place where one used to keep fattened livestock. The Hebrew Text uses the word *Thebbe* <note>original: 'תֵּבָה' (tebah)</note>, which is actually called *Chest* or *Trunk* in Dutch, because the Ark was closed on all sides in the manner of a chest or box. From this, the famous City of *Thebes* in *Boeotia* formerly received its name, and was likewise called a *Small Box* by the Greeks, on account of the little boat or small vessel with which *Cadmus* <note>The legendary Phoenician prince and founder of Thebes.</note> sailed over to *Europe*. Moreover, if one wishes to examine the use of this structure,

one will find that the name of *Ship* or *Vessel*, which the writer of the Book of Wisdom Chapter XIV. v. 6 used, may rightly be applied to the *Ark*.

The material from which the aforementioned Ark or Vessel had to be built was the so-called *Gopher wood*. This Hebrew root-word, because it is found nowhere else in the entire Holy Scripture than in this place alone, is subject to various interpretations. For this reason, it seems to me that those who have kept the original Hebrew word *Gopher* in their translations have taken the safest path. The LXX Translators <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> believed they had overcome all conceivable difficulties by paying less attention to the specific genus or particular species of the tree than to the artistic form or architectural method that one necessarily had to observe in the use and singular preparation of this wood for the heavy construction of this great Vessel. Perhaps for this reason they expressed the Hebrew word *Gopher* in their Greek translations as *four-angled timbers*, by which is understood not so much trees whose branches extend on one side into four corners or regions—as almost all trees do that produce pinecones or similar fruits—but rather the timbers themselves, which are hewn in the manner of square blocks, which are called *square timbers* by *Augustine* in the last chapter of the fifteenth book of the *City of God*. In the common translation, they are known under the name of *smooth* and *evenly hewn timbers*. *Vossius* <note>Gerardus Vossius, a famous 17th-century Dutch scholar.</note> understands the word *Gopher* to mean pitch or resin, as if he wanted to say that Noah had to make the *Ark* of pitch- or resin-tree wood.

But since this tree itself constitutes a genus, everyone is free to consider the Great Cedar or the so-called Pineapple-tree <note>In the 18th century, "Pineapple-tree" referred to a tree bearing pine cones, likely a Stone Pine</note> of Lebanon as such. The Cedar tree, which bears pine cones and has leaves in the manner of a pine tree, which in Greek is called <term>πίτυς</term> <note>pitys</note>, and in Latin <term>Larix</term> <note>Larch</note>. See C. B. This tree is mentioned in very many places in the Holy Scripture. <term>Junius</term> and <term>Tremellius</term> <note>Francis household Junius and Immanuel Tremellius, 16th-century biblical scholars</note> interpret the aforementioned word <term>Gopher</term> as <term>Cedrelates</term>, which has its origin from two joined Greek words, namely from the Cedar- and Fir- or Poplar-tree, and yet does not constitute a distinct variety between the Cedar and the Poplar, but signifies nothing else than the aforementioned great Cedar tree itself. This is openly evident from the clear testimony of <term>Pliny</term>, Book 24, Chapter 5. *The great Cedar tree*, says this writer, *which some are accustomed to call CEDRELATES, which is as much as to say, Cedar-Poplar, produces Pitch, which is called CEDAR-PITCH.* <term>Munster</term> and <term>Avenarius</term> <note>Sebastian Münster and Johannes Avenarius, noted Hebraists</note> make use of the word Pine-tree in their dictionaries, which however will easily be excluded and rejected by all good naturalists, because it is far too twisted and full of knots and gnarls, and consequently much more unfit to build such a heavy vessel than a Fir-tree, see Fig. C. I say quite more unfit than a Fir-tree, because I am surprised that the commentators of Holy Scripture have not even thought of this tree, as it is found nowhere more than in the High German <note>German</note> translation. The Turpentine tree, which is cited by some, is not at all appropriate here, as it should be counted among the shrubs rather than the trees. Possibly those who understand the word <term>Gopher</term> to mean the Cypress tree, Fig. D, have won the prize; all the more because the first two syllables of the word Cypress tree in the Greek, Latin, and German languages, as well as in the Dutch and several other tongues, perfectly express the aforementioned Hebrew root word <term>Gopher</term> <note>Suggesting a linguistic link between the Hebrew 'GPR' and the Greek 'Kypar-issos'</note> according to the letter. Moreover, the wood of this tree is very durable, indeed almost imperishable, and subject to no decay. For this reason <term>Martial</term> Book 6, Epigram 49, says very well:

> *Which fears neither a hundred passed ages*
> *Nor the decay of long old age.*

Which in the Dutch language means as much as:

->*The noble CYPRESS WOOD lasts for a hundred centuries,*<-

The same is very common in Eastern lands, and is used there a great deal, especially for shipbuilding, for which this precious and durable wood is very suitable. For this reason it was also used in ancient times, as a certain writer testifies, for the building of that mighty fleet which <term>Alexander the Great</term> had equipped at Babylon, <term>Arrian</term> in *Life of Alexander*; <term>Strabo</term> Book 15. Possibly since the time of the Deluge the memory of the Cypress tree has remained among the heathens, by whom it was dedicated to the Hellish Prince <term>Pluto</term>, otherwise called <term>Dis</term>, King of the subterranean realms, and for that reason was placed before the houses of the deceased as a recognizable sign of mourning, according to the saying of <term>Pliny</term> Book 16, Chapter 33. Finally, to say everything in short; the matter may be as it is, as anyone wishes: whether one grants the first place to the Cedar tree, or wishes to give preference to the Cypress tree; this at least is undeniable, that this blessed refuge, devised by GOD Himself for the preservation of such a small remnant of the Human Race as <term>Noah</term> and his household were, was built from a kind of tree that produced cones and pitch or resin; all the more so, because in former centuries as well as today, it has been customary to use such wood for shipbuilding. Furthermore, if one wishes to look into this matter even more closely, everyone must confess that it would not be at all contrary to reason, nor even to the content of Holy Scripture, if in this case one allowed both the Cedar- and the Cypress-tree to stand, since one can by no means prove from the Sacred Pages that no more than one kind of tree was used for the equipping of the Ark.

# S P I R I T U A L #

especially for those who wish to travel to warm countries, one must take singular care that the ships are properly provided against all rot and vermin, and above all are tight, so that the force of the penetrating waters does not hinder them. To prevent such inconveniences, the LORD commanded *Noah* to pitch the *Ark* both inside and out. Just as in later times the *basket* <note>A small chest or cradle made of reeds</note> of bulrushes was glued with *slime* <note>The original Dutch "Lym" here refers to bitumen or mineral pitch</note> and smeared with *pitch*, in which *Moses*, still an infant, was placed by his Mother and came floating safely onto the *Nile River*. *Exod. II. v. 3.* Furthermore, it is entirely beyond doubt that the Holy Scripture, by the Hebrew word *Gopher*, did not intend to signify that it was *Camphor* <note>original: "Kamford"</note>, that precious Indian resin, as it is an entirely unsuitable means with which to pitch ships. It is just as unlikely to think that it was a mixture of lime and sand or clay, since one does not usually coat ships with those, but rather masonry buildings. In this case, the so-called *Earth-pitch* <note>original: "Aardpek"</note>, called in Latin *Asphaltum*, seems to come much closer to reaching our objective, as the builders of the Tower of Babylon made use of it for the singular strengthening of the walls. However, one may also understand by this the common *Pitch* or *Resin* that drips from the *Pine-*, *Poplar-* <note>original: "Abeel-"</note> and *Cypress-trees*. Just as today one still coats all kinds of vessels used for seafaring with such. Anyone curious to have a detailed description of its powers and uses should see the works of *Vitruvius* <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman architect and engineer</note> in *Book II, Chapter 9*, where one shall find the same to one's satisfaction.

Just as today all ships equipped for long and arduous voyages at sea have their particular compartments, rooms, and hiding places, for the people as well as for the merchandise, and all provisions and ship's stores; likewise the Ark, that wonderful and heavy vessel, had its *Nests*, as the Hebrew root word sounds, but according to the common translation, its *little dwellings*, or as others wish, its *rooms*. For it was not only necessary that the second *Adam*, I mean the Patriarch *Noah*, with the rest of his household, was well and comfortably placed; all the genera of animals also had to have a suitable hiding place, and above all, be provided with sufficient life-necessities and food for a voyage or duration of an entire year.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, there is nothing certain regarding the number, nor regarding the exact arrangement and size of the mentioned rooms or dwellings, to be reported from the Holy Scripture. Consequently, all architects, painters, and sculptors are free to divide the entire building of the Ark according to the rules of art and even according to their own pleasure, provided that nothing is produced that is contrary to the fundamental rules of architecture, and that one remains with the three decks or floors which one must observe above all in the mentioned construction, so as not to deviate from the very words of the Holy Scripture. However, it is not probable that all the mentioned rooms or small living places were of equal size, as much in their length as in their breadth and depth, since one might consider it an improper arrangement if one wished to give the same amount of space to dogs, hares, cats, and more of that sort of animals as to elephants, rhinoceroses, and crocodiles: although the equality of such stalls or hiding places would better agree with the measures of architecture. However, it will do much for our cause if one wishes to maintain a certain uniformity in all parts of this building, and, as will soon appear, make the ceilings equally high and place them on the same continuous floor; yes, even if one wished to stack the stalls or stables, which were to serve as hiding places for the lesser types of animals, above one another on the same floor. Moreover, it is well to think that the LORD GOD, that supreme and all-wise Master Builder, graciously infused or gave the most perfect idea or pattern, both of the entire design of the Ark and of the uniform division of the same, to the Patriarch *Noah*, who was without doubt quite unskilled in such a rare and unknown handiwork. Just as He afterwards also prescribed to *Moses* the pattern of the so-called Ark of the Covenant. This is absolutely evident from the clear words of the Holy Scripture: *See then that you make it after their pattern, which was shown to you on the Mountain. Exod XXV. v. 40.* Let the same be said in respect to King *David*, who openly confesses to have received the pattern of that precious and world-renowned Temple from GOD himself: *All this was made known to me in writing, says this Prophet, from the hand of the LORD, namely, all the works of this pattern. I Chronicles XXVIII. v. 19.* <note>original: "I. Paralip." refers to Paralipomena, the Greek name for the Books of Chronicles</note>

### PRINT PLATE XXXVI.

->*And this is how you shall make it: Three hundred cubits shall be the length of the Ark, fifty cubits its width, and thirty cubits its height. Genesis 6:15.*<-

Since the present object of our attention—I mean *Noah’s Ark*—is such a perfect and particularly the very first example of shipbuilding, I deem it worthwhile not only to view it from the outside but even to dissect it from within with singular accuracy, and to examine it more closely according to the measures of arithmetic, geometry, and architecture. This is all the more necessary because many among the Heathens—namely *Celsus*, whose own words are cited in the works of *Origen, Book IV* <note>original: *Lib. IV*</note>, as well as *Marcion*, *Valentinus*, the so-called *Gnostics*, and others of their following—consider this wondrous construction an unfounded and ridiculous fiction, and openly dare to mock it. It is to be lamented that the ancient Church Fathers—those religious men, those unshakable pillars of the early Church, those courageous proponents of the true religion—did not offer these intolerable mockers a more powerful resistance, nor more properly restrain the extravagance of that abandoned and unbelieving people. But, if the truth be told, it was their great inexperience in geometry that gave rise to such absurd and ridiculous sentiments, and even strengthened the Heathens in them. Similarly, even today, many capable and pious theologians—yet ignorant scriptural commentators in matters concerning mathematics <note>original: *Wiskunft*</note>—tend to commit such gross blunders. This occurs because they have the imprudence to hide their ignorance of certain uncommon subjects in the Holy Scriptures from people, sometimes putting forward quite unbecoming and unheard-of propositions and interpreting them according to their own whim. Through this, it frequently happens that the esteem and credibility of Holy Scripture is further harmed, and orthodox doctrine is brought far more disadvantage and shame than benefit and luster.

<column-break/>

Certainly *Origen* in his *Second Homily on Genesis, etc., and Book IV against Celsus* <note>original: *Hom II. in Gen. &c. Lib. IV. contr. Celfum*</note>, did not give the aforementioned Heathen mockers sufficient satisfaction, having invented for himself a geometric or so-called *Egyptian Cubit* <note>original: *Egyptifchen Elleboog*; a cubit is a unit of length based on the forearm</note> that was six times larger than the common one. This strange and abominable invention even found acceptance with the famous Church teacher *Augustine*—which is no small wonder—as can be sufficiently shown from his writings *The City of God, Book XV, Chapter 27* <note>original: *De Civ. DEI Lib. XV. C. 27.*</note>. Meanwhile, no one among the ancient writers is found who makes the slightest mention anywhere of such a geometric or so-called *Egyptian* cubit, which, as *Origen* wrongly claims, would be six times larger than the common one. In such a way, it would be by no means surprising that from such a misshapen and unheard-of blunder, a misshapen and unbelievable size of the Ark would consequently spring. For in this case—that is, if one wished to proceed according to the aforementioned cubit of *Origen*—the Ark would be *Eighteen Hundred Cubits Long, Three Hundred Wide, and One Hundred and Eighty High*. Consequently, this entire building in its totality would consist of 97,200,000 square cubits. If one now wishes to measure these imaginary cubits by the common or modern foot-measure, one will immediately find oneself fully convinced that the entire building must necessarily collapse of its own accord due to its too great and immoderate extent, since it would then amount to *Three Hundred and Twenty-eight Million well-measured feet*.

# SPIRITUAL

Although one could bring to light quite a few rare and absurd things about such an unheard-of and fabricated vessel, I will instead, for the sake of brevity, pass over all further improper consequences that could not unfairly be drawn from such an unpleasant fiction with a composed silence. However, I have seen fit, to give the curious reader greater pleasure, to present this shameful wandering of *Origen* in **Fig. II**. **Fig. I** represents *Noah’s Ark*, set in such a manner and measure as it ought to be calculated according to the correct determination of Holy Scripture.

The aforementioned Church Father *Augustine* in *The City of God, Book XV, Chapter 25* <note>original Latin: *de Civ. DEI L. XV. C. 25.*</note> committed, besides the aforementioned error, another one which was certainly no less than the first, by calculating the prescribed measure of the Ark—which GOD the LORD had explicitly commanded to *Noah*—as triple on all sides. For if one wants to calculate the entire size of the Ark according to his opinion, following fixed geometry <note>original: *Meetkunde*</note>, one will find that its true stability then amounts to *four hundred and fifty thousand cubits*: understood as its length, width, and height calculated together. One can be convinced of this as soon as the triple width of 150 is increased by the length of 300, and the resulting forty-five thousand by 1/3 of the height (10), or also the single width 50 increased by the triple length 900, and the result with 1/3 of the height. If that venerable Church Father had tripled his calculation in such a way, he would not have erred so badly. But because he took the entire extent or measure of the Ark, clearly defined in Holy Scripture, as triple from all sides, he committed a mistake of 11,700,000 square cubits; by which the imagined Ark of *Augustine* is that much larger than that of the Patriarch *Noah*. A similar gross error was made by those of *Delos* in former times, as *Vitruvius* <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer</note> in *Book III, Chapter 3, Section 14* <note>original Latin: *Lib. III. C. 3. §. 14.*</note> recounts at length, when *Apollo* advised them to double the altar. This thoughtless people, wrongly understanding the true meaning of the oracle, had the imprudence—instead of making the said altar twice as large as it was before—to double its entire extent in all its parts, by which it happened that they extended the construction of this altar not twice as large, as *Apollo* had declared to them, but eight times as far. Certainly a great misunderstanding in architecture! I have deemed it worth the effort to represent this great mistake alongside the others in **Fig. III**.

But to finally have a thorough and clear idea of the true size of the Ark, that excellent and Divine Masterpiece, it serves above all to investigate with accuracy what the Hebrew measure *Ammah* <note>Hebrew: אמה</note>—otherwise called *El* <note>ell</note>, and by the Latins *Cubitus*, that is, *Elleboog* <note>cubit; literally 'elbow'</note>—actually was and how it must be calculated by us; the more so because even today there is a general and perpetual difference over this measure among the scribes <note>biblical scholars</note>, which can never be settled by any other means than to establish once and for all a well-arranged and determined distinction between the *Sacred* or *Scriptural* cubit and the *common cubit*, about which there is likewise a great dispute among them. To better achieve our aim in this case, it will, in my opinion, be enough for the present to cite here the principal views regarding the said Hebrew measure *Ammah*, called in Dutch the *Elle*, and to choose the safest from many, since one must necessarily know beforehand in what way one shall best calculate it. To that end, I have found it most advisable to present the view of the learned *Eisenschmid* in *Of Ancient Weights and Measures* <note>original Latin: *de Pond & mens. vet.*</note> before all others, as it will provide us with no little enlightenment. This writer on weights and measures assigns the Hebrew cubit 2384/1440 of the so-called French or Parisian feet; that is 1 foot 944/1440 of the Parisian foot-measure, or 1713 1/2 or 1714/1000 Rhineland feet.

<column-break/>

that *Noah* himself and all those of his lineage likewise abstained from all carnal mingling. The lengthiness of this subject does not seem to permit the naming of all the birds in particular or the assignment of each to its specific cage; thus it will be enough to have informed the reader that there is still quite enough room remaining here for twice as many birds as are known. The nocturnal birds, such as owls, bats, etc., can conveniently be placed in the lowest story.

In the second or middle story **Y.**, one finds the stalls for all kinds of four-footed animals, which are all 7½ cubits high, although such a height is hardly required for even six genera of such animals: this is, however, not in vain, as all the others can more easily be cut in two in their height and placed one above the other. On either side, three stalls of a medium size remain, which are 5½ cubits long and wide, alongside four smaller ones, which are 5½ cubits long and 2½ wide, in which one could conveniently place more other animals of all genera. The unclean <term>swine-brood</term> <note>original: *Zwynegebroed* — pigs</note> is separated from all the other livestock and banished to the corners **X.**, which are 5½ cubits long and 2½ wide, where, directly opposite in two particular corners, one sees two necessary places where the people used to retire for the relief of their bodies <note>A polite reference to latrines or toilets</note>. Finally, letter **Z.** points out a place where the most provisions for the four-footed animals could be stored as desired.

One could, however, through more extensive and detailed elucidations of Holy Scripture—of which only the core is presented here—present without much trouble the complete drawing of the entire Ark according to various other suppositions and opinions regarding the <term>Hebrew Cubit</term> <note>original: *Hebreeuwsche Elle* — scholars often debated the exact length of the cubit, which changed the calculated size of the Ark</note>: but, if it pleases the reader, let the aforementioned descriptions suffice...

### PRINT PLATE XXXVIII.

The proposed illustration of *Noah’s* Ark, deliberately cut through the middle for greater clarity, will undoubtedly give the attentive reader a clearer and more intimate idea of this great and wondrous building. In this drawing, the letters **A B C A** indicate the very highest story—namely, the one located under the single roof—where at **a. a. a.**, next to two long galleries that stand five <term>cubits</term> <note>original: *ellen* — a unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18-22 inches</note> high, sufficient space would be found to easily place various bird nests.

**A C D D** is the third story, which is partly assigned to the birds at **a. a. a.** and will further serve as living quarters for *Noah’s* children, as well as for the granaries marked **C. C. C.** This story is 7 1/2 cubits high and also has two spacious corridors or galleries that run through the middle of the entire Ark from one end to the other.

**D D E E** is the second story, where, besides two common galleries at **b b**, one sees the stalls for the four-footed animals at **f f**, and particularly in the middle, those for the largest species at **g g**, properly partitioned. On both sides in the corners are the necessary water pumps, which were required for daily refreshment. This story is 8 cubits high.

**H I K H** is the first, or otherwise the lowest, and also the largest story of all. In its entirety, it consists of nothing but spacious pantries at **I. I. I.** and other large areas where all kinds of provisions and hand tools can be stored. This level is 14 1/2 cubits high, leaving nothing further but the single floor of the Ark at **K. K.**, or the bottom of the ship, which is commonly laden with ballast. Five cubits of height have been allocated to this area.

The calculation being thus made, one will undoubtedly find upon careful inspection—especially when the roof and the aforementioned bottom of the Ark are subtracted—that there remain 30 cubits for the height of the three stories, of which the Holy Scripture explicitly makes mention. Consequently, one must admit that there has been no deviation here from the prescribed measurements.

Furthermore, this significantly clarifies what one reads in various ways, and consequently with a certain obscurity, in the Greek, Common <note>The "Common" translation refers to the Latin Vulgate.</note>, and the Zurich-Latin translations, but which is best expressed in the Dutch with these words: *You shall make it, the Ark, with lower, second, and third stories, Gen. VI. v. 16.* In this passage, the <term>Septuagint</term> <note>original: *LXX Overzetters* — the creators of the influential Greek version of the Old Testament</note> translators, as well as *Leo Juda* <note>A Swiss Reformer and colleague of Zwingli who produced a famous Latin translation of the Bible</note>, seem to have understood not so much three specific stories, but rather their particular divisions, chambers, stalls, and other rooms placed one above the other.

### PLATE XXXIX.

Having thus far laid the foundations for the construction of the Ark, I believe it will be useful to present it half-drawn, both in this and the following plate, in such a way as it should be depicted according to the sense and principles of the famous *Sturmius* <note>Johann Christoph Sturm (1635–1703), a German mathematician and physicist who applied scientific reasoning to biblical descriptions.</note>. I do this not only to fulfill my duty to the original designer of this work—at least in part, if not in full—but especially to provide proper satisfaction to the kind reader. Furthermore, I consider it my duty to attribute any praise this remarkable work might receive not to myself, but to him alone, as he rightly deserves it.

Plate Thirty-nine **A.** shows *Noah’s* Ark floating upon the universal waters of the Deluge, almost invisible through the thick and heavy downpours of rain with which it is flooded from all sides.

### PLATE XL.

In my opinion, it will be neither uninteresting nor, I hope, unpleasant for the curious reader to see some specific depictions of the Ark that others have published, alongside the previous ones.

Based on the premise of *Sturmius* **B.**, the adjacent depiction **A.** seems to come closest; it was published by *Christoffel Murer, son of Josias*, a prominent citizen of *Zurich* <note>Original: "Zurig"</note>. He was also very experienced in history, an excellent poet, a great lover of mathematics, and a very famous painter who made his name renowned at the end of the sixteenth century. For this reason, I have seen fit to share the proposed drawing—just as it remains in my possession among other original works—with the art-loving reader.

One commonly sees *Noah’s* Ark depicted in the manner of a case or chest, see Fig. **D.**, which stands on a flat, elongated, and rectangular bottom.

Regarding our perspective drawing, which is depicted on the thirty-ninth plate, some things should be noted with attention, which one

<column-break/>

must necessarily reconcile with the literal sense of Holy Scripture.

Since the many and heavy household tasks that occurred daily in the Ark could not well be carried out without proper light, an opening was necessary, especially on every floor, to be able to perform everything properly—lest the cramped air, which otherwise could have no passage, cause any harm to humans or animals. Those who, along with the people of *Zurich*, follow the literal expression of Holy Scripture: *You shall make one window for the Ark*, and are of the opinion that there was no more than one opening in this entire building, seem to want to make the Ark into a hideous and dark dungeon rather than a comfortable and suitable dwelling, not only for all those of *Noah’s* lineage, but even for the animals. But with such translations, a good explanation or interpretation is needed, and perhaps even a proper correction: especially if one understands the Hebrew word <term>*Zohar* (Hebrew: צֹהַר): often translated as 'window' or 'skylight,' but more accurately referring to 'illumination' or 'splendor'</term>, as the nature of this sacred language actually requires, not so much as a *window*, but rather as a be-

should come from the *Creation of Light*, or to put it better and more briefly, the bright-shining sunlight itself. By its rays, the entire Ark, especially at midday, could be illuminated and brightened. According to this premise, anyone is free to assign as many windows to the Ark as there were rooms, stables, and chambers. Consequently, one may rightly reject the ridiculous opinion of certain Jewish teachers, who not only shamelessly dare to claim that there was no more than one single tiny window—and specifically only a hand-breadth wide—in this large and heavy building for its illumination; but even more rejectable, in place of this small window, they suggest a certain precious stone, undoubtedly their imagined *Carbuncle stone* <note>original: "Karbonkel-steen." In medieval and early modern lore, the carbuncle was a mythical gemstone, often identified as a deep-red garnet, believed to emit its own light in the dark.</note>, which they believe was powerful enough, through its bright and magnificent glow, to illuminate the entire Ark, even in the darkest and most hidden corners. One might, if one wished, somewhat accommodate the view of *Furtembach*, *Buteo*, and others, who likewise believe there was no more than a single small window in the Ark—especially if it had only been for a single winter, and mostly for the bears, snakes, and the so-called *Alpine* Mountain Rats, commonly called *Marmots* (and in this country called *East Indian Rats*), which spend the entire winter sleeping. It would also not have been inconvenient for bats and night owls, as that sort of bird sees well enough by night and mostly seeks to live in the dark. However, for the nature of eyesight, it would have been an unbearable and entirely contrary hardship, not only for the humans but also for the animals, and especially for *Noah’s* children. They would have spent the entire time they had to remain in the Ark in the utmost sorrow, like slaves or locked-up criminals in a dark and dismal prison. Furthermore, most animals would have run the greatest risk of immediately going blind as soon as they came into the open air and were struck by the bright sunlight after having sat fast in a dark dungeon for an entire year. One could concede that, according to the proposition of *Pelletierus*, there might have been a type of *lattice* or *grate* <note>original: "Rooster- of Traliewerk"</note> which served for illumination before the aforementioned window under the roof, being one cubit high but 300 cubits long. However, it agrees far better with the rules of architecture to assign the Ark a larger number of windows to bring sufficient light into all rooms, stables, and chambers; or rather, to say everything in one word, to use the word *Light*, as mentioned above, in place of *Window*. Without doubt, air vents were necessary everywhere in such a large and heavy building as the Ark; why then no windows? Furthermore, no mention is made in Holy Scripture of what material the aforementioned window was made; thus, one cannot say with certainty whether it was made of a certain transparent stone, or of glass, or perhaps of oiled paper. Therefore, we shall not examine this matter more closely.

Finally, let the roof of the Ark have been as it was—namely, in such a way that it could be moved, or at least opened, so that *Noah* with his wife and children could walk upon it, observe the course of the stars, and keep his logbook, commonly called a *journal* <note>original: "Journaal"</note>, from them, and hang his wet clothes or other damp things there to dry; a view that certainly does not seem strange or unreasonable to me.

Now follows the *door* of the Ark, which, according to the express command of the Supreme Architect <note>A common 18th-century reference to God as the "Great Architect of the Universe."</note>, had to be placed not in one corner or another of the Ark, but in its *side*, as Holy Scripture says—that is, in the middle of the *side*, and even in the middle story, as can be seen in the accompanying ground plan and perspective drawing of the Ark at Letter D. Regarding its size or width, nothing is mentioned in Holy Scripture; but the rules of architecture require that it be proportionate to the size of the building and correspond well with the purpose for which it was to be used. If one wishes to deduce its size by reason, it must have been at least 10 cubits high and 8 cubits wide, in order to serve as a suitable entrance for the elephants. That the same must undoubtedly have been very wide, and even such that it could not be closed by *Noah* and his family, can be sufficiently gathered from what one reads in *Gen. VII, v. 16*, where it is said *that GOD the LORD closed the door of the Ark behind him*; to which is added, *by His Word*.

### PLATE XLI.

For a singular explanation of what has been said so far about the wonderful construction of the Ark, and especially to confirm its proportions and compositions, it should be noted that even today such ships are still found in which the aforementioned proportions are followed and maintained. One does not mean to speak here of a certain freighter or merchant ship that *Pieter Janssen*, a Mennonite and citizen of Hoorn, had built in the year 1647 after the model of *Noah's Ark*, which was 120 feet long, 20 wide, and 12 feet deep. The so-called *Fluyt ships* <term>Fluyt: A type of Dutch sailing vessel originally designed as a dedicated cargo ship with a pear-shaped stern.</term>, depicted in Fig. E, are 80 feet at the bottom, 95 at the top, and consequently about 50 feet long in the middle, 9 high, and 16 feet wide: or else according to *Nic. Witsen, Shipbuilding p. 159* <note>Nicolaes Witsen (1641–1717) was a famous Dutch statesman and author of a definitive text on shipbuilding.</note> 130 feet long, 26 1/2 wide, and 13 feet, 5 inches deep.

To these *Fluyts* are added those small and light boats, depicted in Fig. G, in which a single Greenlander <note>Likely referring to the Inuit people and their kayaks, which fascinated European observers.</note> dares to venture fearlessly upon the wild billows of the boisterous sea, which are 10 feet long, 1 foot deep, and 1 1/3 wide.

However, no one should imagine that these representations are made with the intent to claim that *Noah's Ark*, with all the proportions with which it was built, is a vessel that ought to be imitated today. Certainly, neither warships nor merchant ships, if they

<column-break/>

were built according to this model, could survive at sea, much less ward off the violence of the waves, which, by their uneven striking against this heavy structure, would easily smash the prow or stern to pieces. So that from this it can be sufficiently concluded that the sea at the time of the Flood <note>original: "Zondvloed"</note> must not have been as boisterous nor as violent in its waves as it sometimes is today, but on the contrary, very still and calm of current, at least in those places where the Ark floated. Moreover, it is easy to understand that the first heavy downpours must undoubtedly have fallen without great disturbance of the air, since today it is often found that all violent rain or hailstorms are usually accompanied by heavy storms of wind. Likewise, it is well to think that the waters rising from the Deep <note>original: "Afgrond"</note> caused fewer waves the deeper the water was, as is mostly found at sea. To confirm this, one could even point to an innumerable multitude of shell and crust-like remains <note>A reference to fossils, which were often interpreted as debris from the Great Flood.</note> of the Flood, which for the most part, although they were of a very fine substance, were found whole and undamaged. This is also strengthened by the observation one should make regarding the plants of the earth, whose seeds and roots necessarily had to be replanted on those same soils and places to get their proper growth, where they were before the...

...stood [through] the Deluge. Certainly, it did not well agree with the nature of **terrestrial plants** <term>Aardgewassen: referring to land-based vegetation and crops</term> that those produced in India would be carried over to Europe, or brought to the most remote regions of the North; just as our native plants would undoubtedly not grow in hot climates. If one wishes to establish the matter thus, one might say that *Noah* had no need for a **rudder**, except perhaps only for the first two or three weeks to avoid the cliffs. But perhaps it was not necessary at all to avoid these, since the Ark was not only steered by the **Divine Providence of GOD**, but also so well preserved that it never ran the slightest risk of striking cliffs, or of being overwhelmed by the waves, or capsized by heavy storm winds.

From all that has been said so far, one might nevertheless conclude that a rounded bottom would have suited the Ark much better than an elongated square flat bottom: all the more so because it was not made to stand on solid ground, as one sees with all masonry buildings, but had to float on the

<column-break/>

water, in which all rounded bodies can be moved much more easily because they find less resistance, and can overcome the surrounding fluids with far less effort than flat and angular ones; for these, because of their corners—whether they be right angles and very strong or sharp—suffer much even without violence from light waves and run the risk of being entirely overwhelmed. For the same reason, in previous and even in later times, round towers and **bastions** <term>Bolwerken: defensive fortifications</term> were much more highly regarded by all **military architects** <term>Krygsbouwkundigen: those who design fortifications and siege engines</term> than square ones, according to the testimony of *Vitruvius, Book I, Chapter 5, Section 16* <note>original: "Vitruvius Lib. I. C. 5. §. 16." Vitruvius was a Roman architect whose works were rediscovered during the Renaissance and were highly influential in the 18th century.</note>, which round buildings, however, have today been changed into angular bastions for particular reasons and by virtue of other principles. To be sure, if one considers the matter well, one will find that *Noah's Ark*, had it not been specifically preserved by the all-governing hand of the LORD, would undoubtedly have run the greatest risk of being turned upside down even by weak winds, or of perishing by some other minor mishap.
