confusion of Languages. <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who used allegorical interpretation.</note> Namely, it is clear that a building will be so much larger and thicker as the foundation is wider. The monstrosity and the impossibility of the building are shown simultaneously in Figure I: the round shape with a point; and Figure II: an inverted Pyramid. If someone were to choose only a half-diameter <note>A radius.</note> for the height, and the entire circumference of the Earth for the foundation of the building, then according to Figure III, he would obtain a circle nearly like that of *Saturn*, <note>A reference to the rings of Saturn.</note> surrounding the Earth all around, which building would be equal in weight to the entire Globe.

Regarding the specified Height and Shape of this Tower, there is nothing certain from Holy Scripture. Therefore, one is free to visit secular sources, allowing Architects to exercise their minds—indeed, I might almost say, to invent. Just as certainly, the Jews dally with nonsense in the book *Yalkut*, <note>The Yalkut Shimoni, a medieval compilation of midrash (scriptural commentary).</note> putting the height at 27 miles, and in the book *Pirke* at 70 miles. *Jerome*, in the fifth book on *Isaiah*, from the testimony of eyewitnesses, counts 4,000 paces. *Ado* in his Chronicle has it at 5,174. The very oldest Monumental record we have after Holy Scripture is *Herodotus* in *Clio, Book I, Ch. 32*, consisting of eight Towers built one above the other, of which the lowest had the length and the breadth of a stadium: *a stadium in length and in breadth*, <note>original: "stadion tou meykos kai to euros" (Greek: στάδιον τὸ μῆκος καὶ τὸ εὖρος)</note> which, if you—following the lead of *Stephanus*—understand "breadth" to mean height, would have been 574 Parisian feet, therefore no larger than the Strasbourg Tower. <note>The Strasbourg Cathedral was one of the tallest buildings in the world at the time of this writing.</note> But regarding this Tower of *Herodotus* itself, it is uncertain whether it was our Babylonian one, or another dedicated to *Belus*? *Benjamin* <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a medieval Jewish traveler.</note> in *Bochart’s Phaleg*, Chapter 13, arrives at a height of 900 feet.

### P L A T E  LXX. LXXI.

In order that the first requirement be met, Figure I shows the ground plan of the top platform of the Tower, 198 feet in diameter, upon which both the Temple A in its center, and around it four buildings, suitable also for housing families, could be built C. C. C. C. Between the Temple and the houses is the platform B, under the open sky, or the circular street 32 feet wide, and in addition another D, outside the buildings—whether of the priests or the treasurers—of 25 feet; the first 1,632 [square feet], the latter 7,400. Four passages from the inner street to the outer one 780. Therefore, all are comfortably able to accommodate 9,812 persons, assigning 4 square feet to each person, so that on this entire surface 4,000 people could have gathered together, moving to and fro quite unhindered, and conducting their affairs. This open place stands upon a Tower 283 feet high, at whose base a staircase E rises neatly, running around the Tower, and the same being four times 8 feet wide, along which 16 people could continually climb at once toward the four quarters of the world. The second Figure also shows these stairs and the open place immediately below this uppermost Tower; and there are in total 17 such towered blocks set one above the other, the dimensions of which the following table shows.

One may freely conjecture, based on the architecture of the Egyptian Pyramids, that a building of such immense size was not entirely divided into rooms. For this reason, our architect constructed a solid central pillar (marked A, B, C, D in Figure II) in the center of each section, filled with earth, sand, and unhewn stones, upon which the subsequent sections could always be built. Around this pillar, he placed ladders and vaulted arches for each section, as can be seen in the ground plan of the uppermost tower in Figure II, and in Figure III, the elevation drawing <note>Original: "Standaafteekening", a technical term for a vertical architectural drawing showing the height and external features.</note> of the building.

The ratio of the height of the entire tower to its thickness is approximately 12 to 1; certainly not too much for a tower built in the manner of a pillar, nor even for one shaped like a spire.

<column-break/>

### PLATES LXXII. LXXIII.

Plate LXXII shows the ground plan of the entire tower, and finally, Plate LXXIII shows the elevation drawing.

It would be far too tedious, and perhaps annoying to the reader, if I were to calculate the number of laborers required for that building, as well as the number of people who could have lived at that time. Likewise, the time required to complete a building of such a vast undertaking. It will suffice to have stated in general that all the laborers—including those who relieved the others by turns every eight days, the officials, the farmers, and those who transported the provisions—amounted to the number of 1,763,128. The total population living at that time was 9,094,468 according to the lowest estimate; therefore, even if only one-fifth had been assigned to the work, it would have been sufficient. Finally, the time required was twelve years, in which the Tower of that astonishing size could have been built. Those who desire more detail may consult the renowned *Sturmius*. <note>Johann Christoph Sturm (1635–1703), a German philosopher and mathematician known for applying scientific principles to biblical accounts.</note>

All these things now are sufficient to silence those who treat this entire history of the building of the Tower of Babel as a mere fable—a charge that the heathens of old had thrown at both Christians and Jews—comparing this intention to the enterprise of the *Aloadae*, <note>In Greek mythology, the Aloadae were giant twins who attempted to storm heaven by piling the mountains Ossa and Pelion onto Mount Olympus.</note> the—

### NATURAL HISTORY. ###

The riches of the Patriarchs, as is also evident from the example of **Job**, did not consist of tons of gold or silver, nor of precious stones from both the Indies, nor of costly woven tapestries, nor of purple or purple-dyed goods, nor of silks or even more expensive fabrics, nor of long rows of gold and silver vessels of great weight. Their entire treasure consisted of livestock; **Abraham** had **sheep, oxen, and male and female donkeys and camels**, and those whom he needed—be it to graze the herds or to drive them out and in—**menservants and maidservants**. A life such as many "milk-eaters" <note>A term for people living on a simple dairy-based diet, here compared to the rural Swiss.</note> among our Swiss countrymen lead today.

**Tson** <note>Hebrew: צֹאן</note> signifies a **sheep** and a **goat**, much like the Greek **Meylon** <note>Original: *Meylon* (μῆλον), meaning sheep or small cattle.</note>. Indeed, sheep and goats have many things in common: their size, their divided hooves, the fact that males have more teeth than females, their diet, their mating season, the period of gestation, their birth, rumination, shearing, their communal life, similar diseases, and the same herbs that are harmful to both, as well as the same remedies for their illnesses. But **Tson** is a collective or plural term, meaning **sheep** as a flock of sheep, distinguished from the singular **Ze**. This is clear from **Ezekiel 45:15**: *Furthermore, a lamb from the flock, etc.* Related to this word is the word **Zain** among the Arabs, in the plural **Zeen**; the female **Zainet**, and in the plural **Zemaim**, which words signify a **sheep**. See **Meninski’s Lexicon, page 3025**.

Likewise, the word **Bakar** <note>Hebrew: בָּקָר</note> does not lack an extended meaning, being common to an **ox**, whether male or female; one might call it the **bovine species**. Indeed, it is also used for a group of **oxen**, and by the Syrians, through a misuse of the word, for all kinds of herds. Otherwise, **Bakar**—from which the Latins seem to have derived **Vacca**, a cow—signifies an ox of full age; for this reason, a calf or a young bull is called in **1 Samuel 14:32**, **Sons of Bakar**. To this belong the Arabic **Bakere, Bykar, Bewakyr** for a cow, **Baker** for an ox, and **Bakuret** for both an ox and a cow. See **Meninski’s Lexicon, pages 857, 2959, 5907**.

Next follows **Chamor**, a **donkey**, specifically a

<column-break/>

tame or **house-donkey**, so named from **Chamar**, or the Arabic **Chamara**, meaning **to be red**. For those that are gray or ash-gray in Europe are generally reddish in the East. This is why the Egyptians held the donkey in abomination, as being the same color as the red **Typhon**, <note>Original: *onodeyteinchroan* (ὀνοειδῆ τὴν χρόαν), meaning "donkey-like in color."</note>. See **Plutarch in Isis and Osiris**. From this, the Spanish call it **Burro** or **Burrico**, and the French **Bourrique**, from the Greek **Purros, Purrikos, Purrichos**, meaning **Red**; for which the later ages of the Latin language used **Burrum** and **Burricum**; and modern Greece uses **Bourrichon**. Related to this **Chamor** is the Turkish **Hymar**, with the plurals **Hamir, Humür**, and **Æhmire**, likewise **Humr, Humer**, plural **Hymar** and **Ehmer**. See **Meninski’s Lexicon, pages 1802, 1805**.

After that, following the menservants and maidservants, come **Athonoth**, the **female donkeys**, and not **Hymionoi** <note>Greek: ἡμίονοι, meaning mules.</note> or mules, as the **LXX** <note>The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators have it. It corresponds to the **Etan** of the Arabs, in the irregular plural **Meetune: Etaneb**, and in the plural **Metuna** and **Atiin**, by which they designate a **female donkey**. See **Meninski’s Lexicon, pages 4226, 5661, 5659**. Perhaps the Greeks derived **Onos** from this, the Latins **Asinus**, and the Germans **Ezel**.

The procession of **Abraham’s** livestock holdings concludes with **Gamal**, the **camel**, a word which—whether Hebrew or Chaldean—has provided the name in most other languages. The Arabs and other Easterners have very diverse and almost innumerable terms for **camels**, regarding their age, size, color, and quality. Our **Gamal** is related to **Gemel** or **Geml**, an adult camel, and **Gimal, Egmal, Gimalet, Gimalat**, plural **Gemail**. See **Meninski’s Lexicon, page 1652**.

It appears then from these enumerated riches of **Abraham** what kind of life the Patriarch led, namely a pastoral and nomadic one. His food from milk and meat and his clothing from skins were provided by the sheep and bovine species; the donkey and camel species provided transport; and to graze the herds and perform labor, the menservants and maidservants served him.

It provides linguistic connections between Hebrew, Arabic, Greek, and Latin to show how these animal names evolved and spread.</summary>

This Promise, repeated again in *Gen. XXII. 17.*, signifies a very numerous procreation, and provides an opportunity to clarify the Text through <term>modern Astronomy</term> <note>In the context of this 18th-century manuscript, "modern" refers to the era of the Enlightenment and the early use of telescopes.</note>. In the age of the Patriarchs, the knowledge of the Stars was very limited: they did not know what they could not see with their naked eyes. See the very beautiful confession regarding this by *St. Augustine* in the *City of GOD* <note>original: *Stad GODS*, referring to *De Civitate Dei*</note> in *Book XVI, Chapter 23.* Those things which he did not see, but which he foresaw with Scripture and Reason lighting the way, have been discovered—and are discovered daily—by voyages directed toward both <term>Poles</term> <note>The rotational axis points of the Earth.</note>, and by <term>Telescopes</term> <note>original: *Verrekykers*, literally "far-seers."</note>; but even where these cannot reach, perhaps *Abraham*, his eyes being enlightened by GOD who had shown him the entire array of the Heavens, saw through. And where the eyes of the Patriarch could not penetrate, even when irradiated by Divine light, there reaches the infinite Wisdom and Power of GOD himself. He, and He alone, *counts the number of the Stars; he calls them all by name, Ps. CXLVII. 4.*

The Ancients separated all the <term>fixed Stars</term> <note>Stars that appear to stay in a fixed position relative to one another, unlike planets.</note> into six or eight Ranks, and the moderns still distinguish them as such, and record them on the *Globes*, or celestial spheres, of which one must know, however, that they are depicted as they appear to

<column-break/>

our eyes: for there are perhaps among them dark and nebulous ones, which might be equal in size to, or even surpass, the Dog Star, *Sirius*, itself the brightest of the constellations. *Ptolemy* counts 1022 in total. *Tycho Brahe* 1225. The moderns, having put aside the telescopes, climb higher: *Kepler* and *Bullialdus* to 1292. *Bayer* to 1709. The renowned *Johann Gabriel Doppelmayr*, having brought the Celestial Globe into *Plate VI*, to 1949. But these are nothing at all if they are compared to the exceedingly numerous hosts discovered in the last Century by telescopes, particularly in the <term>Milky Way</term> <note>original: *Melkweg*</note>, which is a gathering of innumerable Stars. The Stage of this new World was opened by the sharp-sighted *Galileo* in *The Starry Messenger* <note>original: *Nuntio Sydereo*, p. 311</note> and *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* <note>original: *Syst. Cosm. Dial. IV. p. 509*</note>, which places must be consulted for others. I would go astray if I wished to enumerate the Stars discovered by *Galileo* himself, as well as by *Hevelius*, *Huygens*, *Hooke*, and *Cassini*. As an example, in the present Print, 78 Stars are enumerated from *Hooke's Micrographia* <note>original: *Hookius Micrograph. Obs. 50. pag. 241.*</note>, of which only six or seven were known to the Ancients.

It appears sufficiently from what has already been said, and abundantly so, that the host of the Heavens cannot be counted, nor the sand of the Sea [be measured]...

*And he said unto him: take for me a heifer of three years old, and a goat of three years old, and a ram of three years old, and a turtledove, and a young pigeon. Genesis XV. v. 9.*

<margin>* Others read *Meshulesheth* <note>original: "Meſchuleſcheth"</note> not as "three years old," but as "cut into three parts," so that the number three is applied not to the age, but to the divisions of the animals.</margin>

In this historical account of the Covenant which GOD made with Abraham, a very special ceremony appears, involving selected beasts.

*Gnegela Meshulesheth* <note>original: "Gnegela Meſchuleſcheth", Hebrew: עֶגְלָה מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת</note>, a *three-year-old Calf*; not as Kimchi, Onkelos, and others would have it—a threefold calf, or three calves, or a calf born at the third birth, which is stronger. Much less should it be understood as three types of offerings: the Burnt Offering, the Sin Offering, and the Peace Offering. Both our translations approve of *Jonathan* and the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> translators, who have *damalin trietizousan* <note>original: "damalin trietizouſan", Greek: δάμαλιν τριετίζουσαν</note>, meaning "a heifer of three years." See Jerome, who has "a three-year-old calf," and others. This animal is now "taught" or "instructed," *milmada* <note>Hebrew: מְלֻמָּדָה</note>, accustomed and willing to thresh, *ohabti ladonsch* <note>Hebrew: אֹהַבְתִּי לָדוּשׁ</note>, as in Hosea X. 11. Virgil says in the third Eclogue:

> — — — *I offer this heifer, lest you perhaps refuse,*
> (*She comes twice to the milking pail, and feeds two calves from her udder*)
> <note>original Latin: "Ego hanc vitulam, ne forte recuſes, (Bis venit ad mulctram, binos alit ubere fœtus) Depono."</note>

There follows *gnes meshulesheth* <note>Hebrew: עֵז מְשֻׁלֶּשֶׁת</note>, a *three-year-old Goat*. This noun *gnes* <note>goat</note> has passed into many other languages: from this comes the word of the Phoenicians *Aza* found in *Stephanus* where he speaks of Azotus. The *gnissa* of the Syrians and Chaldeans, in the

<column-break/>

plural *issan*, from which comes the Greek *izanei*, a *goat skin* in *Julius Pollux Book IV. Ch. 18*. The *maz, mayz, anz* of the Arabs, and *Kecy* of the Turks. See *Meninski's Lexicon pages 806, 2367, 3885, 4241*. Among the Greeks it is *aix, aigos*, among the Germans *Geiss*, and even closer among the Swiss, especially those of *Glarus*, *Giz* or *Gizlin*.

*Ail meshuballas* <note>original: "Ail meſchuballas", Hebrew: אַיִל מְשֻׁלָּשׁ</note>, a *three-year-old Ram*. The word *ail* comes from "strength." From this also comes "strong GOD" <note>El</note>. For this reason, the Pagans also depicted *Jupiter* with the face of a Ram. Because of this, *Jupiter Hammon* was attributed with ram's horns, which the *Sons of Jupiter* <note>Rulers like Alexander the Great who claimed divine lineage.</note> requested to borrow. See *Alexander* and *Lysimachus*. That ram from Asia with a larger and fatter tail is called *ejelat*. *Meninski Lexicon p. 5817*, of whom we speak elsewhere.

Then follows *Thor, Turtledove, Trugoon*. From the Hebrew *Thor* <note>Hebrew: תּוֹר</note> the Italians derive their origin *Tortora* or *Tortorella*, the French *Tourterelle*, and the High Germans *Turteltaube*.

*Gozal* <note>Hebrew: גּוֹזָל</note> signifies a *chick* of all sorts of birds, including the brood of pigeons and also of a turtledove. The Arabic word of the same name is *ganzal* or *gewzel*. *Meninski Lexicon p. 1677*. The Syrians say *zogal* for *gozal* by a transposition of letters. The Carthaginians in ancient times said *gozol*.

Abraham is commanded to offer to GOD a *Heifer*, *Goat*, and *Ram*, perhaps three years old, because these animals are at the peak of their strength at this age. Similarly, *Ganymede*, in *Lucian’s* *Dialogues of the Gods*, after being abducted by *Jupiter* and demanding to be released, promises to sacrifice to *Jupiter* *a large three-year-old Ram, which leads the flock in the meadow*. Such a Ram is called *arneios* <note>original: "arneios"</note> and *moxias* in Greek. *Hesychius* defines *arneios* as a *trieteys krios* <note>Greek: "trietēys krios", meaning a three-year-old ram</note>. The Poets call it *trikouros* <note>Greek: "trikouros"</note>, which means "thrice-shorn."

---

*And the wild Birds came down upon the carcasses, but Abram drove them away.* Gen. XV. v. 11.

Whoever understands the distinction between grain-eating and meat-eating birds—not only by their different diets but also by their body shape, particularly the beak and stomach—will not deny that by *gnait* <note>Hebrew: "Ayit", typically translated as a bird of prey or vulture</note> here, one should not simply understand a "bird" in general, but specifically a meat-eating and predatory one, such as those lured by the scent of the dead and falling upon them. The same word appears in *Job XXVIII. 7: The Bird of Prey has not known the path*: and from the Hebrew, the Greek *aetos* or *aietos* <note>Greek: "aetos", meaning an eagle</note>, an *Eagle*, the foremost among the birds of prey, perhaps originated. However, the meaning of *gnait* also extends further to other four-legged predatory wild beasts.

it lay buried under the ashes. <note>The author is citing Hesychius of Alexandria, a 5th-century grammarian.</note> Hesychius says: *an ash-cake is a type of bread made in embers, which serves as the oven.* <note>Original Greek: *enkruphias artou eidos ho en spodo genomenos to mey einay klibanon*</note>. Likewise, he mentions the *hidden hearth-cake* <note>Original Greek: *enkruptos esgarites*</note> from *eschara*, the hearth in which it is baked. *Exod. 12:39; Num. 11:8; 1 Kings 17:12, 19:6; Hos. 7:8; Ezek. 4:12.* See there, then, the delicacy of the Patriarchs! The tasty dishes for guests arriving unexpectedly. A lump of unleavened dough, kneaded with water or milk, buried in a heap of warm ash, roasted there, and cleaned of the ash with which it was sprinkled. With this food, several types of baked cakes can be compared, which nowadays are fried in a pan, either made from flour and eggs with milk, or from bread itself with eggs—pancakes—or from a lump of flour with almonds.

<margin>The *Seah* or *Satum* was the fourth rank of measure for dry goods, being the third part of an *Epha*. It *equals one and a half Italian modii* <note>Original Greek/Latin: *ischuei modion kay eimisu italikon*</note> according to *Josephus, Book 9, Chapter 2*. Consequently, the three measures in our text were one *Epha*. The size of a *satum*, the third part of an *Epha*, is set by Eifenbach in his work on weights and measures (page 172) at 674 Parisian inches; calculated by our Zurich measure, it is 6.2 small measures. I have had this depicted in the shape of a cube, with the resulting side being 8 inches and 9 Parisian lines.</margin>

<column-break/>

But the Shepherd *Abraham* also prepares a pastoral meal for his most holy guests. He entertains them as an *Alpine inhabitant of the Cevennes* <note>A reference to the simple but generous hospitality of the mountain people in the Cevennes region of France.</note> might receive a Prince in his hut. He gives what he has; the herds and the dairy are at hand. He runs with joy to the *bakar* <note>Hebrew: cattle</note>, and *takes a calf, tender and good*, which to the Jews was not only food but a delicacy. And indeed it is; if any meat is tender, it is veal, being very easy to digest and dissolve into the best chyle <term>chyle: a milky fluid produced during digestion</term> and gastric juices, overflowing with parts suitable for nourishing the body.

There is *Milk* as well, the noblest fluid separated from the blood in the breasts or udders—the "flower of the blood." Its dried part provides cheese, its fatty part butter, and its liquid part whey; all very necessary components capable of nourishing the body, which is evident in those who live primarily on milk, for whom it is very pleasant. To the milk, butter is added, as seen in *Deut. 32:14* and *Judges 5:25*. The word used is *Chemea*, and in *Job 19:16*, *Chemah*, which perhaps finds its origin in the Arabic *Chamah*, meaning to be thick or clotted.

A completely different cause is attributed to the Rain which is now being discussed. From Heaven, elemental sulfur was cast down; it was not scattered as insensitive, very light fibers, but was poured out of jars—not as a non-flammable substance, but ignited, namely by the breath of GOD’S wrath.

*Brimstone and Fire* <note>original: "Ferith Vaësch"</note>, an example of a more earnest preparation of Fire, through which all houses, trees, humans, and beasts encountered were slain. *Brimstone mixed with Salt and Pitch*, as is evident from *Deuteronomy 29:22: When they shall see the plagues of this land and the sicknesses thereof, wherewith the LORD hath afflicted it. v. 23. That the whole land thereof is brimstone, and salt, and burning, that it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein, like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the LORD overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath.* Those Sodomite villains had not only to perish, but the region itself had to be devastated—the land which had carried the most ungodly of all that walked on two feet—the Cities and the entire plain (the surrounding region) together with the vegetation of the Earth [*all that lived*]. That Garden of the LORD *Gen. 13:10* was changed into a Wilderness, even into a Salt Sea. *Gen. 14:3.*

The saddest Monument, namely of this overthrow, is the Dead Sea, called the *Asphaltic Lake*, from *Asphaltus* or Pitch mixed with Brimstone, which floats in abundance upon that water. *Salt Sea* <note>original: "Jam Hammelach"</note>, so called as much for its excessive saltiness as for its infertility. See *Justin, Book 36. 3. 6; Diodorus Siculus, Book 19. 98; Tacitus, History, Book 5, Chapter 6.* And that the Ancients judged from the remains, which were susceptible to

flame, that the devastating Fire had been there in former times, is evident from the 16th Book of *Strabo*. And who would not judge from this, *the turning of fruitful Land into salty ground (Psalm 107:34)*, just as one judges the Flood from the monuments of the Deluge? The Sodomites had to perish by Fire, just as the inhabitants of the first world perished by Water; and those who were delighted by the stench of their flesh <note>A reference to their perceived moral decay and carnal sins.</note> had to be consumed by the stench of Brimstone and Pitch.

So hideous is that execution of punishment by Fire and Brimstone taken upon those of *Sodom*, that it can show, as in a Painting, that final burning of the Earth *Luke 18:29, 30; Jude verse 7.* Regarding the precise manner in which this punishment will be carried out, nothing specific can be determined, nor should it be: burning sulfur falling not only as drops mixed with salt, but a terrifying storm having arisen, the thunderclaps breaking the air and causing it to tremble, the lightning shooting out here and there, the flashes of light cast out abundantly, through which, according to the Scriptures, four Cities were overturned. *Strabo 13.* But it is also probable that the Earth contributed its part to this, that Fire flowed from torn-asunder cracks—even streams as of burning Pitch, previously hidden in the bowels of the Earth. This reasoning can be confirmed by the remains of that sulfurous earth, the transformation of the most fertile Valley into a most stinking marsh, and the swallowing up of the *Jordan*, which flowed through the Valley, of which *Strabo* gives testimony *Isaiah 1:9.* None of the Sodomites had the power to escape, but *Lot* with his Daughters was led out by the Angels.

THE Wife of Lot looked back, *into the things behind* <note>original Greek: "eis ta opizoo" (εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω)</note>, that is, backwards, being on the same journey with Lot and the Daughters, in the same company as is commonly depicted. *From behind him*, like the Hebrew *from behind him* <note>original Hebrew: "meacherau" (מאחריו)</note>, similar to our Latin translation; namely, that Lot had already entered the City of Zoar. Thus the Latin does not agree with our Dutch version, since the latter simply has, *behind him, behind himself, after him, she after him, Lot*. Yet both could have occurred: she may have curiously looked behind herself and behind him, or even stepped back, or thought of returning, which may be guessed from the warning of the Savior in *Luke 17:32: Remember Lot's wife.*

Of greater importance and difficulty is the dispute over the *Pillar of Salt*, into which Lot's Wife was transformed. Some say she was burned by sulfur, as *Aben-Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (1089–1167), a significant Spanish Jewish scholar and biblical commentator.</note> maintains; others take the word *salt* <note>original Hebrew: "melach" (מלח)</note> metaphorically as a sign of eternity, so that a *pillar of salt* <note>original Hebrew: "netziib melach" (נציב מלח)</note> is a pillar of eternal destruction, intended to last forever: just as in *Numbers 18:19*, a *Covenant of Salt* is taken to mean a lasting agreement that shall never cease. From this has sprung the embellishment regarding the durability of this Monument, which *Josephus* <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note> confirms with his own eyesight. The over-credulous Church Fathers, such as *Tertullian* in *On Sodom* <note>original Latin: "De Sodoma Carm." (a poem attributed to Tertullian).</note> and *Irenaeus* in *Book IV, 51*, go so far as to claim that until their times it had not only retained its external shape but also the distinction of its sex, and even undergoes the female cycles <note>A legendary claim that the pillar of salt continued to menstruate.</note>. All antiquity has a way of growing larger. We believe before we see. We approach holy things as if pickled by prejudices, and our eyes become enchanted, so that the soul stops investigating. And what if those who live nearby draw foreigners to them and perhaps find a profit therein—one not to be despised? It becomes a sort of Religious Pilgrimage, or at least a curious one. There have indeed been covenants confirmed by Salt, just as Sacrifices were introduced with Salt; yet Salt is no symbol of eternity, as a body can be dissolved by water, whereas Iron and Flint are far more durable.

<column-break/>

*Heinsius* in his *New Testament Exercises* <note>Daniel Heinsius (1580–1655), a famous Dutch scholar and poet.</note> fills in the meaning of the phrasing. A *pillar of salt* <note>original Greek: "Steyley halos" (στήλη ἁλός)</note> is as much as an "evil" *pillar of salt*, just as in the Song of Solomon: *Your eyes are Doves' eyes*, meaning, like those of a Dove. Namely, the one looking back had her affection fixed [on the city] rather than undergoing a physical transformation into a Pillar of Salt. A sensible interpretation, provided it were true.

Other Interpreters are not so much pleased by the destruction of her physical substance as by the addition of something of another nature. They claim that she became stiff, being filled with Salt inside and out. And lest anyone think that this Monument would be no less eternal than modern petrifactions—which often last scarcely a few months or years—they bring as examples the eternal rocks of mined Salt in *Africa, Tartary, India, Arabia, Poland, Transylvania, and Spain*, of which *Pliny* writes in *Book 21, Chapter 7*: The same Salt is invincible even against Iron. One also finds the Houses of Salt of the *Gerrheans* in *Strabo*, Book 16. Also mentioned are those Bavarian Peasants with their Cows who, being seized by an earthquake and infectious air, were changed into salt Statues, according to *Aventinus* <note>Johannes Aventinus (1477–1534), a Bavarian Renaissance humanist historian.</note> in the *Bavarian Annals*. Such stories are suspicious; natural history provides corrections.

The question has long been contested: should the transformation of *Adith* (as the Jews call Lot’s wife) into a pillar of salt be counted among the miracles? Some are for the affirmative opinion, others for the negative. Perhaps both are not entirely right, because the manner in which this happened is not known. It is certainly a very rare proof,

...yes, the only thing, of Divine severity.

God did not lack for materials in nature itself to overturn the cities of **Sodom** and to make the wife of **Lot** stiff. The resources were at hand. And a Philosopher <note>The author uses "Philosopher" here in the historical sense of a "natural philosopher" or scientist.</note> is free to devise means by which this *salt-transformation* could have been brought about. One is free to suggest on this stage various petrifications, wrappings, embalmings, or even vitrifications <note>The process of turning a substance into glass through heat.</note>. Indeed, the body of this wretched woman could have been so filled, inside and out through all the pores, by salt-earth particles that what was previously soft and yielded to the touch became as hard as a stone: that which was previously subject to decay and decomposition thereafter became incorruptible and resistant to the touch. There are countless examples of such petrifications involving wood, fruit, shells, bones, animals, and plants: she could have been covered with a stony or saltpeter-salty crust and thus preserved from the decaying action of the air, and **Adith** <note>Adith is the traditional name for Lot's wife in Jewish Midrash.</note> could thus have been embalmed while still alive. Examples are provided by fruits and small animals encased in amber, others in stone-turning waters, and everything that appears when thrown into a crust-forming liquid. She could have—as **Wedelius** <note>Georg Wolfgang Wedel (1645–1721), a German physician and scholar.</note> suggests in his work *On the Destruction of Sodom and the Form of Salt*—been turned to glass by the fire of lightning: which happens to all kinds of translucent bodies placed at **Tschirnhausen** <note>Refers to the experiments of Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhausen (1651–1708), who used large burning mirrors to melt materials.</note>: the wretched woman could have—as **Sturmius** <note>Johann Christoph Sturm (1635–1703), a German philosopher and mathematician.</note> argues in *Inquiry into Holy Scripture, p. 167*—been seized by a sulfurous stream, wrapped in liquid sulfur-earth, buried under other sandy substances and earthen materials, and found in such a grave after the sad event had ended.

**Le Clerc** <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Genevan theologian known for his rationalistic approach to the Bible.</note> weakens this matter, according to his custom, in his *Treatise on the Pillar of Salt*. To him, ***Netzib*** <note>The Hebrew word used in Genesis 19:26 for "pillar."</note> is not a *Statue*, but generally something *hard, stiff, and unmoved*. According to **Philo**, they are said *to be turned into a pillar in the manner of a lifeless and mute stone* <note>original Greek: "apsychou kai kophys lithou tropon stylitheusthai"</note>. The High German <note>Meaning the German language.</note> way of speaking agrees with this: *He stands like a stick: He stares or towers like a log.* The word ***melach*** signifies not only salt, but also barren earth, salty-tasting, like that found at the Dead Sea. *Deuteronomy 29:23, Psalm 107:34*, where the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint (LXX), the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> have *briny* <note>original Greek: "halmuris"</note> and *salt* <note>original Greek: "halmy"</note>. Thus **Lot's** wife would have perished in a salty

<column-break/>

land, being stiff with fear, falling down dead, or perhaps smothered by the vapor of sulfur and pitch. Using such a figure of speech, the heart of **Nabal** is said *to have died within him, so that he became like a stone. 1 Samuel 25:37.* **Ariadne**, in **Ovid**, is related to the name of **Adith** in this regard:

> Or looking out at the sea, I sat cold upon a rock; And as much as the seat was stone, so much a stone was I myself, <note>original Latin: "Aut mare prospiciens in saxo frigida sedi; Quamque lapis sedes, tam lapis ipsa fui." From Ovid's Heroides.</note>

From this comes the transformation of **Niobe**, the daughter of **Tantalus**, into a stone, which in **Cicero’s** *Tusculan Disputations III* signifies a constant sorrow arising from the loss of her children. But **Clemens of Alexandria** places this history of **Niobe** in comparison with this one of ours regarding the Wife of **Lot**, *Exhortation, page 65.* Anyone who wishes to see these thoughts of **Le Clerc** refuted at length should consult the *Treatise of Witzius on the Wife of Lot* <note>Herman Witsius (1633–1708), a Dutch theologian who defended traditional orthodoxy.</note>. He cannot tolerate that **Le Clerc** presumes to force the Scripture into the twisting of his logic, and he shows that ***netzib*** nowhere in the Holy Biblical page signifies someone being stunned, like a statue unmoved, but rather a statue or a fortification: that **Philo** himself has stated in express words the transformation of that woman into a Statue: that ***melach*** means salt, but ***melecha*** means barren Earth, and if the meaning that **Le Clerc** gives to these words were adopted, the Text would have to be translated: *And the Wife of Lot became very stunned, a barren ground, which is an entirely nonsensical meaning.*

On the same bench with **Le Clerc** deserves to be placed **Hermannus van der Hardt** <note>Hermann von der Hardt (1660–1746), a German historian and orientalist known for his unconventional theories.</note> regarding the *Monument of the Wife of Lot*, who maintains that **Lot's** wife, just like the citizens of **Sodom**, perished entirely by fire, but that afterwards either **Lot** himself, or his descendants, the **Ammonites** and the **Moabites**, erected a Memorial or Grave-statue in memory of what happened.

This same Monument to this wretched woman has been found in Europe, in the field near **Bologna**, according to **Hermann’s** *Treatise on the Fate of Lot's Wife*, in that inscription which has tortured the minds of the Learned until now, which epitaph he skillfully applies to the **Wife of Lot**. Behold the same, translated according to the letter:

*And to Sarah he said: See, I have given your Brother a thousand pieces of Silver. Genesis 20:16.*

The word *keseph* <note>Hebrew: כֶּסֶף</note> has many meanings: it signifies 1. Silver, the Metal. 2. Silver money, just as the French use the word *Argent* <note>meaning both "silver" and "money"</note>, indeed money made from any kind of metal: as the Greeks say, "money is any coinage, whether in copper, in silver, or in gold" <note>original Greek transliteration: "varinus argurion pan nomisma eit en kalko eit argurio eit en chrusoo"</note>. A piece of silver refers to any coin, whether in copper, silver, or gold coinage. 3. All kinds of goods and riches. This is how the complaint of *Rachel* and *Lea* must be understood in *Genesis 31:15, 16.* The triple meaning of the word finds no place here because of the added number *thousand*, unless one establishes that *Abimelech* intended to express a large but uncertain number through a specific one,

<meta>This page continues the philological discussion of the Hebrew word for "silver" (keseph) and transitions into a numismatic study of ancient Jewish coinage, specifically the shekel. It links the previous page's mention of Abimelech's gift to Abraham with historical weights and measures.</meta>

<page-num>124</page-num>
<header>SPIRITUAL</header>
<meta>catchword: to</meta>

just as we High Germans often say: *I would not take a thousand Guilders and do this or that.* <note>original German: "Ich wolte nicht tauſend Gulden nehmen, und diſs oder jenes thun."</note> This is why we prefer, in the fourth place, to understand *keseph* <note>Hebrew: "silver"</note> as a coin known to the Hebrews made of silver, called a shekel.

It is not at all clear from this text whether the Shekel was weighed by the balance scales or the steelyard, or if it was minted money. But it is certain from other passages, and the entire description of the Shekels, that they were weighed. *Genesis 23:16. And Abraham weighed to Ephron the silver which he had named in the audience of the sons of Heth, four hundred shekels of silver, current money with the merchant.* Indeed, even today the most learned scholars maintain that the Jews in the Old Testament, except perhaps in the time of the Maccabees, had no minted money. <term>Maccabees: A Jewish dynasty that ruled Judea in the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, known for revolting against the Seleucid Empire.</term> If anyone suspected the quantity, whether together or separately, they could resort to weight, or test the quality of the metal with a touchstone or another trial. Mention of weighing is also made long after these times. *1 Chronicles 21:25. Jeremiah 32:9. So I bought the field from Hanameel, my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth: and I weighed him the money, seventeen shekels of silver.*

But the value of the shekel, *sekel*, both in weight and in currency, remains to be investigated. The guiding torch shall be the passage in *Matthew 17:24*, from which it appears that a *stater* <term>stater: an ancient Greek silver coin</term> was equal in value to a quadruple *didrachme* <term>didrachme: a silver coin worth two drachmas</term>, because it was sufficient to pay the didrachmas for the Savior and for *Peter*. And on the other hand, that every Jew had to pay half a Shekel every year for the Temple, which was this very same Didrachme. A Shekel is therefore a quadruple Didrachme. However, *Josephus*, who was very experienced in Jewish affairs, teaches us in *Book III, Chapter 9 of the Antiquities of the Jews*, that a Shekel consists of four *Attic Drachmas*. Therefore, the weight of an *Attic* quadruple Drachma must be examined. On this point, *Eisen-schmid* in *Weights and Measures, page 53*, is more pleasing than others. He, and before him *Montanus*, *Mersennus*, and *Villalpandus*, found the weight of the Hebrew Shekel to be 268 Paris *Azen* <term>Aas (plural Azen): a very small unit of weight used in Northern Europe for precious metals; about 0.05 grams</term>, which is 8 more than the old Roman half-ounce, but 64 grains lighter than the *Attic* quadruple Drachma; this same weight corresponds to 320 barleycorns, which is how many the old Rabbis give to a Shekel. These 268 *Azen* converted into a medicinal pound give 3 Drachmas, 2.8 Scruples, 90 Grains. *Bernardus* has it differently, who

<column-break/>

gives a quadruple Didrachme of the Jews 288 mint-grains, which correspond to 351 Paris grains. But in monetary value, a Shekel is worth 45 German *Kreutzers*. Therefore, the 1000 Shekels given or weighed by *Abimelech* to *Abraham* would amount to 475 ounces, 9 grains, or 950 *Lothonen* <note>Loths: a pre-metric unit of weight equal to about half an ounce</note> and 9 grains, or 750 guilders: thus, other passages of Holy Scripture occurring here and there which mention Shekels must and can be interpreted.

However, however consistent the proof may be from the scholars of this age—that in the Old Testament until the time of the Second Temple no coins with any image were struck by the Jews, but only silver plates weighed by weight, and that all those Shekels marked with Samaritan letters do not date back further than the age of the Maccabees, and those bearing Hebrew letters not even to that time—it will nonetheless, I hope, not be unpleasant to the reader of this work if I set down in a full print-plate the list of these coins, which has been gathered both from various writers and from coin cabinets by *Joan Baptist Ottius*, Archdeacon of the Church in Zurich, a man very famous for his linguistic scholarship and splendid merits.

N. 1. Shows on one side the name of *Simon*, and a *Palm Tree*, on the other side the leaf of a *Balsam Tree*, or rather of a *Vine*, with the inscription: *The redemption of Jerusalem.*

N. 2. Has the same inscriptions, but on one side a Palm Tree with two vessels or earthenware pots: on the other side two other vessels, from which a plant sprouts.

N. 3. On one side the name of *Simon*, within a crown or wreath, on the other side an earthenware pot or jug with a handle, and a branch of the redemption of Jerusalem:

N. 4. 5. 6. On the front side they show the building of the Temple with the name of Simon; on the back side, the Redemption of Jerusalem, and a bundle, seemingly of grain.

N. 7. The name of *Simon* on the front with a bunch of grapes, the Redemption of Jerusalem on the other side with a lyre.

N. 8. Under the same inscriptions it depicts a lyre, on the other side a branch of a tree, or an ear of corn in a crown.

N. 9. Is said to show the second year of Zion's Redemption, which falls in the 139th year before the birth of the Savior.

N. 10. 11. The fourth year after the permission—

# SPIRITUAL MATTERS

...[crea]ted, and has been preserved for so many centuries for this special use <note>A reference to the Jewish midrash that the ram offered by Abraham was created at the twilight of the sixth day of creation</note>. Thus speaks *Jonathan* in his commentary, and *Rabbi Solomon Tanchuma* <note>Rabbi Solomon refers to Rashi, and Tanchuma refers to a collection of homiletic midrashim</note>. The Providence of infinite wisdom has provided for it there, in which *Abraham* trusted when he said to his son in *verse 8*: "**God will provide himself a lamb for a burnt offering**." This Providence also gave the name to the place in *verse 14*: "**The LORD will provide**," or "**THE LORD SHALL BE SEEN**" <note>original: "De HEERE ZAL GEZIEN WORDEN," a translation of Jehovah Jireh</note>. We do not inquire too anxiously where this Ram came from, as it could very easily have wandered away from a flock and, through God’s governance, fallen into *Abraham's* hands.

Something similar is read in the mythology of the Greeks regarding *Iphigenia* and her father *Agamemnon*; she was dedicated to *Diana* <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Artemis</note> and, when she was about to be sacrificed by the hands of *Calchas*, was rescued by a Hind, which boldly placed itself before the Altar. You have here our own history, if you change *son* <note>original Latin: "filium"</note> into *daughter* <note>original Latin: "filiam"</note>, changing the "u" to an "a"; *Isaac* into *Iphigenia*, *Abraham* into *Agamemnon*, and the *Ram* into a *Hind*. In the same way, the fable of *Helena* can be substituted, and in her place a heifer-calf put by *Aristodemus*; there, *Helena* having been placed at the altar so that she might be sacrificed for the welfare of the people while the Plague raged, a descending Eagle snatched the sword and, flying down upon a heap of beasts, placed it upon a heifer. Or even this similar tale from the *Italica* of *Aristides* regarding *Valeria Luperca*.

The Ram tangled in the bushes by its horns also tangles the interpretations of the Commentators—namely, whether it was a thick thorn-bush or merely a tangled one. *Jonathan* says that it was held in the woods; *Onkelos* <note>Author of the famous Aramaic Targum of the Torah</note> says in the *Tree*; the *Syriac Translation* says in the *Branches*; the *Arabic* version published in Paris says in the *Branches of the Trees*; the *Arabic* version of *Erpenius* <note>Thomas Erpenius, a 17th-century Dutch Orientalist</note> says in the *thorns*; *Aquila* <note>A 2nd-century translator of the Hebrew Bible into Greek</note> uses *dense* <note>original Greek: "fuchuo" (συχνοῦ), meaning frequent or thick</note>, namely of trees. *Symmachus* uses *in the net* <note>original Greek: "diktuoo" (δικτύω)</note>; the *Septuagint* and *Theodotion* use *a Sabek plant* <note>original: "phuto sabek"</note>, which *Sabek* is translated by *Hesychius* as *depth* <note>original Greek: "bathos" (βάθος)</note>, where without doubt one should read *bramble* <note>original Greek: "batos" (βάτος)</note>; *Cyril* and *Phavorinus* use *Golden-herb* <note>original: "Chryfolachanum," likely referring to Orache</note>, a kind of mild herb, though *dense* <note>original Greek: "puknos" (πυκνὸς)</note> is better, as *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart, a French Protestant biblical scholar</note> reads. *Chryfogonon* <note>Golden-knee or Leontice chrysogonum</note>, according to *Dioscorides*, is a *shrub* <note>original Greek: "thamnus" (θάμνος)</note>, a thick bush whose leaves resemble those of oak trees. At this point, I would grant the Painters and Sculptors the same freedom they are otherwise accustomed to using.

I leave the Literary details to the Critical Remarks; for the Jews, the matter of a ram 2000 years old, tangled in the trees by the Devil; for the Jurists, the dispute of whether *Abraham* could make an offering to GOD of someone else's property; and finally, for the Theologians, the spiritual Application of the Ram to CHRIST.

->*And the first came out, red; he was entirely like a hairy garment; therefore they named him Esau.* Gen. XXV. v. 25.<-

->*Red-haired ESAU, in what state do you appear?*<-

Of the twins whom *Rebecca* had carried, *Esau*—otherwise also called *Seir* and *Edom*—emerged first, "the first-born came out red, all over like a hairy skin" <note>original Greek: "exeilthe o prototokos purrhakis holos hosei dora dasus"</note>, in a word, red and hairy, just as the Poets depict the *Satyrs*. For this reason, those who played the roles of the Wood-gods <note>the Roman *Silvani* or *Fauns*</note> in the theaters were clothed in the skins of goats or young deer. *Pliny* <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist</note> makes mention in his *Book V, Chapter 8* and in his *Book VI, Chapter 30* of *Satyrs* dwelling in the neighborhood of *Ethiopia*. Nowadays, there is no certainty regarding such creatures. Thus, there is no doubt that the Ancients mistook beasts of human stature—such as Apes, Guenons <note>long-tailed monkeys</note>, and Simians, which imitate human form and manners—for *Satyrs*. To this category belongs especially that *Orangutan* <note>at this time, the term was often used for chimpanzees or other great apes</note> brought over from *Angola* and presented to his Highness FREDERICK HENRY, Prince of *Orange*. *Tulp* <note>Nicolaes Tulp, a famous 17th-century Dutch physician</note>, in his *Observations, Book III, Chapter 56*, calls this creature a "man of the woods" and titles it with the name of an Indian Satyr. As we present this creature in the accompanying Print, it will not be beside the point to add the description itself to the image:

> "into the pillow, and covering his body
> "becomingly with the blanket,
> "he tucked himself in just as if
> "the most delicate person had lain there.

Meanwhile, I do not intend by this comparison to suggest that *Esau* was a Wood-god, a *Satyr*, or that the *Esauite* lineage were animals in human form. I regard *Esau* as a "monstrosity" <note>Dutch: *wandrogtigen*, referring to a biological anomaly</note> or as a fetal birth whose hairiness may have been shaped by the mother's imagination <note>a reference to the historical theory of "maternal impression," where a mother's thoughts or sights could affect the fetus</note>, or perhaps he was simply born with a red complexion, although there are many children who come into the world with red or ruddy coloring.

### ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXV.

> And Jacob gave Esau bread, and the lentil stew: and he ate, and drank, and he stood up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright. Gen. XXV. vs. 34.

->*Softly, ESAU! contemplate your reckless existence,*<-
->*The lentil stew shall betray you through its taste,*<-
->*And wring the birthright out of your hands:*<-
->*But it seems you cannot restrain your lust and greed,*<-
->*The pottage compels you by its scent to its delicious flavor,*<-
->*And JACOB gives it to you with joy and delight,*<-
->*For the birthright, which he has obtained.*<-
->*So little can man sometimes curb his desire,*<-
->*That he gives the most precious pledge for a little pleasure,*<-
->*When he lives too unthinkingly and only for himself;*<-
->*This is evident in ESAU, who the right of the firstborn,*<-
->*Through JACOB'S lentil pottage, has forever lost.*<-

---

See here the simplicity in eating, and the contempt for the most precious thing, the Right of the Firstborn! See there, sons! even the thrifty children of a very wealthy Father! devoted to frugality! *Esau* living from the hunt, bringing home dishes from the wild game of the field; *Jacob* eating bread, and Lentils *Gnadazim* <note>original Hebrew: "nezid adashim" (lentil stew)</note>, or a dish, a porridge of lentils! A food—the simpler, the better; the older, the simpler. Nature and Necessity taught the Ancients simplicity: "That the *Arcadians* eat acorns, the *Argives* apples (which are called *Appia*), the *Athenians* figs, the *Tirynthians* wild pears: the *Indians* reeds: the *Caramannians* dates, the *Sarmatians* and *Maeotians* turpentine <note>likely terebinth resin</note>, and the *Persians* garden cress," as *Aelian* testifies in his *Various History, Book III*. 

Now, excess and the variety of food corrupt the inhabitants of the Earth; in the old days, the stomach's juices were healthy and simple, but here they are diverse, a fruit made of many complex parts. In that time, the stomach easily submitted to common things, though they were not necessarily of the noblest sort, such as legumes, and among them this *Lentil*. The Lentil—called *gnadas* <note>likely a corruption of "adash"</note>, *phakey*, or *phakos* <note>original Greek: "phake" or "phakos"</note>—was held in great value by the Greeks and was particularly pleasing to the Philosophers. One reads in *Athenaeus* that *Zeno* <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism</note> cooked lentils. Indeed, in the same author's fourth book, it was a commandment of the *Stoics* "that a wise man must do everything rightly, and diligently pickle lentils." And in *Pliny*, one finds in his *Book XVIII, Chapter 12*, that a certain tolerance arises in authors who eat them. From this perhaps, whether by the guidance of Reason, Experience, or Prejudice, the *lentil* was the food of the *Stoics*, who became slow and gentle from eating lentils. 

"We find the bean to be the food of the *Egyptians*, for there in *Egypt* it grows abundantly, which is why the *Alexandrian* bean is highly esteemed and is imported into our lands, as if no bean grew here. Therefore, *Esau*, through his desire for *Egyptian* food, lost the first place." *Augustine on Psalm XLVI.* Nevertheless, the *Egyptian* lentil was food for poor people and was not of high value among the Romans of old. We have *Martial* as a witness:

<column-break/>

> *Receive the Nilotic lentil, the Pelusian gift;*
> *It is cheaper than spelt, but more precious than the bean.*
<note>original Latin: "Accipe Niliacam Pelusia munera Lentem / Vilior est Alica, carior illa Faba."</note>

Indeed, even among Physicians, this food is not much praised; it is full of bad humors, *kakochumos* <note>original Greek: "kakochymos," meaning producing bad bile or fluids</note>, and hard to digest, *duſpeptos* <note>original Greek: "dyspeptos"</note>, hindering bowel movements and causing wind, although in medical practice it is considered an infallible remedy for driving out smallpox. What kind of Lentil this actually was that was set before *Esau*—whether the common Lentil or the Great Lentil—is not sufficiently clear. In this illustration, Figure I represents the former, Figure II marks both, and Figure III represents them all. The doubt falls over the red color of that stew...

stew, *red pottage* <note>original Greek: "hepsematos pyrrou," meaning a boiled red dish</note>, that red [dish] of verse 30. From the Text, it does not sufficiently appear whether this color should be attributed to the Lentils or to the sauce. ### ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXVI.

*And he dreamed, and behold a ladder set up on the earth, and the top of it reached to heaven: and behold the angels of God ascending and descending on it.* Gen. XXVIII. v. 12.

->*Sleep, Father JACOB! sleep peacefully on your stone,*<-
->*Where GOD, through your dreaming, makes you hear His prophecy!*<-
->*A rank of Angels climbs from above to below,*<-
->*And back up again, while this sound flies through your ears.*<-
->*This land, upon which you rest, is for you and your Seed;*<-

->*My favor shall always accompany you wherever you go,*<-
->*And your Progeny shall live here on these grounds,*<-
->*Until it spreads to the North, and South, and East, and West;*<-
->*Yea, I shall bless all other Nations in your Seed.*<-
->*I am with you, and always ready for your protection,*<-
->*So that, wherever you travel, no disaster shall befall you.*<-
->*Refreshing Dream! how you have awakened the mind*<-
->*Of JACOB to praise his GOD,*<-
->*Who foretold him the salvation of such abundance,*<-
->*That one could sooner count the Stars than his Progeny.*<-

<column-break/>

There is in all Dreams something that exceeds our understanding, indeed, something in all sensory perception that leads us immediately to GOD. For what similarity, I ask you, is there between a physical thing and the idea of the soul? What connection is there between a thing seen, heard, tasted, or felt long ago, and the thoughts which I renew in my mind while sleeping? And yet the distinction is very great, the chasm immeasurable, between natural and Divine Dreams. In the former, the matter is imagined according to the guidance of Nature, according to the Laws given by GOD; here, however, GOD works independently of His usual Laws, immediately upon the mind of Man, and reveals to him that which He wills. Entirely in the same way as He has revealed Himself to others through a Vision, and to others *mouth to mouth* <note>meaning direct, face-to-face communication</note>; so here to *Jacob* He reveals Himself through a *dream*. In such a manner, GOD has revealed still-hidden matters in dreams to *Abraham*, *Abimelech*, *Laban*, *Joseph*, *Pharaoh*, *Solomon*, *Nebuchadnezzar*, *Daniel*, *Judas Maccabeus*, *Joseph* <note>the husband of Mary</note>, *the Wise Men*, *Pilate’s Wife*, and *Paul*. But in the Men of GOD, the interpretation of Dreams is Divine; in others, it is vain and ridiculous. The Ladder which the Patriarch saw belongs to another place and is not within our current scope <term>scope: the "bestek" or specific plan/framework of this natural history series</term>.

S P I R I T U A L

# ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXVII.

> *Then Jacob rose up early in the morning, and took the stone that he had put for his pillows, and set it up for a pillar, and poured oil upon the top of it. And he called the name of that place Beth-El: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first. Gen. XXVIII. v. 18, 19.*

->*The Patriarch anoints the stone on which he rested,*<-
->*And calls the land of Luz now BETH-EL, as if reborn,*<-
->*And chosen as a possession for his Lineage,*<-
->*Thus he finds through sleep a pleasant delight;*<-
->*The body is refreshed, his senses are exalted*<-
->*By the salvation which GOD allowed him to envision while sleeping.*<-

Who would believe that this text belongs to the discourse on Minerals <term>Mynstoffen: a 17th-century term for minerals or fossils</term>, specifically the discourse on Stones—indeed, the history of Thunderstones—or at least that it would provide enlightenment regarding the obscurities of the most ancient writers? I will willfully pass over the trifling stories of the Jews regarding this Stone, which *Jacob* used for a pillow and which he erected into a pillar: that it was set as a navel on the center point of the Earth, indeed, that it is the foundation of the entire Earth, particularly of the Temple of the LORD, and is therefore called the *Stone of Foundation*. They say that GOD sealed the mouth of the great Abyss with it; that it was placed by *Solomon* in the Sanctuary; and that the name *Jehovah* was engraved upon it—which, having been stolen, allowed JESUS to perform his miracles <note>These references come from Jewish commentaries like the *Pirke Rabbi Eliezer* 235, *Targum Jonathan* on Exodus 28, and the Talmudic tractate *Yoma* f. 53, 54</note>. Whether it was the Stone itself, the memory of it so sacred to the Jews, or even the name, it passed over to the Pagans. He who gave the name to *Beth-El* also gave it to *Bætylus* or *Betulus* <note>A "Baetyl" is a sacred stone, often of meteoric origin, worshipped in the ancient Near East</note>.

Observe in what manner: The *Phoenicians* revered this stone, but also others, which they consecrated, made famous by the name *Bætyli*. Thus speaks *Sanchoniathon*, the interpreter of *Philo of Byblos*: *God Uranus devised the Baetylia, by contriving living stones* <note>original Greek: "Epenoeyse theos ouranos baitylia lithous empsuchous mechaneizamenos"</note>. Regarding this passage, one should consult *Bochart* in his *Sacred Geography, Book II, Ch. 2*, where those who transformed anointed stones into "living" stones are discussed. *Asclepiades*, near Heliopolis, a city in Syria, is said to have found *Baitoulia* or *Baitulous* while climbing the mountain, according to the testimony of *Photius* from *Damascius*. The same stone is said to have given its name to *Saturn* when it was consecrated in place of *Jupiter* in the writings of *Hesychius*. It is also called *Abdir*, *Abadir*, or *Abaddir*, from *Adir*, meaning *Glorious Father*, or *aben dir*, meaning *round stone*, because this was the shape of the *Betulus*.

Listen to *Pliny* in his *37th Book, 9th Chapter*, where he speaks of Thunderstones <term>Dondersteenen: prehistoric stone axes or meteorites once believed to fall from the sky during lightning</term>: *Sotacus identifies two other kinds of Thunderstones, black and red, and states they look like axes. By those which are black and red, cities and fleets are conquered, and these are called Betuli, though those that are long are called Ceraunians.* The *Bætylus* of the ancients is therefore the *Ceraunian* Thunderstone of the moderns. They are of one shape, either round and black, often pierced through; such stones are very frequently found near burial urns in the graves of the ancient Germans, primarily in the North, and in the judgment of the most experienced writers, they were used to slaughter sacrificial animals. See more on this in *Büttner’s Diluvian Remains, p. 92; New Baltic Literature 1699, p. 96; 1700, p. 341. 21. 23; Wolfart’s Natural History of Hesse, 46. Plates XXII and XXIII; Dan. Major’s Populating of the Cimbri, ch. 39; Arnkiel’s Cimbrian Antiquities, Book II, p. 166.*

What if these Stones, the shapes of which are represented in the present Plate, were placed in graves so that the deceased might rest all the more comfortably, just as the Patriarch lay resting upon his Stone? This conjecture, which I do not wish to force upon anyone, cannot be further explored due to lack of time. I could also add the shape of the stones, often hollow, like a pillow where a head has rested.

### ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXVIII.

*And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found Dudaim in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah: then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's Dudaim.* Genesis 30:14.

> *O DUDAIM, O beautiful fruit!*
> *How could you so please Rachel’s eye,*
> *That she came to beg you from Leah,*
> *While she sighed for you inwardly?*
>
> *What scent, what color, what taste, what power*
> *Are truly contained within your form?*
> *Can you increase the passion of love?*
> *Or is this a false claim brought forward?*
>
> *Who can show me the right path here,*
> *As to what fruit or flower this might be?*
> *I hold my peace, for there is much to fear,*
> *Since everything remains in doubt.*

In treating the *Dudaim* <note>A transliteration of the Hebrew word דּוּדָאִים (dûdā’îm), traditionally identified as Mandrakes</note>, I can promise hardly any other satisfaction than that which depends on the enumeration of various sentiments, or rather opinions, and the viewing of the illustrations. Nevertheless, the study of herbs <term>Kruydkwekery: Botany or the cultivation of medicinal plants</term> must be undertaken, the fields and forests walked through, and the gardens and meadows inspected, to see if perhaps the fruits, so long and anxiously sought, might be found along the way. Regarding the *Dudaim* of Reuben, many have occupied themselves with entire treatises or tracts: Heidegger’s *Dissertation on Reuben's Dudaim*, which is the 19th of the 2nd Volume of the *History of the Patriarchs*; Drusius *on the Mandrake*; Anton Deusing’s *Treatise on the Mandrake: and primarily on Mandrake Apples generally taken for Dudaim*; Jakob Thomasius’s *Treatise on the Mandrake*; Christiaan Ravius, Professor at Uppsala, *Treatise on the Dudaim*; Michael Liebentanz’s *Treatise on the Dudaim: Rachel’s Delicacies*. I omit other interpreters, literary scholars, and philologists. However, the freedom that others have taken in choosing an interpretation, I shall also take for myself.

Our Latin translation has *Mandrake* [Mandragora] instead of *Dudaim*, and rightly so, if the matter must be decided by a majority of votes. For we have supporting us the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>, the *Targum of Onkelos* <note>An ancient Aramaic paraphrase of the Torah</note> which uses the word *Yabrochin*, as well as Josephus, Aquila the Syrian, the Arabian, most Jews, Fuller, Drusius, and others. Nor are we devoid of weighty evidence. Let us examine them, with a judgment added to each, though modestly. The Ancients describe the Mandrake as suitable for love potions. For this reason it is called *dircaea* and *circaea* <note>Refers to the sorceress Circe, implying magical or aphrodisiac qualities</note>, "since the root is thought to be effective in making love charms." <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ δοκεῖ ἡ ῥίζα φίλτρων εἶναι ποιητική," Dioscorides, Book IV, c. 76</note>. The word *Dudaim* itself is derived by lexicographers from *Dod*, meaning "beloved" or "friend." It is for this reason they say that Rachel very greedily desired the Mandrakes, and Leah granted them only with great difficulty, so that each might draw the love of their husband to herself. These same authors also mention the sleep-inducing power of the Mandrake, and for that reason it is pleasing to Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love</note>. They even claim that it is beneficial for promoting conception, which is perhaps why Venus is called *Mandragoritis* by Hesychius. That the shepherds—such as Jacob was with his pastoral household—used a white variety of Mandrake is testified by Dioscorides: "By the eating of them they are satisfied." Finally, they argue that Reuben's apples, by sight alone, appealed to Leah and Rachel because they were lovely, fragrant, beautiful, and of a golden color: "saffron-like in color, fragrant with a certain heavy scent." <note>original: "κροκίζοντα τῇ χροιᾷ, εὐώδη μετὰ βάρους τινός"</note>. However, few among the moderns subscribe to this view. Indeed, these aforementioned very ancient interpreters are not even certain of themselves. The Hellenists on Jeremiah 24:1, 2...

<header>SPIRITUAL NATURAL HISTORY</header>

<columns>
1, 2. Some interpret *Doudai* <note>original: "Doudai," a variation of Dudaim</note> not as *Mandragora* (Mandrake), but as *Calatbos* or *Camistra*, and the *Targum* <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> on *Song of Solomon 7:13* translates it as *balsamon*, or balsam. This at least suggests that the *Dudaim* spread a very pleasant scent, rather than the sleep-inducing, heavy, or oppressive odor that *Pliny* <note>A Roman author and natural philosopher</note> ascribes to the *Mandragora* in *Book XXV, Chapter 13*. Whether the Mandrake truly possesses love-inducing powers, or whether love potions are actually effective in the way commonly claimed, is very doubtful. It is even more doubtful that this was the intent of those godly women—that they hoped to stir affection or aid conception through the use of love potions. The very best and most natural "love potion" was *Rachel’s* own exceptional beauty. And what purpose would a love potion have served? That her husband should be bound as if by a spell, running like a madman to his wife’s embrace? He certainly had no need of such a remedy, but rather one that might cure infertility; yet such remedies are of a nature that they often hinder immoderate *Venus* <note>original: "Venus omhelzingen," a classical euphemism for sexual intercourse</note> rather than encourage them. Indeed, that Rachel was not driven by lust is evident from the fact that she traded her husband’s company for the *Dudaim*, granting that right to her sister. Finally, it is difficult to determine anything certain regarding the fertility-inducing power of the *Mandragora*, or Mandrake, or of *Opium* and other sleep-inducing substances; one might just as easily conclude they have the opposite effect. Furthermore, the loveliness or fine appearance of the Mandrake is no greater than that of other flowers or fruits, many of which are even destructive. I would have skipped over the Jewish fable found in *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a prominent medieval Spanish-Jewish scholar</note> on *Numbers 11:2* regarding the human figure on Reuben’s banner, and likewise the idea of the Mandrake having a human shape—already known in antiquity to *Pythagoras* and the ancient Romans—were it not for the fact that this fable has passed from the Jews, Arabs, and Persians to Christians. Indeed, the superstitious tell wonderful things about the power of this root to bring luck, banish infertility, and discover hidden treasures, especially if buried in a particular way under a gallows. Such tales were told long ago by *Josephus* in *The Jewish War, Book VII, Chapter 25*, and *Pliny, Book XXV, Chapter 13*; these stories are more worthy of mockery than serious refutation. Meanwhile, Figure I displays the *Mandragora*.

*Franc. Georgius*, a Venetian Friar Minor, translates *Dudaim* as white lilies. The bulb of a lily, resembling a breast <note>original: "mamme"</note>, supports this view. So too does the month of May, during which the wheat harvest took place among the Jews; the pleasant scent praised in *Song of Solomon 7:13*; and finally, the supposed fertility-inducing power. However, all these points are speculative and could apply to other plants as well. See Figure II.

*Jarchi* <note>Rashi, the medieval French rabbi and commentator</note> considers this plant to be a violet, called *figle*, or *Jesmin* (Jasmine) by the Arabs. *Mattheus Silvaticus* translates it as *leukoion* <note>original: "leukoion," Greek for a white violet or wallflower</note>, a white violet. These and other Jewish scholars were swayed to this opinion by the beauty and pleasant scent of the flower, which is why *Theophrastus* (quoted by *Athenaeus* in *The Deipnosophists, Book LXV*) counts it among the most important *stephanomatikois* <note>original: "stephanomatikois," Greek for plants used to weave crowns or wreaths</note>. But anyone can see how uncertain these claims are. See Figure III.

There are those who, led by taste rather than sight, prefer to search beneath the earth rather than gather from above it. These find underground "tree-fruits" called *Trufes* or *Truffles* by the French; we call them "earth-apples" <note>original: "Aardappelen," here referring to truffles or similar tubers, not the modern potato which was still relatively new or different in context</note>, a food served even on the most magnificent tables, having a pleasant taste, especially when prepared with a sauce. These scholars argue from our text and *Song of Solomon 7* that they are gathered in the field, that they have the shape of *dudim* (breasts)—being not only round but having nipple-like growths—and that they contain a spongy internal substance resembling a woman’s breast, and are also aphrodisiacs. This opinion is held by *Daniel Ludovici* and others in the *Breslau Collections*. See Figure IV.

<column-break/>

### ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXIX.

We return now to a beautiful sight, which most people find pleasing. *Deusing* proposes that the *Dudaim* is a type of melon or pumpkin, very common in Syria and Egypt, much like a *colocynth* <note>A bitter cucumber or desert gourd</note>, mixed red and yellow, with a pleasant taste. In support of this, he cites the Arabs, who translate *Dudaim* as *Luffahb*; with this word, they mean not only Mandrake-apples but also a type of pumpkin or melon, according to the testimony of *Ibn Beitare*. The Persians call the same fruit *Destanbouie*, which means "scent of the hand," because of the pleasant fragrance it leaves in the hand...

I would have skipped the fable of the Jews, which appears in *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar</note> regarding *Numbers 11:2*, concerning the figure of a human on *Reuben's Banner*, as well as the *Mandrake* having a human form—already known in ancient times to *Pythagoras* and the ancient Romans—were it not that this fable passed from the Jews, Arabs, and Persians to the Christians. Indeed, the superstitious tell wonderful things about the power of this root to bring luck, banish infertility, and discover hidden treasures by burying it in a special way under a gallows. Such things were previously told by *Josephus* in *The Jewish Wars*, *Book VII, Chapter 25*, and *Pliny*, *Book XXV, Chapter 13*, which are more worthy of laughter than a serious refutation. Meanwhile, Figure I displays the *Mandrake*.

*Dudaim* is translated as white Lilies by *Franciscus Georgius*, a Venetian <term>Friar Minor</term> <note>A member of the Franciscan religious order</note>. The bulb of a Lily, resembling a *mamme* <note>A breast</note>, supports this. The month of May, during which the wheat harvest took place among the Jews, the pleasant scent praised in *Song of Solomon 7:13*, and finally the fertility-inducing power [all point to this]. All these things, however, are speculative and common to other plants as well. See Fig. II.

*Jarchi* <note>The medieval commentator Rashi</note> considers this plant to be a violet, *sigle*, called *Jesmin* by the Arabs. *Mattheus Silvaticus* translates it as *leukoion*, a white violet. These and other Jews were persuaded to this view by the beauty of the flower and its pleasant scent, which is why *Theophrastus* (cited by *Athenaeus* in the *Deipnosophistae, Book LXV*) counts it among the primary <term>stephanomatikois</term> <note>Greek: plants used for weaving wreaths or crowns</note>. But anyone can see on what uncertain footing these things stand. See Fig. III.

There are those who, led by taste rather than sight, prefer to search under the earth rather than gather above it. These find underground tree-fruits, called *Trufes* or *Truffles* by the French; we say <term>Aardappelen</term> <note>Literally "earth-apples." In the 18th century, this often referred to truffles or similar tubers rather than the modern potato</note>, a food also placed on magnificent dinner tables, having a pleasant taste, especially if a prepared sauce is added. These scholars argue from our text and *Song of Solomon 7* that they are gathered in the field; that they have the shape of *dudim* (breasts), being not only round but also having nipple-like growths; and likewise possess an internal spongy substance resembling a woman's breast, and that they are also aphrodisiacs. This opinion is held by *Daniel Ludovici* and others in the *Breslau Collections*. See Figure IV.

<column-break/>

### ILLUSTRATION PLATE LXXXIX.

**W**e return to a beautiful sight, which pleases most. *Densing* proposes that the *Dudaim* is a type of melon or pumpkin, very common in Syria and Egypt, just like a *colocynth*, mixed red and yellow, and of a pleasant taste. In support, he cites the Arabs, who translate *Dudaim* as *Luffah*; with this word they mean, besides mandrake-apples, a type of pumpkin or melon, according to the testimony of *Ibn Baitar*. The Persians call the same fruit *Destanboue*, which means "scent of the hand," because of the pleasant fragrance it leaves in the hand...

### PLATES XC. XCI.

Christianus Ravius considers the *Dudaim* <note>Hebrew: דּוּדָאִים, usually translated as mandrakes, associated with fertility and love in the Bible</note> to be twigs specifically from Fig trees. He argues primarily with evidence gathered from etymology, placing the root of the word in many instances such as *Song of Solomon VII. 14* and *Jeremiah XXIV. 1, 2.*, through the comparison of these two passages, and the consensus of the Rabbis and the most prominent translations. The *Septuagint* <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> translators, in the book of *Jeremiah*, translated *doudae theenim* as *baskets of figs* <note>original Greek: "kalathous fukoon"</note>. The common translations and *Onkelos* <note>The famous Aramaic translation (Targum) of the Torah</note> agree on this. Our very famous *Heidegger* would rather understand them as branches of flowers, or lovely-smelling fruits, coming close to the translation of *Junius* and *Tremellius*, who interpret *Dudaim* as "lovely flowers." The VIIth and VIIIth Figures, in which you can see various opinions on the *Dudaim* tied into a small bouquet, perhaps bring these views into agreement.

That the *Dudaim*, whether they be fruits or flowers, must be sought in the East, no one will deny. There they might appear more quickly to an unlettered person traveling there than to the most learned philosopher who rarely sets foot outside his study, and never outside of Europe. Better service is rendered to us here by those who, applying themselves to the things found in Nature—especially plants—cross the seas, rather than the most learned interpreters who seek the *Dudaim* in our cattle pastures or fields. This path has been taken by the famous *Ludolf* in his *History of Ethiopia, Book I, ch. 9, Commentary p. 139.* He considers the fruit of an *Indian* Fig tree, called *Muz* or *Mauz* by the Arabs <note>The banana plant</note>, to be the most excellent. They are very numerous on the same stem, for 50 figs of the shape and size of a cucumber hang from one stalk, possessing a very pleasant smell and juice, which ripen in *June*. Such a place exists near *Damascus* in *Syria*, where the Prince *Radzivil* saw them: the time being that of the wheat harvest,

<column-break/>

which occurs there in the middle of *June*. Given the excellence and the rarity, the very outstanding fruit, smell, and taste: the tree itself—as we learn from the travel descriptions of *Rauwolf*—is 9 or 12 feet high. The leaves are a beautiful green, like a reed, so long and so wide that they equal the entire body of a man. You would sooner call it a herb than a shrub or tree. This plant is described by *Garcias ab Horto* in *Indian Plants, Book II, ch. 10*, *Leo Africanus, Book IX*, and *Pliny, Book XII, ch. 6*, where he speaks thus: "The other larger fig tree, more excellent in fruit and sweetness, upon which the *Indian* sages live; the leaf resembles the wings of birds, having a length of three cubits <note>original: "ellen"</note> and a width of two. The bark of the fruit (*Clusius* reads 'the stem') yields a wonderful sweetness of juice, such that one (namely a cluster) can satisfy four people. The name of the tree is *Pala*, the apple *Ariena*; it is very common in the region of *Sidrach*, the final boundary of *Alexander's* campaigns. There is yet another apple sweeter than this, similar in appearance, but harmful to the health of the bowels. *Alexander* had forbidden the touching of this apple by his entire army." Five types are mentioned by the *Nubian* geographer in *Climate I, Part 7.* Even more are described by the Honorable *Hendrik van Reede* in the *Hortus Malabaricus*. By *C. Bauhinus* this plant is named: "A low Palm tree with long and wide leaves, called *Musa* by many writers." *Ludolf* draws to his advantage the root-stem of the word *Dudaim* itself, taking it simply to mean "kinsmen" or "close blood-relatives" <note>original: "Neven"</note>, applying this etymology to the many fruits hanging from a single stalk. Regarding the fruits, he understands the passage in *Genesis*; regarding the flowers, the passage in the *Song of Solomon*. This opinion appealed to me above others, to which the LXXXIXth Plate belongs.
