# PRINT PLATE XCII.

> *I will pass through all your flock today, removing from there every speckled and spotted beast, and every brown beast among the lambs, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and such shall be my wages.*
> *So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come, when you shall come concerning my wages before your face: every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and brown among the lambs, that shall be counted stolen by me.* Genesis 30:32, 33.

->*After long service rendered with care and sweat,*<-
->*Jacob shall finally receive his wages from Laban.*<-
->*What servant has shown such patience as he,*<-
->*Or spent his time and diligence with such alertness?*<-

->*Consider, Laban, you gave him your daughters*<-
->*For fourteen years of service: Now the speckled cattle*<-
->*Must be the six-year wage for the help he gave you;*<-
->*Therefore, let your greedy nature by no means strive against this;*<-

->*A higher Supreme Power has prepared that wage for him,*<-
->*Before he would approach his father’s house or land again,*<-
->*The Divinity has promised to make Jacob great,*<-
->*Thus the will of the Supreme Majesty is fulfilled.*<-

This is an agreement between the best son-in-law and a greedy father-in-law, between Jacob and Laban, and one made under conditions whose outcome depends not on a fixed set wage, but on God's blessing.

Just as the entire composition of animals is the work of the Creator, so too is the form of the hair and its color. *We cannot make one hair white or black*, <note>original: "Wy konnen geen hair wit of zwart maken"</note> Matthew 5:36. The formation of hair is the same in humans and in animals: oblong, round, and hollow, through which a tiny vein descends, bringing the nourishing sap to the end; its use is the same. The hairs are also excretory tubes through which excess moisture evaporates: I shall remain silent on other uses, including those which come from the hair of beasts for the service of human society.

Here, both the irrational animals themselves and the colors with which they are "dyed" come into consideration. *Tson* <note>Hebrew: צֹאן (tson)</note> signifies small livestock and is common to both *sheep* and *goats*, Genesis 27:9. Likewise, *Seh* <note>Hebrew: שֶׂה (seh)</note> signifies a kid or a lamb. This is evident from verse 32, as well as from *Exodus* 12:5, *Numbers* 15:11, and *Deuteronomy* 14:4. Lexicographers and the Hebrews agree on this. Among

<column-break/>

the Arabs, *fat*—in the plural *fa, faün, fahet, sijah, siwah*—is a sheep. See Meninski's Lexicon <note>Franciszek Meninski (1623–1698) was a famous Orientalist and court interpreter</note> pages 2741, 2742. *Keseb* <note>Hebrew: כֶּשֶׂב (keseb)</note> instead of *Kebesch* is a lamb of middle age, between *thela*, a little lamb, and *ail*, a ram, from the first year to the third; *Guizoum* are goats.

From the genus, we descend to the species, or rather to the individuals—the varieties of small livestock in terms of colors. *Nakod* <note>Hebrew: נָקֹד (nakod), meaning speckled or spotted</note> is properly "spotted" <note>Greek: "stikton"</note>, and is not well rendered by the Septuagint <note>The Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> as "variegated" <note>Greek: "erhauton" (likely a typo for erythron/reddish) or "poikilon"</note>. Our Latin version has it better: *bestrewn with spots*. For *stiktia* are marked, spotted animals, or those varied with spots, as in *Electra* by Sophocles <note>An ancient Greek tragedian; the reference is to line 569</note>. The term *Achates* <term>Achates: Agate, a gemstone known for its multicolored bands and spots.</term> wonderfully illustrates the power of the word: "marked with bright spots and white, black, and green spots" <note>original Greek: "katastiktos spilaaessi purfaisin leukais te melanomenais chlueraeis"</note>, in *Orpheus Lapidarius* <note>A 4th-century Greek poem about the magical properties of stones</note> page 230, lines 10, 11. This is perhaps the *Panther-stone* of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History"</note> in his 37th Book, Chapter 11, and *Porphyrites* <term>Porphyrites: Porphyry, a hard igneous rock containing crystals of feldspar, often purple and white.</term>, which is red with intervening white spots, called *leucostrictos*. See *Pliny*, Book 36, Chapter 7. Jerome translates the word *nakod* as "varied"; *Jonathan, Onkelos*, and the *Samaritan* <note>Referring to the Targums (Aramaic translations) and the Samaritan Pentateuch</note> use *namood*, as if one were to say "leopard-like" <note>Greek: "pardaleion"</note>,

# NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.
## Ll 2

various and spotted. The *rhannoton* <note>original: "rhannoton"</note> of the Greek linguists means *sprinkled* or *strewn*; they add that this is through spots, or *from drops* <note>original: "apo toon ranidoon"</note>, meaning distinguished in the manner of drops. See Figure I.

It signifies, as we have just seen, *dotted*, *speckled*, or *small spots*; but *talu* <note>original: "talu"</note> means *large*, as if sewn on, for *tala* <note>original: "tala"</note> is properly the sewing together of many patches or colors. This is why our translation correctly uses *sprinkled*. Most among the Ancients understand this to mean white spots. Thus also Onkelos <note>A famous 1st-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note> has *rakoa*, and among the Turks *rak-a* is a sheep marked with white on its side. See Meninski’s Lexicon, 2348. The Septuagint uses *marked with white* <note>original: "dialenkos"</note>, notably through white spots. For *marked with white* is the same as *white-centered* <note>original: "mesoleukon"</note>, where the outer edges consist of various colors. Similarly, the purple outer robe of the Persian Kings was woven with white in the middle. See Quintus Curtius <note>A Roman historian known for his biography of Alexander the Great.</note>. A sheep is therefore *speckled* when it has broad white spots in the middle of a black or red fleece. See Figure II.

*Chum* <note>original: "Chum"</note> is dark brown. The Septuagint uses *dusky* <note>original: "phaios"</note> from *to be warm* <note>original: "chamam"</note>, to become warm, and likewise to make black. *Alchemy* <note>original: "Chymia"</note> stands for black, which is in the eye, or the pupil. See Plutarch in *On Isis and Osiris*. We translate it as yellow <note>The author notes a discrepancy in the Dutch translation of the time, which sometimes rendered these color terms inconsistently.</note>.

<column-break/>

*Thais* <note>original: "Thais" (Hebrew: *tayish*)</note> is not a ram, as Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated it in Proverbs 30:31, nor a Tabis-tree, but a male goat. The consensus of the commentators makes this certain: the Chaldean language, which uses *Thaseja*, and the Arabic, in which *Thais* signifies a male goat. See Meninski’s Lexicon, 1505. *Theis* in ancient Hebrew was *tujus*, *etias*, or *tijase*. Finally, see <unclear>other</unclear> passages of Scripture besides this one: Genesis 32:14, 2 Chronicles 17:11, and Ezekiel 27:21.

We translate עקודים <note>original: "akudim"</note> as *goats bound around*. *Akud* stems from the word *akand*, *to bind*, specifically a sheep for shearing or slaughter (Genesis 22; 2 Kings 10:12), because it was the custom to bind such livestock by the feet. See Rabbi Solomon <note>Referring to Rashi, the preeminent medieval Jewish commentator.</note>. *Akudim* means *differing in the place of binding*, that is, in the pasterns <note>original: "hamertjes"</note> of the front and back feet; this is how the Jews and others have it. Symmachus <note>An author of one of the Greek versions of the Old Testament.</note> calls it *white-footed* <note>original: "leukopodas"</note>. See Figure III.

There remains *Laban*, the *white color* (which Laban chose for himself) as more characteristic of wool, as is evident from Isaiah 1:18, Daniel 7:9, and Revelation 1:14; which is also why snow is compared to wool in Psalm 147:16: *He gives snow like wool.*

# SPIRITUAL PHILOSOPHY
<note>original: "GEESTELYKE," likely referring to Spiritual Philosophy or History.</note>

> *The Patriarch JACOB cuts the green HAZEL,*
> *CHESTNUT and POPLAR their sprouting branches*
> *From the high tree trunk, and peels them here and there,*
> *And throws them thus spotted into the livestock's water troughs,*
> *Whereby the Sheep then bears speckled Lambs,*
> *While the unspotted Livestock had to serve as LABAN'S portion.*
> *O wondrous invention! which has pleased the Deity,*
> *To cover JACOB with his favor and blessing,*
> *To show the greedy LABAN how His power*
> *Always blesses virtue, and despises treachery.*

Jacob plays here the role of both a very experienced Shepherd and a very close observer of his affairs. Helped by a completely singular, Divine blessing, having entered into his agreement with Laban, he tips the scales in his own favor through a very innocent and at the same time very ingenious trick of three kinds. Namely: to the Son-in-law was to be added all that was of various colors, and to the Father-in-law all that was of a single color.

Let us first see the trick which Jacob utilized. He took rods of green *Poplar* wood. The Greeks have "a green rod of storax" <note>original: "rhabdon styrakinen chloran"</note>. If this translation is exact, the *Storax* presents itself for our consideration, a tree very common in *Syria* according to *Pliny* <note>A Roman author and natural philosopher (23–79 AD).</note> Book XII, Chapter 25. See Figure A. Its resin or sap is usually brought to *Europe*, and is of three kinds: red, reddish-brown, and soft. Yet the *Storax* shall not detain us, because it pleases neither us nor others; for us, as we have seen, it is the *Poplar*, as it is for the common Latin Translator and *Onkelos* <note>A famous 1st-century translator of the Torah into Aramaic.</note>. The Syriac Translator has "white moist rods"; the Arabic "rods of moist Libanum." According to the power of the word, *libbena* <note>A Hebrew term related to whiteness.</note> signifies a tree with a white bark. Under this name, therefore, can be included not so much a specific kind of tree, but all trees with a white bark. If the outermost bark was white, the second layer, once the first was cut away, must be understood as green; if that was green, this was white. If you seek a white bark, the white Poplar tree (see Figure B) will satisfy you. Yet our translations do not seem to have meant this one; the Latin has simply a *Poplar*, and it does not specify whether it wants a white or black one. The Dutch <note>The author uses "Duytsche," which in this period could refer to either the Dutch or German vernacular translations.</note> seems to have intended *Willow* much sooner (see Figure C), which is a black *Poplar*; otherwise they would have put *Sarbachen* or *Aspen* (see Figure D).

The third rod which *Jacob* used was *Armon*, which we translate as *chestnuts*, Figure G. On what grounds, I do not know. The common translator prefers *Platanus*, a *Plane tree* <note>The original Dutch uses "Ahornboom," which usually means Maple, but here refers to the Plane tree mentioned in the Latin text</note>, Figure H. The Greek also has *Platanos*. *Onkelos* translates it as *Dulb*, a word found in *Stephanus* and in medical law-books. Our *Heidegger* also gives his consent to the Plane tree in the cited passage.

These things so far concerning the trees whose rods *Jacob* took and peeled, so that the whiteness would shine through, exposing what was white within the rods. This is something our shepherds often do when they have nothing to do, for a pastime; however, the Patriarch applied it to a certain end, for his own great use and profit. But this very ingenious shepherd does not peel off the entire bark, so that if it were completely peeled, the rods would appear entirely white; rather, either with a curling stripe (Figure I) or many parallel stripes (Figure K), he cuts into the bark. He removes the cut portions at intervals, so that bands were seen in turns, one white, the other green. In this, namely, consisted the first cleverness of *Jacob*: that a mixed color of white and green would make an impression on the sheep as they were becoming pregnant. *Verse 38.*
> “And he laid these rods, which he had peeled, in the gutters and in the watering troughs where the flock came to drink, over against the flock; and they conceived <note>literally: "became heated"</note> when they came to drink. *v. 39.* And the flock conceived before the rods, and the flock brought forth ring-streaked, speckled, and spotted lambs.”

The second skill of *Jacob* consists in this: that he, having now produced many spotted lambs, separated them from the

<column-break/>

other flock and gathered them together, always placing them before the eyes of *Laban’s* sheep, so that this sight would strike the eyes of the pregnant ewes and drive them to breed similar lambs. *Verse 40.* “Then *Jacob* separated the lambs, and he turned the faces of the flock toward the speckled and all the brown among *Laban’s* flock; and he set his own flock apart and did not put them with *Laban’s* flock.”

The third skill consists in this: that *Jacob* did not employ these artifices regarding all of *Laban's* lambs without distinction, but only regarding the healthiest and strongest, having reserved those that were lesser and not so strong for his father-in-law. *Verse 41.* “And it came to pass, whenever the stronger <note>literally: "early-born"</note> cattle did conceive, that *Jacob* laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods. *Verse 42.* But when the cattle were feeble <note>literally: "late-born"</note>, he put them not in: so the feebler were *Laban's*, and the stronger *Jacob's*.” Through the first two skills, *Jacob* looked to the quantity; through these last two, to the quality.

The difference in our translations will not detain us, while the Latin has *stronger sheep*, the marginal notes have *the first*, the High German has *the early-spring flock* <note>original: "Frühlinger Heerde"</note>, and we have the *early-born*. *Onkelos* has *the first* or *the firstborn*; the Arabic has *of the Spring*; *Aquila* uses *early-born* <note>original Greek: "proimous"</note>; *Symmachus* uses *firstborn* <note>original Greek: "protogonous"</note>. These are set against *hagataphim*, translated by us as *weak*, or in the margin as *late-born*; *Aquila* has *late-born* <note>original Greek: "opsimous"</note>; *Symmachus* has *second-born* <note>original Greek: "deuterogonoi"</note>. The reconciliation of these terms is not difficult. There are sheep, especially in Eastern regions now and then, that give birth twice a year—according to *Homer’s Odyssey, Book 8*, though with a poet's license, three times. The first gestation period must, according to the Jews, be brought to the month of *Nisan*, which corresponds with *March*; the other to the month of *Tishri*, which almost corresponds with *September*, and none is better to be placed above these. However, *Pliny* in his *Book VIII, chapter 47* and *Columella* in *Book VIII, chapter 3* testify to the contrary. Indeed, we have others more in agreement with us, who understand the breeding of sheep, and reason supports this. For in winter, bodies are more constrained by the cold and as if bound, and for this reason they are of a more tightly bound composition, which is why the pregnancies of the earlier sort are called <term>קשורים</term> <note>Hebrew: Keshuirim; meaning bound or tied together, interpreted here as "strong" or "sturdy"</note>, as much as to say bound or fastened. Yet it seems to me that better attention should be paid to the distinction of the spring-born lambs among the—

Certainly in Saxony, where countless herds are found, those offspring of the sheep cast around Easter are less valued, because when brought into the pastures they do not grow strong due to constant insect stings. For this reason, they are usually slaughtered for the table rather than kept for milking; indeed, they cost barely half as much as the first-born. For this reason, *Jacob* took the strong ewes, so that strong lambs would be cast from them, while the tender ones were saved for his father-in-law.

There remains a primary question for investigation: whether the artifice which the Patriarch employed to increase the flock was wrought by the forces of nature, or if it surpassed them? The Greek Church Fathers take refuge in a miracle. *Chrysostom, Homily 57 on Genesis*, to whom this effect seems miraculous and exceeding natural consequences. *Cyril, Glaphyra on Genesis, Book V, p. 547:* <note>original Greek: "Arrhyton kai tais hymeterais eunoias astibes"</note> "Inexpressible and untrodden by our thoughts." We also agree with the latter. History does not lack examples that clarify the present matter—Natural history, Medical history, and indeed daily experience with so many monstrosities and defects. The narrowness of the space does not allow for transcribing testimonies from the families of men and the ranks of beasts. In the public writings of *Breslau* <note>Referring to the first medical journal, the Miscellanea Curiosa</note>, compiled by the famous *Kanolaus* page 326, a monstrous goat is mentioned, which, being born

That is: "Then he who breeds tame birds subtly concealed his intention: namely, that he places many purple garments close to the females, and they, having their wandering eyes fixed upon them and being rejoiced in spirit, bring forth purple-colored chicks."

But what does the Philosopher say to all these things? What are the natural causes of this wonderful phantom-effect? Is it the sight, bringing the image of the painted thing to Nature, according to *Galen*? Or a certain collection of images and a mental painting of likenesses, according to *Heliodorus*? Or a strong imagination impressing the form of a thing upon the spirits, and impressing that same form into the blood? All these things are too clumsy. It is difficult to conceive, indeed impossible: the transfer of Likenesses, Images, Little Figures, and Paintings from the object to the imagination, and from there to the fetus. Many of the moderns also have much to say about the imagination of Men and Beasts, but few things for the Learned. Often we cast mists over our eyes and minds, and we give occasion for a thousand doubts. For what, I ask you, is the imagination of Beasts? Is it a Body, or a Spirit? In what way does the idea of a perceived thing pass from the brain to the womb, and from there to the fetus? Surely through the nerves, which are merely bundles from the medullary brain. In what way is this Painting performed? Where are the Brushes? Where are the paints? Where is the hand guiding the Brush dipped in the paints? In what way shall a body, perhaps formed in the tiny egg itself long ago—yes, perhaps in the first creation—become deformed? I confess that I, as in many other matters, so also in this, am ignorant among the most ignorant. Here is an uncultivated Field, an unknown Land, into which observations have indeed penetrated, but almost no conclusive reasonings. In the very harbor, the Formative

I leave it to the Theologians and those experienced in the Law to judge this question: whether *Jacob* was permitted to deprive his father-in-law and Uncle of his livestock—that is, the greatest part of his possessions—by employing such artifice. Arguments against *Jacob* seem to be the true sense of the contract: that while the sheep of various colors were to be credited to him, *Laban* intended this to happen by chance, not by a trick. Other arguments include: a lack of sincerity, the suspicion of ambiguity, the use of deception, and the Law of God itself, which dictates that he should not have repaid the evil done to him by his father-in-law with evil, but should have overcome evil with good (**Romans 12:21**), waiting for God to be his avenger and defender. Pleading for *Jacob* is his steadfast faithfulness toward *Laban* in the midst of so many wrongs inflicted upon him; but primarily the will of God, who rightfully transferred a portion of the goods—which *Laban* had obtained through the labor and sweat of his son-in-law—over to *Jacob*.

# SPIRITUAL [NATURE]

Through wonderful little tricks, shepherds nowadays deceive their masters, so that it is a great art to protect oneself against their impositions; yet in this place, *Jacob*—the best and most meticulous caretaker of the goods of his father-in-law *Laban*—portrays him as shameful, greedy, and perverse. *That which had been torn by wild beasts, or stolen away, the shepherd gave back: this the very greedy Laban demanded from Jacob’s hand*, and most unlawfully so, because such things were taken despite the shepherd's efforts and his vigilance against them as much as he was able. We have an express Law in **Exodus 22:10, 11**: <note>This law establishes the liability of a bailee (someone entrusted with property).</note> "If a man delivers unto his neighbor a donkey, or an ox, or a sheep, or any beast to keep; and it dies, or is hurt, or driven away, while no man is seeing it: *v. 11.* Then shall an oath of the LORD be between them both, whether he has not put his hand unto his neighbor's goods; and the owner of it shall accept thereof, and he shall not make it good." And in *verse 13*: "If it be torn in pieces, then let him bring it for witness, and he shall not make good that which was torn." Nature itself teaches this Law, because all guilt in such a case, and all deceit on the part of the shepherd, is absent. The crime of *Laban* is all the greater because he demanded the return of torn or stolen sheep without distinction, even if the misfortune occurred at night. For in the writings of the <term>Talmudists<note>Jewish scholars and commentators on the Torah/Talmud.</note></term>, exceptions are made regarding the cited Law. If, for example, there was only a single wolf; if the shepherd himself drove the cattle into a place made unsafe by wild beasts or highwaymen; if he neglected to call the neighbors for help: all of which excuses, even if they were lawful, could not have harmed *Jacob*, who without doubt performed his entire office very industriously, providing himself with weapons necessary to ward off wild animals and thieves, and guarding the flock with strong dogs—all marks of a good shepherd. See *The Honest Shepherd, chapter 8*.

What, I ask you, could *Laban* demand more of *Jacob* than what he testifies further of himself? *v. 40. In the day the heat consumed me, and the frost by night.* In the Greek translation, the word *sunkaionenos* <note>original: *συγκαιόμενος*</note> appears, meaning *robbed* or *scorched*, which pertains both to the night frost and to the day heat. Thus is *funkaufei* used of the Moon 

<column-break/>

and of the Sun in **Psalm 121:6**. From both these places, someone might easily conclude that the Moon warms, even burns (*sunkaiein*), just as well as the Sun. <term>Suidas<note>Referring to the Suda, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopedia.</note></term> on the word *selene* (Moon): *Phasi tyn feleyneyn my monon hugran etene. Nai alla kai thermanein homoioos to hylio.* That is: *They say that the Moon is not only moist, but also warms just like the Sun.* Yet modern Philosophy knows nothing of this warming power of the Moon, even though the rays of this "Guardian of ours" are brought to a point through the largest burning glasses. Therefore, one must assign another explanation to these passages; and in the *Psalm* one must fill in *frost for night*. Indeed, even without this addition, it can be understood that the *heat by day consumed Jacob, and the frost by night*. He suffered the burning by day, properly so called, from the burning rays of the Sun piercing his body, dispersing the fluids, and agitating the entire blood; by night, he suffered a "burning" by accident, the sweat pores of the skin being closed up, whereby the blood was again agitated by uneven and often feverish movements, increased by the motion of the internal organs, the circulatory motion having been hindered. Who is there that does not know that when the degree of cold increases and the circulation is prevented by extremes, the limbs are indeed "burned" (*funkaieflai*) and attacked by gangrene, and that in a lesser degree a burning pain is felt in the tips of the fingers? Our shepherds must have frequently felt something of this sort, staying overnight in the field, as was the custom, the sheep being enclosed within wicker hurdles so that they would not wander hither and thither by night. Regarding this matter, one finds a passage from *Nicander* <note>Nicander of Colophon, a Greek poet and physician from the 2nd century BCE.</note> in *Theriaca, v. 403*:

> — When around the tall fir trees
> The shepherds, who dwell in the fields, catch the cold,
> Having ceased from the work of tending the cattle.

What wonder is it, finally, that *Jacob* suffered hardships from the night watches? *Sleep*, he says, *departed from my eyes.* Thus the spirits, which usually descend to the center, were scattered by the waking, and the most vigilant shepherd was consumed, unless Divine and most excellent providence had preserved him.

This is a gift which *Jacob* offers to his brother *Esau* from the goods he had acquired, intending to reconcile the anger previously felt: in this regard, note the proportion of goats and sheep to the bucks and rams is ten to one, a ratio which *Varro* <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a Roman scholar and writer known for his works on agriculture.</note> also praises in *On Agriculture, Book II, Chapter 3.*
<margin>“Regarding the males and females, there is nearly the same distinction, so that some pair one buck to every ten goats, as I do. For the cows to the bull, it is fourfold.”</margin>
*Par* <note>Hebrew: פַּר</note> among the Hebrews is an *Ox*, and *Parah* <note>Hebrew: פָּרָה</note> is a *Cow*. The dictionary writers explain the word as a *young ox* and a *young cow*; *Maimonides* <note>A highly influential medieval Sephardic Jewish philosopher and Torah scholar.</note> calls it a *two-year-old ox*. That *Par* is certainly more than a calf is evident from *Psalm 69:31*, where it is called a horned bullock, and *Parah* is already fertile by giving birth. *Job 21:10*: *Their cow calves, etc. Their calves are already nursing.* Yet that the animal is younger is evident because *Par*, in at least thirty places in Holy Scripture, is called *Ben Bakar*, meaning *Son of the Herd* <note>original: "Ben Bakar"</note>, and *Parah* in *Numbers 19:2* is *A perfect heifer, upon which no yoke has come.* Therefore, the Jewish Masters conclude that *Par*, an *ox*, and *Parah*, a *cow*, are named such around their second or third year. The origin of the word must be sought in the Arabic language, in which *firar, furar, ferir, ferur, furarur, furfur* signifies the young of a sheep, of a goat, and of a wild cow. *See Meninski Lexicon, pages 3482, 3503.* *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a French Protestant biblical scholar who wrote a famous natural history of the Bible.</note> in *Hierozoicon, Part I, Book II, Chapter 27* has *phurar, phurar, pharir, phuraphir, purphur, phurphur*, from *pharra*, meaning he has bared the teeth of the young beast or livestock to see how old it was. For this reason, it is probable that a calf is called *Par* when it sheds its first teeth so that others may come in their place. A two-year-old changes its teeth, according to *Aristotle's History of Animals, Book VI, Chapter 21.* From the Hebrew or Arabic word comes the word *Farren* <note>Young bulls or bullocks</note> used by the Germans.

*Athon* <note>Hebrew: אָתוֹן</note>, a female donkey, from *Ethan*, meaning strength, because she is more capable of carrying a load

[...can] carry more than any animal of the same weight. This is why *Jacob* says in *Gen. 49:14: Issachar is a strong-boned donkey, lying down between the packs.* Among the Arabs, a wild donkey and a she-donkey are called *Etan* and *Etanet* <note>original: "Etan, Etanet"</note>. In the irregular plural, it is *Meetuna*. *Atun* is the plural of *Etan*. *See Meninski's Lexicon, pages 5659, 5661.* <note>Franciscus a Mesgnien Meninski (1623–1698) was a famous linguist whose "Thesaurus" was the standard dictionary for Oriental languages in Europe.</note>

*Ghair* <note>original: "Ghair"</note>, in Chaldean *Ghail*, refers to a small donkey, or as *Lalisius* <note>Likely referring to a classical or Renaissance-era philologist.</note> says, a young donkey: with this, the Arabic names *air* agree, which in the feminine is *airet*, and in the plural *a-jar, u-juret, yarat, me-jura*, by which both a tame and a wild donkey are signified, as well as *ujeir, ayr*, and incorrectly *uweir*, meaning a "little donkey." *See Meninski's Lexicon, pages 3361, 3368.* From *Lalisius*, and perhaps even from *Guair*, comes our word *Lali* <note>A Dutch term for a simpleton or a clumsy person.</note>, by which we signify a dull, clumsy person who pays no attention to how things are done.

Nn 2

opposing, although he was the victor, he felt the strength of his adversary, so that he would receive the victory not through his own power, but from the conquered one himself. This one touched the socket of his hip, and the socket of Jacob's hip was wrenched while he wrestled with him.

The injured part *Caph* <note>original Hebrew: כַּף, meaning the hollow or palm</note> must be considered more closely, which word properly signifies the hollow or the palm of the hand, and the hollow of the foot. For this reason, our Translator renders it *the hollowness of the hip*. The German <note>referring to Luther's translation</note> expressed it as *the joint itself, das gelenke seiner huft* <note>original German: "the joint of his hip"</note>. But what is the hollowness of the hip? An expression, as far as I know, used by none of the Anatomists. One must look for some hollowness or curve, which the Greeks translate as *platos tou meyrou* <note>original Greek: πλάτος τοῦ μηροῦ, meaning the breadth or flat of the thigh</note>, and search for it either in the joint with the shinbone from behind—which would have caused the dislocation of the shinbone, not of the hip—or rather in the joint of the hip with the bone *Ischius* <note>the ischium, part of the pelvis</note>, where the hollowness is deep. It is called the little cup, *kotulei* <note>original Greek: κοτύλη - the acetabulum or hip socket</note> by the Greeks, into which the head of the thigh bone is fitted, primarily by means of a round ligament; when this is relaxed and the head or small cap slips out, a true dislocation occurs, as we call it. However, this requires a greater force than that which depends on a wrestling match, and indeed, by a mere touch, it cannot happen through the forces of nature. Therefore, the sense is that that strong Man, indeed that *El* <note>original Hebrew: אֵל - God or a powerful being</note>, exceedingly strong, the strongest of all, touched the hip or the thick part of Jacob's leg, strengthened by many ligaments and muscles and their tendons, and that through a truly Divine power, a loosening occurred in Jacob's thigh, and that it did not merely become weak—which the common Latin translation suggests, and the Greek expresses by the word *enarkeife* <note>original Greek: ἐνάρκησε - became numb or stiff</note>—but that such a relaxation occurred as one often encounters in exercise, whereby the loosened thigh leaps out of its socket, the ligament having been made loose, and can be restored again with little effort, though limping follows. Or perhaps Jacob was healed by the departing victor, yet the pain remained in the touched part, which caused the limping; how long this lasted, one does not know. For there is no evidence that he came to Esau limping.

Greater difficulties are posed to us by *gnid hannaze* <note>original Hebrew: גִּיד הַנָּשֶׁה - gid hanasheh</note>, *the benumbed nerve*, or according to others, *the displaced* or *the overstretched nerve*. To this day, it remains a memorial sign for the Jews (v. 32). According to the interpretation of the Arabic Translator, this nerve is the "female nerve"; some Jews also understand it as the *reproductive organ*, which *Aben Ezra* <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a 12th-century scholar</note> rightly mocks as being devoid of sense. Most Jews call it *the nerve of forgetfulness*, and describe it as follows:

As God inclines hearts, the deadly hatred of Esau against his brother *Jacob* is transformed into the most tender movements of love. In the same way, the *Kadmeian* brothers <note>likely a reference to the legendary brothers Eteocles and Polynices, though here used to illustrate brotherly reunion</note> met in former times, separated from each other by a long series of years; they throw themselves into each other’s embraces, they give mutual kisses, and they weep. The hearts are touched; tears are pressed from the eyes. The strings are plucked and moved in sweet-sounding harmonies. This is what daily experience teaches. Yet the reason for that phenomenon must be drawn from the description of the nerves, from the "sympathy" or connection of the facial nerves and the intercostal nerves, which simultaneously reach the heart. For the intercostal nerve consists of the distribution of the branches of the nerves of the fifth and sixth pairs; and the second branch of the fifth pair, called the *Oogmeester* <note>The Ophthalmic nerve, literally "Eye-master"</note>, is divided into four or five small shoots, which all pass above the muscles of the eye and, being passed to some extent through its glands, are almost all consumed in the eyelids. ->### SACRED HISTORY<-

"...when I traveled through Africa, they called a coin a *Kesitham* <note>original: *Kesitham*; a Hebrew unit of currency mentioned in Genesis 33:19</note>. What use comes from that? That the hundred *Kesithen* spoken of in the Law of Moses are explained as being one hundred *danakes* <note>original: *danakes*; a small silver Persian coin</note>. The first martyr, Stephen, provides the explanation for this in **Acts 7:16**: 'And they were carried over into Shechem, and laid, Jacob and the Patriarchs, in the sepulchre that Abraham had bought for a sum of money from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem.' From which it appears, at the very least, that the field was sold and bought for money, *argurio* <note>original: *argurio*; Greek for 'with silver' or 'by money'</note>, not obtained through bartering, which was in use in the earliest centuries. Abraham had—as we have seen in its proper place—bought the field of Ephron for 400 shekels, a contract also attributed to him in the cited passage from the Acts of the Apostles; yet in our text, it is attributed to Jacob. Why is that? Others may take that into consideration. Jacob had given his sons money to buy corn when they were about to depart for Egypt. *Arias Montanus*, *Masius*, *Serarius*, *Bonfrerius*, *Cajetanus*, and others, add to this the forms of the money or the penny, and of the sheep; they propose that the image of a sheep was imprinted on those pieces of money, just as the Romans formerly called money *pecunia* <note>Latin term for money</note>, from *pecus* <note>Latin term for cattle</note>, and marked it with the image of cattle, according to *Plutarch* in the *Life of Publicola*, and *Pliny* in Book XVIII, Chapter 3, who says: 'King Servius was the first to mark copper with the image of sheep and oxen.' and it is known from *Varro* and from *Gellius* in *Attic Nights 11* that in the most ancient times, money itself appeared under the title of 'sheep.' Thus the Peloponnesians struck a tortoise, *chelone* <note>original: *cheloneyn*</note>, on their coins, and the Athenians an ox on their didrachms <note>two-drachma coins</note>; or otherwise an owl. I pass over other examples in silence. Whatever the case may be, as it is indeed difficult to attribute coins stamped with the image of sheep to the Israelites, no modern writer is so arrogant as to wish to determine the exact value of the *Kesitha*.

Now, as for the deed performed in these regions; let us discuss for a little while the circumstances of the time in which this circumcision of the Shechemites was carried out, based on the mechanical principles of modern medicine. Experience teaches us that the pains arising from wounds become sharper on the third or fourth day. This observation could

<column-break/>

not have been unknown to Jacob's neighbors, whose foreign servants had to be circumcised and therefore suffered that sharpness of pain. The initial pain from the injury follows immediately upon the dissolution of the solids, the emptying and dissolution of the nervous fibers and blood vessels, which is instantly followed by an irregularity in the movement of the fluid parts—the blood and the fluid of the nerves <note>Refers to the 18th-century medical theory of "animal spirits" or nerve fluid</note>. For some of it flows out through the open mouths of the vessels, while some begins to coagulate at the lips of the wound; from this comes the swelling and the repulsion of the nerve fluid back toward the brain, where the Mind is presented with the form of tension—that is, Pain. Therefore, the more the fibers are stretched at the injured site, the more intense the pain is; and it is all the more intense if many nerves converge there, for then the many repelled 'spirits' <note>nerve impulses</note> retreat from the seat of the mind with even greater force—indeed, they pour upon it. They pour upon it, I say, because a new path must be opened for the blood and the spirits, which these fluid substances cannot find except through force. Now, the blood outside its vessels, which is sweet and soft at the beginning, gradually becomes sharp; the balsamic, more volatile particles fly away, leaving behind those that are more saline and earthy, which, through putrefaction on the third day, cause pus. This pus, by its sharpness, gnaws at, agitates, and stings the bare nervous fibers, consequently causing pain, and very sensitive pain at that. And these same sharp salt particles, mixed with the returning blood through the mouths of the veins, excite irregular, feverish, surging movements throughout the entire vital fluid, from which wounds cause fevers. From these principles, it is easy to judge why wounds lead to swelling, inflammation, redness, pain, fever, and even occasionally convulsions and delirium. It is for this reason that surgeons, who are experienced in their art, do not disturb the injured parts on the fourth or fifth day, but treat them gently. Behold here the Golden Rule of *Hippocrates* in his book *On Fractures*, section 33: 'For one must by no means move any wounds on the third or fourth day; and to say it in one concept, it is also useful during those days to avoid all use of probes and other things by which wounds are provoked.' The blossom consists of square thin stems, at certain intervals full of moss, composed of green points growing from the same spot, so that now and then they crown the little "tongue" <note>This likely refers to the bract or a specific part of the flowering structure.</note> from which they hang. Also, the beginnings of the acorns are perceived as the very smallest spheres, purple-colored and hairy. The acorns, sitting in their buds or cells, either hang very close to the branch or are suspended from it by long and thin stalks, usually an inch long, covered by a bark-like membrane, reddish or ash-gray, with a hard, bitter, and sour pit—much like the raw outer cap, which is smooth on the inside and much thicker than the aforementioned skin, barely containing a third of the acorn. At the top of the acorn, a short, dull point protrudes. This tree belongs to those flower-bearing plants where the blossoms are separate from the fruits, and the seeds have a covering as if made of leather. See the distinguishing marks clearly expressed in the margin, according to the opinion of *Tournefort*. <note>Joseph Pitton de Tournefort (1656–1708) was a foundational French botanist whose system was widely used before Linnaeus.</note>

Just as constant mention is made in the Holy Scripture of the Oak tree, so has its memory been held in honor among various peoples; its use was religious to the point of superstition, and further, it was subject to use, or rather, abuse. Occasions for this were provided by the firmness of its material, its strength (which is the very namesake of the Oak), <note>In many languages, the name for "Oak" shares a root with "strength"—for example, the Latin *robur* means both oak and strength.</note> its wide-spreading reach, and various matters conducted under this tree. Its strength perhaps relates to the opinion of the Ancients that it was the very first thing to spring from the Earth, just as the *Arcadians* <note>People from the central Peloponnese in Greece, often associated with ancient, rustic traditions.</note> were the first of men and, for that reason, were related to the Oak tree. From this it also came that *Socrates*, in contempt of the Gods of his time and people, swore by the Oak tree—namely, by a GOD, according to the explanation of *Tertullian*. <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD) was an early Christian author from Carthage. He argued that Socrates's famous oath "by the dog" or "by the oak" was a way of acknowledging a higher, singular Creator without naming Him directly.</note> Serving the Ruler of Heaven and Earth, older than the Oak tree itself, yet holding the GODS of the *Athenians* or of other Greeks to be younger than this tree; this "heresy" was the cause of both the hatred and the death penalty which this great man—worthy of a better fate and a happier age—brought upon himself. Its towering greatness was the reason why this tree was hallowed and dedicated to *Jupiter*, as it was given to men for their life’s sus-

<column-break/>

tenance, since they first ate acorns. *Ovid* says thus:

> And the open acorns which had fallen from Jupiter's tree. <note>original: "Et quae deciderant patula Jovis arbore glandes." from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*.</note>

So that there have been those who, by *dios balanon*, <note>Greek: Διὸς βάλανος — literally "Jupiter's Acorn."</note> understood not so much chestnuts as the acorns of Oak trees, as in the proverb, *polloon panegyreoon dios balanon ephagen*: *He has eaten Jupiter's acorns at many festivals*, <note>Greek: πολλῶν πανηγυρεῶν Διὸς βάλανον ἔφαγεν.</note> said of an old man made learned and experienced through the practice of many things. For this reason, the Oak tree was sacred, from which it was customary to give the Roman Civic Crown, as well as to the gods of the underworld and the Fates. <note>The *Corona Civica* was a chaplet of common oak leaves given to a Roman soldier who had saved the life of a fellow citizen in battle.</note> *Catullus* says:

Yet with our mournful Oak tree can very fittingly be compared that Oak near *Priene*, a city in *Ionia*, close to which a thousand *Samians* were defeated by the *Prienians* in a mutual struggle; and after seven years, the best and most prominent citizens [were lost] to the *Milesians*. From this arose the custom that the *Prienian* women, in matters of the greatest weight, testified by oath *by the darkness at the Oak*, because at that place they had lost their fathers, husbands, and sons. They used this proverb on the occasion of a very great and deadly calamity. *Plutarch* wrote this of the *Prienians* in *Greek Questions*: <note>original: "Σάμιοι καὶ πριηνεῖς πολεμοῦντες... παρὰ δρυὶ σκότος..." This passage describes the bloody history of the border wars between Samos and Priene.</note> The Samians and Prienians, being at war with each other, harmed one another in various moderate ways, but a great battle occurring, the Prienians killed a thousand Samians. In the seventh year afterward, fighting the Milesians at the place called the Oak, they lost the best and first of their citizens at once... for the women of Priene, the suffering then and the lamentable disaster became an oath concerning the greatest matters, "the darkness at the oak," because their children, fathers, and husbands were slaughtered there. Yet regarding these, writers have various opinions, as well as several motives for the reason of that theft. There are those among the Jews who hold that the Daughter secretly took the Idols from the Father so that he would not be able to consult these Idols, nor by looking into them come to know the way which her Husband *Jacob* had taken. Thus speaks *Rabbi Eliezer* in *Chapters [of Eliezer] chapter 36*, *Aben Ezra*, and *Albilda* in *The Continual Burnt Offering, page 99*, who are joined by *Tostatus* and *Bonfrerius*. However, *Flavius Josephus* in *Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, Chapter 19* suggests it was so that she could take refuge in the Idols against her Father's wrath. Others, such as *Chrysostom* in *Homily 57 on Genesis*, *Pererius*, and *Osiander*, suggest she took them to serve them herself, or that she took them as a reward for her Husband and as a dowry for herself and her sister—whether these Idolatrous figurines were made of gold or silver. Regarding the material, the shape, and the use of these Idols, various Interpreters again differ wonderfully. *Rabbi Eliezer* in the place cited, and with him other forgers of "old wives' fables," claim that it was the head of a slaughtered firstborn male, soaked in salt and oil, under whose tongue they placed a gold plate with the name of an unclean Spirit written upon it; they would then fall down to the earth before this head, and the image would speak with them. Most Rabbis, alienated from such godlessness on the part of *Laban*, say they were certain instruments made by specific art according to the positions of the Stars, through which, by speaking, they could come to know future things. Others from the number of the Circumcised Teachers <note>A reference to Jewish scholars.</note>, namely *Rabbi Moses Nachmanides*, say they were Clocks or Star-height meters, *Astrolabes*. *Pfeiffer* believes they were Idols, specifically Household Gods, as appears from the history of *Michal* in *1 Samuel 19:13*, varying in material—silver, copper, wood—and that the Devil answered through the *Teraphim*. *Spencer* in his *Book on the Laws of the Hebrews* derives the origin from the *Egyptians*: that GOD, in place of the *Teraphim* of the *Egyptians*, actually gave the *Urim* <note>Part of the High Priest's breastplate used for determining God's will.</note> to the *Israelites*, having the same service and form, namely small figurines as Oracles, so that He might serve the stubborn people. This opinion, which is harsh in truth, is extensively refuted by *Hermann Witsius* in *Egyptiaca*, showing that the *Teraphim* were Household Gods whose use displeased GOD—instruments of superstition that served for Divination, Idolatry, and Sorcery; that speech was provided to them through magical conjurings; and that GOD had granted an entirely different instrument for an Oracle, distinct from the *Teraphim*. This is one of the most difficult passages from Holy Scripture, whose clarification is sooner to be expected from general Scholars than from diligent Researchers of Nature. For the whole question here comes down to what must be understood by *Jemim*, which word we have translated as *Mules*, and with us *Jonathan* <note>Referring to the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, an Aramaic translation/paraphrase of the Torah.</note> in the Commentary *Bereshith Rabbah* <note>A midrashic collection on Genesis.</note> the 82nd *Section*, and so many Translations and Interpreters, that the number would defend it, like armies joined by their shields.

Yet the most powerful arguments fight for the contrary. 1. A Mule is called *Pered* by the Hebrews. Also, you shall find among no Eastern Peoples that anyone called this kind of Beast *Jemim*. 2. He who had devised the way to breed Mules would not be said by *Moses* to have found them. *Maza* <note>Hebrew *matza* (מצא), meaning to find or encounter.</note> signifies in Holy Scripture the finding of a thing which already exists. Although the Greeks’ *exeuriskein* <note>Greek: ἐξευρίσκειν, to find out or invent.</note> and the Latins’ *invenire* <note>Latin: to come upon or find.</note> are taken for diligently thinking something up. # NATURAL HISTORY.

...and a female donkey, or the mating of a wild donkey with a mare or female donkey. Yet here no mention is made of horses. 3. We do not read that the Jews used mules before the time of *David*, who lived about 700 years after *Anah* <note>Anah is a figure in Genesis, the son of Zibeon</note>. Before those times, mules are nowhere listed among the livestock of the Patriarchs and the nations. See <margin>Bochart, *Hierozoïcon*, Part 1, Book 1, Chapter 21.</margin>

For this reason, others translate *Jemim* <note>The Hebrew word *Yemim* in Genesis 36:24</note> as *pools, springs, seas, or warm waters*. See *Jerome*. The common translation <note>The Latin Vulgate</note> has *warm waters*. The Syriac has *waters in the desert*. *Diodorus of Tarsus* says *a spring in the desert* <note>original Greek: *pēgēn erēmō*</note>. Against this view is the fact that *Jemim* is indeed written with the same letters as *Jammim* (*Seas*), but with very different vowel markings. 2. *Jammim* is not used by the Hebrews to describe all gatherings of water, but specifically *Seas* or large lakes that are open to everyone. 3. Waters are called *Mayim* by the Jews, not *Jemim*.

Given such great difficulty in interpretation, the Septuagint <note>The early Greek translation of the Old Testament</note>—as well as the later Greek translators *Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion*—preferred to keep the original *Jemim*, transliterating it as *Iamein*. This leads us to another and perhaps the very best guess. *Onkelos*, in the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> translation, has <term>Gabbaraia<gloss>Giants</gloss></term>; the Samaritan version has *Emaen*, who were those same tall people as the *Anakim*; the giants were considered the same as the *Anakim* in *Deuteronomy* 2:10, 11—the *Enakim* is written there. To these translators, *Jemim* are the same as the *Emim* <note>A race of giants known as the "Terrible Ones"</note>.

This meaning is clear: that *Anah*, the son of *Zibeon* and father-in-law of *Esau*, "found" the *Emim* <note>the giants</note> in the desert. In the Hebrew style of speaking, to have "found" enemies refers to someone who unexpectedly falls upon or encounters them. We have examples of such a finding or encounter in *Judges* 1:5, 1 *Samuel* 31:3, 1 *Kings* 13:24, and elsewhere.

<column-break/>

It adds weight to this interpretation that the *Horites*, over whom *Zibeon* (the father of *Anah*) ruled, were neighbors of the *Emim*. Now, the *Emim* possessed *Ar* and the field of *Kiriathaim*, and the *Horites* held Mount *Seir*, until the former were driven out by the *Moabites* and the latter by the *Edomites*. This is why the region of the *Emim* is called the land of *Moab*, and that of the *Horites* is called *Idumea*. This proximity is confirmed by what we read in *Genesis* 14:5, 6 and *Deuteronomy* 2:9, 12. This view is favored by *Bochart* and *Heidegger* in his *Dissertations on Esau*, Thesis 17.

Therefore, the discovery of mules, which has until now been attributed to *Anah*, is very uncertain. The father-in-law of *Esau* loses the honor of the invention. If we listen to the oldest of poets, *Homer*, in the *Iliad*, Book 2, line 852, then the *Heneti* people are the inventors of mules.

> *From the Heneti, where the race of wild mules is found.* <note>Original Greek: *Ex enetōn, hothen hēmeionōn genos agrotēraōn*</note>

->The breed of wild mules comes from the city of Henetum.<-

However, the honor of the invention would return to our same *Anah* if—as *Louis de Dieu* <note>A 17th-century Dutch orientalist</note> believes—the *Henetians* are descended from the same *Enan* mentioned by the Septuagint. They were a people neighboring the *Paphlagonians, Cappadocians,* and *Galatians*, from whom other Greeks like *Theophrastus, Strabo,* and *Plutarch* claim they first originated. If we give credit to the Arabs, *Karun* (who seems to have been *Korah*) was the first of all who had a donkey cover a mare, or a horse cover a female donkey. For further study on this text, see *Fortunatus Scacchus*, *Myrothecium*, Volume 3, Chapter 25, where he defends the common Latin translation and the "gathering of waters" at length.

<summary>This page explores the biblical mystery of what Anah "found" in the wilderness, debating whether the Hebrew word "Jemim" refers to the invention of mule-breeding, the discovery of hot springs, or a surprise encounter with a tribe of giants (the Emim).</summary>
